**Learned 2026-09-03** putting 88 vFlat iPhone scans of the Myszka football book into page
order. Cost several wasted OCR-tuning passes before the right method surfaced.

## Do not trust OCR for the page number

Three tuning attempts; **one made it worse** (80 of 88 unread). Two failure modes:

- A bottom-strip crop catches **body text and citation years**. Taking the longest digit
  token then picks a 4-digit year over a 2-digit folio.
- Tesseract **confuses 5 with 9**. It read page **50 as 90 with 8/8 unanimous votes** — a
  confident wrong answer, which is worse than an unread one. Vote counts do not rescue this.

## What actually works — read a contact sheet

1. Crop a tight band around the **centred** folio: `x 0.36–0.64`, `y 0.900–0.952` of the
   page image. Autocontrast, grayscale.
2. Tile ~44 of them into one PNG with the capture index labelled beside each.
3. **Look at it.** Two sheets covered 88 pages, unambiguously, in two passes.

Folios are large, bold and isolated — trivial to read by eye, and the thing OCR keeps
getting wrong. Do not keep tuning tesseract; switch methods after the second failure.

## Ordering traps

- **Sort by mtime, never by filename.** macOS appends ` (1)` on download collisions, and
  `…17-35-17 (1).jpg` sorts *before* `…17-35-17.jpg` while the timestamps say the reverse.
- **Same-second captures land out of page order.** Two pairs were swapped this way.
- A page shot out of sequence (67 before 66) looks exactly like a **missing page** if your
  sample happens to skip the tile it is on. Verify a "gap" before believing it.

## Other findings

- **A zero-word OCR page may just be blank.** One page returned no text and was genuinely
  blank in the book — but still carried a printed folio.
- **Bad pages cluster in time**, not randomly: all 7 poor scans fell inside one two-minute
  window. Re-shoot the window, not the whole book.
- **The scan folder is live** while the human is still working. Any script must re-verify
  its map rather than assert on a file count — a new shot broke an `assert` mid-analysis.
- Rename via a **temp prefix in two passes** so no collision is possible, and always write
  an old→new manifest so the rename is reversible.

## Quality bar that worked

vFlat Scan on iPhone, ~2000×3200 px (~360 DPI) — above the 300 DPI OCR target. Median
tesseract confidence **95.0**. Turn the app's OCR off, or just use
`ocrmypdf --force-ocr`, which discards any text layer the app added and makes the setting
irrelevant.

Pipeline: `img2pdf` (page order) → `ocrmypdf --force-ocr --rotate-pages --deskew` →
`ingest-book` at **full-text tier**.

## Second batch, 2026-09-05 — what changed

157 more pages finished the book (printed 14–253, 240 pages). Median confidence **95.5**,
consistent with the first batch, so the quality bar above holds.

**All of this is now code:** `DEV/RTP_Constraints_Course/scripts/scan_pipeline.py`. Read
its docstring before the next book rather than rebuilding the method. `verify_pdf.py`
beside it proves page order afterwards.

**The arithmetic gate is the highest-value thing learned.** `files − duplicates == last −
first + 1`. It costs nothing, it is enforced in code that *refuses to rename*, and it
caught the batch's structure immediately: 157 − 5 = 152 = printed 102…253. **It does not
catch a transposition of two adjacent pages, or two errors that cancel** — say so rather
than implying the gate proves order on its own.

**Collision pairs are not rare.** Twelve same-second ` (1)` pairs this batch against two
last time, and one pair (`08-08-44`) was genuinely inverted on disk relative to capture.
The mtime rule handles it; filename sort would not have.

**Re-shoots cluster into runs.** Printed 170–173 were each shot twice, in two passes ~30 s
apart, with the *first* pass interleaved so 170 and 171 shared a second. Resolve duplicates
by **measured OCR confidence**, not by eye or by assuming the later shot is better — here
the earlier copy won three of the four.

**Blank versos carry folios.** Printed 62, 194 and 236 are blank in the book and each still
prints its number. Open the page before calling a zero-word OCR result a failed scan.

Base directory for this skill: /Users/kristinarash/.claude/skills/ingest-book

# Ingest Book

Turn a book into atomized, citable entries under the library subtree, grouped by domain and book, ready for the `advisor` skill.

**Library root:** `/Users/kristinarash/SecondBrain/Knowledge/library`
**Paths:** canonical vault locations live in `/Users/kristinarash/.claude/skills/_shared/config.json` (`vault_library`, `vault_root`) — load it if unsure; if a literal path here ever disagrees, the config wins.
**Extractors:** `~/.claude/skills/ingest-book/lib/extract_epub.py`, `extract_pdf.py`
Run extractors inside the context-mode sandbox (`ctx_execute`, language python) so raw book text never enters the conversation — only the atomized entries you write do.

## Model split (cost vs quality)

This skill mixes three kinds of work with very different model needs:
- **Extraction & structure mapping** (probe, chapter map, text cleanup) — deterministic
  Python in the sandbox. **Zero model tokens; model choice irrelevant.**
- **Orchestration** (searches, `_book.md` updates, dedup checks) — mechanical.
  **Haiku-tier is fine.**
- **Atomization** (Phase 2/3: distilling prose into accurate entries with correct
  mechanism-vs-claim, honest confidence, and a real "when NOT to apply") — this is where
  the advisor's entire value is created. **Run on Sonnet or stronger. Do NOT use Haiku
  for atomization** — a weak distillation becomes a permanent low-quality entry, and the
  generated output is only ~3K tokens/chapter, so quality-per-token matters far more than
  price-per-token. Cost levers that DON'T hurt quality: atomize only chapters you'll
  consult, and checkpoint + `/clear` between chapter batches (see Rules) so context
  doesn't compound across the book.

## Schema for every entry note

Filename: `<kind>--<kebab-slug>.md`, `kind ∈ {principle, framework, case-study, heuristic, claim}`.

```yaml
---
type: library-entry
kind: principle
domain: <domain-slug>
book: <book-slug>
chapter: "N"            # or section label; "" if highlights with no location
topic: <2-5 word topic>
category: [tag, tag]
confidence: proven      # proven | supported | untested | contested
ingest-tier: full-text  # full-text | highlights | framework-only
created: <YYYY-MM-DD>
---

# <Human title of the idea>

**What it is** — one tight paragraph.
**Why it works** — mechanism, not restatement.
**When to apply** — concrete triggers.
**When NOT to apply** — scope limits. (MANDATORY — never omit.)
**Example** — one concrete instance.
```

**Confidence is bounded by tier:** full-text ≤ proven; highlights ≤ supported;
framework-only ≤ untested. Set `contested` by hand when sources conflict.

## Phase 1 — Intake

1. Identify: book title, author, source type (PDF/EPUB | Kindle highlights | physical), target domain.
2. Compute `<book-slug>` = `kebab(title)--kebab(lastname)` (e.g. `supertraining--verkhoshansky`).
3. If the domain folder/`_domain.md` doesn't exist, create them (mirror the S&C `_domain.md` format).
4. Build `_book.md` chapter map:
   - EPUB/PDF: run the extractor with `--list` / `--probe` to get the chapter or page structure.
   - Physical: ask the user for the chapter list, or assemble from a verified public listing.
   Write `_book.md` (template below) with every chapter `status: pending`.

`_book.md` template:
```markdown
---
type: book-index
book: <book-slug>
title: <full title>
author: <author>
domain: <domain-slug>
ingest-tier: full-text | highlights | framework-only
source: "<file path or 'physical' or 'kindle-highlights'>"
created: <YYYY-MM-DD>
---

# <title> — ingest map

| # | Chapter | Status | Entries |
|---|---------|--------|---------|
| 0 | <title> | pending | 0 |
```

## Phase 2 — Extract (by tier)

**Full-text (PDF/EPUB):**
- First run `extract_pdf.py --probe`. If `scanned: true`, STOP the full-text path:
  tell the user the PDF is image-only, and fall back to framework-only tier (set
  `ingest-tier: framework-only`, cap confidence at untested). Never emit full-text-
  confidence entries from a scanned file.
- Work **one chapter at a time** (EPUB `--chapter N`; PDF `--pages A-B`). For each:
  extract candidate ideas → atomize per the schema → write entry notes.
- **After each chapter**, update that row in `_book.md` to `status: done` with the
  entry count. This is the resume checkpoint — never batch this update.

**Kindle highlights:**
- Parse `My Clippings.txt` or the highlights export in the sandbox. Cluster highlights
  by theme; write one entry per theme. `ingest-tier: highlights`, confidence ≤ supported.
- Attribute `chapter` from the highlight's location metadata when present, else "".

**Framework-only (physical / scanned):**
- Briefly interview the user for their takeaways. Supplement with *verified* public
  chapter summaries. Write 5–15 framework-level entries. `ingest-tier: framework-only`,
  confidence ≤ untested.

## Phase 3 — Quality gate (run before writing each batch)

- One idea per note. If an extracted point is compound, split it.
- "When NOT to apply" present and non-trivial.
- **Dedup + converge:** before writing, `memsearch search` the library for the same
  concept. If an existing entry (any book) covers it, DON'T duplicate — instead add a
  `[[wikilink]]` + one line to both notes recording the agreement, and only add a new
  note if it contributes a genuinely new angle.
- Never overwrite an existing file; on slug collision append `-2`.

## Phase 4 — Close-out

1. Set all done rows in `_book.md`; if partial, leave pending rows for next session.
2. Add the book to `_domain.md`'s `books:` list and the "Books in this domain" section.
3. Add the book-slug to the advisor persona's `books:` list (`advisors/<domain>.md`)
   if an advisor exists.
4. Run `memsearch index "/Users/kristinarash/SecondBrain/Knowledge/library"`
   so entries are searchable immediately (don't wait for the SessionEnd hook).
5. Commit the vault: `git -C "/Users/kristinarash/SecondBrain" add Knowledge/library && git commit -m "ingest(<book-slug>): <N> entries, ch X-Y"`.
6. Report: entries by kind and confidence, links created, chapters remaining.

## Rules
- Raw book text stays in the sandbox; only atomized entries enter context/the vault.
- Resumable by design: `_book.md` is the source of truth for "where am I".
- A 300-page book is a multi-session job — stop at a chapter boundary, never mid-chapter.

# The Eight Objectives of Training

**What it is** — Bompa frames athlete preparation as targeting eight developable attributes, not just physical output: (1) **multilateral physical development** (general fitness base), (2) **sport-specific physical development**, (3) **technical skills**, (4) **tactical abilities**, (5) **psychological factors** (discipline, courage, perseverance, confidence), (6) **health maintenance**, (7) **injury resistance**, (8) **theoretical knowledge** (the athlete understanding *why* they train). Each is pursued by means appropriate to the athlete's age, experience, and talent.

**Why it works** — Performance is multi-factorial; a gap in any objective caps the others. Technique is limited by physical capacity; physical capacity is wasted without tactical and psychological readiness; durability (health + injury resistance) determines whether training can accumulate at all. Theoretical knowledge improves the athlete's own decision-making and buy-in.

**When to apply** — Auditing a program for blind spots ("we develop physical and technical, but are we addressing psychological and theoretical?"); designing a holistic athlete-development plan; explaining why S&C is necessary but not sufficient.

**When NOT to apply** — Not all eight get equal weight at all times — emphasis shifts by training phase, sport, and athlete maturity. It's a checklist for completeness, not a prescription to load all eight simultaneously. Injury resistance and multilateral base dominate early/youth development (see [[principle--multilateral-before-specialization]]).

**Example** — A pre-season review scores each athlete across the eight objectives and reveals that a physically elite group is under-served on tactical and theoretical development, redirecting some staff time accordingly.

===== p15 =====
CHAPTER 1

The Current Performance Landscape in American
Football

Try entering the term “football practice” into an internet search engine and look
at the images given in the results. What you will see are players: hitting tackling
dummies, running around obstacles on the ground (e.g., agility ladders and tires),
running plays or patterns with no defense, and coaches giving lots of instructions
about the specifics of their technique (e.g., pointing at their knees). For a long
time, this has been what practice is supposed to “look like” for most people. But
why do we practice this way? In this chapter, our goal is to highlight some of the
key features of the current practice landscape in American football and pull out
the underlying assumptions about skill acquisition on which they are based. We
will next address the various gaps and shortcomings of current football practice
while suggesting potential opportunities for growth and evolution. A particular
emphasis will be placed on areas where traditional practice deviates from
contemporary, yet evidence-based, principles of skill acquisition and motor
learning research. Finally, we will introduce the concept of a Skill Acquisition
Specialist (SAS), a staff member who aims to support teams and coaches in

designing and facilitating more effective practice and performance environments
for individual athletes.

Traditional Approaches towards American Football Practice

In this section, we highlight six of the key (typically, unstated) assumptions about
skill that underlie traditional football practice. In the following section, we will
look at the research evidence (or lack thereof) to support these ideas.

1. The value of assessing C training out of context action capacities

Although football is a team sport played with 11 players on each side, it is
commonly accepted that we can pull one player away from the other 21 to
evaluate and train them in isolation, out of the context of the game. The
assumption here is that the level of skill of a player is directly related to (and
predictable from) their raw action capacities (e.g. speed, agility, accuracy,
strength, jump height). Players' action capacities are measured by having players
run a 40-yard dash, bench press 225lb as many times as possible, or perform a
max distance throw at the National Football League (NFL) Combine. In practice,
players are trained by having them run through agility ladders, push tackling sleds,
and run routes and catch balls without defenders present. Assessing these action
capacities is assumed to be valuable for talent identification: a faster 40 makes for
a better running back (RB) than a slower time. This seems obvious, right?! It is

15
===== p16 =====
i.

further assumed that training these action capacities will have positive transfer of
training to game performance. For example, improving the standing jump height
of a wide receiver (WR) will result in more receptions and touchdowns on Sunday,
and improving the sprint speed of a RB will result in more yardage in the game.
As will be discussed in more detail next chapter, we have long taken this
asymmetric, organism-centered approach to skill. The individual player “acquires’
skill and is “skillful”. Skill lives within the player.

2. Task decomposition

A related assumption is that the most effective way to train football skills (e.g.,
receiving a deep pass, tackling a ball carrier) is by breaking them apart into pieces
in some way, training these pieces, and then putting the full skill back together—
an approach called task decomposition. There are two primary motivations behind
using this approach. First, it reduces the overall cognitive load (attentional and
memory demands) on the player, making the task easier. Second, from a practical
viewpoint, we can train football skills without always needing a full team. There
are three different types of task decomposition commonly used in American
football: (1) perception-action decoupling, (ii) part-task training (aka part practice),
and (iii) scaffolding.

Perception-action decoupling involves breaking apart the natural linkage
between the pick up of information from the environment (perception) and
movement (acting to achieve some goal in the environment). Examples include
RBs making cuts around cones placed on the ground or quarterbacks (QB)
throwing a ball through a tire. In these situations, the information that the player
uses to successfully perform the skill in the game (discussed in detail in both
chapters 2 and 3) has been removed. A RB changes their direction of movement
based on the position and movement of other players (e.g., the rate at which a
gap between two defenders is closing). A QB throws a ball to a WR with specific
bodily dimensions (e.g, height, arm length) and action capacities (e.g., vertical
jump height), moving in particular direction and speed, with a position relative to
the defensive back (DB). None of this information is available from many of the
inanimate objects used frequently across many practice environments. We are
training the action separate (or decoupled from) the perception. Similarly, we can
train perception separate from action. Two commonly used examples of this
occur at the QB position. The first consists of running through progressions
while watching a video replay of a specific play. Here, the player is perceiving
information—albeit from a different viewpoint than they will have in the game—
and the only action includes saying something like “I would drop the ball to the
RB in the flat.” The second is the use of perceptual-cognitive computer-based
training tools like $2 Cognition or Neurotracker. For example, in a test of
“processing speed,” a player perceives an object on a screen and performs a
simple action (tapping the screen), completely unlike the complex actions they
will need to perform on the field.

Part-task training involves dividing an action into distinct movement

16
===== p17 =====
phases and training each of these in isolation. For example, Figure 1.1 shows the
four phases of a football throw (early cocking, late cocking, acceleration, and
follow-through) identified using kinematic and EMG analyses of the action. Early
cocking is initiated at the rear foot plant and continues to maximal shoulder
abduction and internal rotation. Late cocking starts at maximal shoulder
abduction and internal rotation and ends with maximal shoulder external rotation.
The acceleration phase began with maximal shoulder external rotation and ended

with ball release. Finally, the follow-through can be defined as the phase from
ball release to maximal horizontal adduction.

(2002).

An example of part practice based on this type of phase analysis, is
training QB dropbacks without having them complete the rest of the throwing
action. So, for example, a coach might have a player take the snap and complete
the early cocking phase while giving them prescriptive technical feedback about
the execution (¢.g., the amount of knee bend, height they are holding the ball,
amount of hip rotation). In a separate drill, the focus could be switched to the
late cocking phases by having the player start from the loaded position. This type
of phase-based training has increased in popularity due to the availability of
markerless motion capture systems, making it easier to break skills like throwing
into their biomechanical parts so they can be assessed (e.g., this player has less
shoulder abduction than the average NFL QB) and trained.

In part-task training there are two different ways a skill can be broken
apart: segmentation and fractionation (Wickens et al., 2013). Segmentation
involves separately training phases of a skill that occur in sequence (i.e., are
separable in time). For example, training the early and late cocking phases of
throwing in separate drills. Fractionation involves separating and training phases
of skill that normally occur simultaneously when the full action is performed. This

17
===== p18 =====
iB

is commonly used in American football such as in drills that focus on footwor
separately from throwing or pushing a defender out of the way.

The final example of task decomposition is scaffolding. Much lik.
scaffolding on a building, this technique involves building a complex skill by
breaking it into its sub-skills. So, instead of breaking a skill apart into movemen,
phases like in part-task training, we are breaking it apart at the task level. These
sub-skills are then trained separately, which allows the learner to progressively
build new sub-skills on the foundation of ones already learned. Another way of
thinking of this would be in reducing the problem space, that is, the gap between
where the learner is currently at and the desired goal, by creating a simpler version
of the skill. This method is commonly used in American football when teaching
a youth player how to tackle a ball carrier. For this, we could first reduce the task
to executing the sub-skill of the player getting their feet in front of the ball carrier.
Once they can do this, we could next work on getting their head in the “correct”
(and safe) position to make a tackle. Finally, we could work on having a strong
wrap on the opponent and finishing with a leg drive through the tackle. A critical
aspect of this is that we need enough practice (strict repetition) for the sub-skill
to become automatic before we move on to the next sub-skill. Scaffolding in this
manner is proposed to reduce the cognitive load by allowing a player to focus on
only one or two movements (in each sub-skill) rather than the whole thing at
once.

3. Being skillful in football involves automatizing the fundamental movements / techniques
through rote repetition

A long-held belief in most sports, including American football, is that a player
must learn the “fundamentals” of their sport before they can effectively play the
game. The term fundamentals is commonly used to refer to an ideal/correct
technique (movement pattern) for basic skills like throwing, blocking, tackling,
catching, and kicking. For example, the “proper” technique for catching a
football is thought to involve the following steps:

i) Follow the flight of the ball with your eyes.

ii) Extend your arms toward the incoming ball, creating a large target area allowing
you to reach the ball with your fingertips.

iii) Form a diamond shape with your hands by touching your index fingers and
thumbs together while keeping your other fingers spread out to create a pocket
for the ball.

iv) When the ball arrives, try to catch the ball with your fingers, not your palms,
to incur a soft, controlled catch.

v) Bend your elbows slightly to cushion the impact of the ball and prevent it from

bouncing off your hands.
vi) After catching the ball, quickly tuck it to your chest to secure it.

Based on the model of skill acquisition developed by Fitts & Posner (1967),
illustrated in Figure 1.2, it is proposed that we go through three distinct stages

18
===== p19 =====
when learning fundamental skills like this. When we first start learning a new skill,
we use controlled processing. That is, we recall how we have been instructed to
position our different body parts (e.g., the steps involved in catching described
above), hold these steps in out working memory, and focus attention on our body
to determine if the positioning is correct. But, if we keep practicing and practicing
(Le., repetition), we can reach the other end of the acquisition spectrum, called
automatic processing, ultimately moving from a cognitive stage to an autonomous
stage. Put simply, being automatic means that you can perform an action without
thinking about the execution of the movements involved. A term that you will
often hear in association with automaticity is that of “muscle memory.” This is
basically used to represent the idea that control of the movement no longer
requires attention and conscious control. Instead, through practice, expert
performers essentially develop internal routines or programs for executing the

movement. Once the routines are activated, they are able to run pretty much on
their own.

Figure 1.2 - Fitts & Posner’s (1967) Skill acquisition model.

As you may be able to tell, the key to skill development following this
model is lots of rote repetition. We practice catching balls thrown at the same
height and speed (often using a ball projection machine to reduce any variation)
until we have mastered the basic fundamentals of catching a football. Again, this
typically involves task decomposition: the fundamentals of catching are practiced
without a defender present, without running after receiving the ball, or without
running a route in a manner to get open (ie., separating away from a defensive
player) before catching. Within the traditional view of skill, thinking about, or
paying attention to, what you are doing is a burden that must be lifted. This is
why we have long called them practice dri//s. Borrowing from the military, the idea
is that we want to train you in practice (following the same repetitive path as a
drill bit) so that when you ate in the heat of competition, skill execution becomes

19
===== p20 =====
-

reflexive, habitual, and automatic. This is expressed in the common saying
“perfect practice makes perfect.”

4. Variability for adjustability

Of course, not every ball thrown to a WR will allow for use of this idea]
technique—the player needs to be able to successfully catch balls that are thrown
low, high, or behind them. The typical way in which this is taught is by adding
some variability to the practice conditions (e.g,, balls thrown at different heights),
but only after the fundamentals have been learned. The player is then instructed
(by the coach) how to adjust their ideal catching to account for these variations,
For example, to catch a ball that was thrown low, a player might be told to cup
their hands in front of them with their pinky fingers together, essentially creating
a "basket" to scoop the ball up, while keeping their elbows slightly bent and using
soft hands to secure the catch.
Thus, in the traditional approach, there are few key points about how
variability is added to practice:
e Variability in conditions should only be added after the player has
mastered the fundamentals (ie., the proper technique for the skill).

e The variations added to practice should be situations the player might
encounter in a game (e.g. a low ot high pass). Since the purpose of
adding this variability is to learn how to adjust their basic technique, there
is little value in having them practice variations that never occur in a game
(e.g., catching a ball that is a different shape or weight than a regulation
football, catching a ball projected at a higher speed than will occur in a
game).

e Adding variability to practice should be accompanied by the coach telling
the athlete the adjustments that need to be made to their technique.

5. Coach as the expert instructor

In the traditional approach to coaching in American football, the coach is the one
that has the answers (i.e., they know the proper technique for catching, passing,
running, and tackling). Their job is to transmit this knowledge to the players
through direct, prescriptive instruction. That is, to prescribe a movement solution
(e.g., your knees should be bent this much, your hands should be in this shape)
to the player and then give corrective feedback whenever there is a deviation from
the ideal solution. As described in assumption #4 above, part of their job also
involves anticipating the different variations of the skill that must be performed
in the game and giving prescriptive instruction and corrective feedback about the
adjustments that must be made for these variations.

Stated another way, in the traditional approach, practice is coach-centric
(.e., it centers around the coach rather than the athlete). Here, knowledge
transmission is unidirectional (from the coach to the player), and the player has
little role in deciding how, or what, they are taught. This is why football coaches

20
===== p21 =====
have long been portrayed as military generals, giving orders.
6. Effective teamwork comes from the development of shared mental models

The final assumption concerns the best way to develop teamwork, making sure
teammates get on the same page. That is, how do we teach players to coordinate
their actions collectively to produce effective outcomes like executing a play-
action pass in football? The mental model approach argues that this type of team
coordination is based on shared information players have stored in memory (e.g.,
concepts or principles related to a specific play call).

A mental model is an internal representation of a system (e.g., a football
defense). Through observing lots of diagrams on whiteboards and watching lots
of game film, a player develops a mental model (stored in their memory) of, for
example, a 4-3 defensive formation. This model contains information about the
positioning of each player on the field and how they will specifically move once
a play is run. This mental model also includes explicit, rule-based information
about what the player should do (their responsibility and where they should move
on the field) for the specific play that was called (e.g., if this, then that cules; if the
middle linebacker (LB) blitzes, I need to do X).

When such individual mental models are shared amongst team members,
a shared mental model (SMM) develops (Filho & Tenenbaum, 2012). SMMs provide
teammates with the ability to coordinate thoughts and actions without necessarily
explicitly communicating in dynamic situations. Over the years, SMMs have
become a common way to articulate how teammates coordinate with each other,
making them a popular method for studying team cognition (DeChurch et al.,
2010). It has been suggested that team members must share mental models that
describe when and how they must interact with one another to accomplish the
task.

For a specific example, consider a QB throwing a deep ball to an open
receiver. In the SMM account, this type of team coordination occurs because both
players have a stored schema for the execution of a “long pass,” and both decide
to execute this action after processing the available perceptual cues (i.e., the
relative positions of the players). This may also involve an intermediate step of
identifying the defensive strategy that is being played by the opponent (e.g., man-
to-man coverage). In this account, the perceptual cues are non-informative in and
of themselves—instead, they have come to be associated with this particular
action or play through extensive practice and/or a coach’s instruction (e.g., being
told that when the defenders do X, you should do Y). Thus, the keys to team
coordination in this account ate that (1) both players have stored a similar set of
schema (i.e., they learned the same set of plays) and (2) these schemas are
associated with the same perceptual cues for each player.

In this approach, a key element of developing team coordination is
developing &vowledge about football (Gibson, 1966). This knowledge about
facilitates our conceptual, indirect “understanding” of our environment. It is
demonstrated either verbally or by using symbols or pictures (e.g., drawing a

21
===== p22 =====
football play out on a whiteboard). It is scaled in units of physics (e.g., when you
are 10 yards from the receiver) rather than being body-scaled because it refers to
the typical, the ideal. In terms of action, knowledge about can only be used to
describe what to perceive and what to do (e.g., turn right when you get to the 50-
yard line).

This traditional SMM approach to teamwork provides support for the
commonly used practices of: (i) team reviews of game footage in the film room,
(ii) coach explicitly explains the plays using a whiteboard, and (fii) an unopposed
walkthrough of plays.

Problems with these Assumptions: A Contemporary View of Skill
Acquisition

Contemporary research and theories of skill acquisition have identified several
limitations with the assumptions laid out in the last section.

Action capabilites are not reliable predictors of football skill

Most football fans can readily cite examples of players that had poor combine
showings followed by excellent careers in the NFL (e.g., Tom Brady) or had great
combines but only mediocre NFL careers (e.g., Vernon Gholston). Research has
shown that, in fact, performance in the NFL combine is a very poor predictor of
success in the NFL. For example, Kuzmits and Adams (2008) performed a
correlational analysis looking at potential relationships between combine test
scores (times for the 10, 20, and 40-yard dash; 20-yard shuttle; 60-yard shuttle; 3-
cone drill, number of bench press repetitions; height for the vertical jump; and
distance for the broad jump) and NFL game statistics in the first three years after
the combine (games played, QB rating, average yards per carry, and average yards
gained per reception). For both QBs and WRs, there wete no significant
correlations between any of the combine scores and any of the game statistics.
For RBs, there were significant negative correlations between yards per carry (in
years one and two after the combine) and times in the 10, 20, and 40-yard dashes.
So, in other words, lower (faster) times were associated with more yards per carry
in NFL games. None of the other correlations were significant.

Rishis et al (2023) recently conducted a systematic review on all the
studies that have attempted to address this question. Their search revealed a total
of 12 studies evaluating the relationship between combine test results and NFL
performance. While many of the studies found significant correlations (as was the
case for the RBs in Kuzmits and Adams study, described above), there was no
consistent pattern across studies (i.e, the combine measures that were
significantly related to NFL performance were different for the various studies).
This suggests that the positive correlations were most likely due to chance (i.e.,
were the result of doing multiple statistical tests, commonly called Type I error).

As we will discuss more in the next chapter, the problem here is we are
conflating action capacity (an individual constraint) with skill. Consider a RB

executing a sweep play. To successfully gain yardage (a skill), they need to be able
to adapt their movement (speed and running direction) based on the relevant
information they are picking up ftom the envitonment (e.g., the position of the

defenders). Having greater raw speed over a short distance (i.e., an action capacity

5. Coach as the expert instructor

In the traditional approach to coaching in American football, the coach is the one
that has the answers (i.e., they know the proper technique for catching, passing,
running, and tackling). Their job is to transmit this knowledge to the players
through direct, prescriptive instruction. That is, to prescribe a movement solution
(e.g., your knees should be bent this much, your hands should be in this shape)
to the player and then give corrective feedback whenever there is a deviation from
the ideal solution. As described in assumption #4 above, part of their job also
involves anticipating the different variations of the skill that must be performed
in the game and giving prescriptive instruction and corrective feedback about the
adjustments that must be made for these variations.

Stated another way, in the traditional approach, practice is coach-centric
(.e., it centers around the coach rather than the athlete). Here, knowledge
transmission is unidirectional (from the coach to the player), and the player has
little role in deciding how, or what, they are taught. This is why football coaches

The final assumption concerns the best way to develop teamwork, making sure
teammates get on the same page. That is, how do we teach players to coordinate

coordination is based on shared information players have stored in memory (e.g.,
concepts or principles related to a specific play call).

A mental model is an internal representation of a system (e.g., a football
defense). Through observing lots of diagrams on whiteboards and watching lots
of game film, a player develops a mental model (stored in their memory) of, for
example, a 4-3 defensive formation. This model contains information about the
positioning of each player on the field and how they will specifically move once
a play is run. This mental model also includes explicit, rule-based information
about what the player should do (their responsibility and where they should move
on the field) for the specific play that was called (e.g., if this, then that cules; if the
middle linebacker (LB) blitzes, I need to do X).

a shared mental model (SMM) develops (Filho & Tenenbaum, 2012). SMMs provide
teammates with the ability to coordinate thoughts and actions without necessarily
explicitly communicating in dynamic situations. Over the years, SMMs have
become a common way to articulate how teammates coordinate with each other,
making them a popular method for studying team cognition (DeChurch et al.,

action or play through extensive practice and/or a coach’s instruction (e.g., being

associated with the same perceptual cues for each player.

technique. One of the instructions given to players in this group was “move the
racquet low to high by turning the shoulders to the side and contacting the ball
in front of the forward foot.” The other group was given an analogy-based
instruction: “hit the ball like the shape of a rainbow.” In the traditional group, the
coach prescribes a movement solution to the athlete by making specific reference
to your body movements and positions (i.e., a specific technique)—“turn your
shoulders” and “in front of your forward foot.” In the analogy group, the coach
is guiding the athlete to find a more authentic solution that has the key
characteristics they are looking for without telling the athlete the specifics of how
that is to be achieved (i.e., the technique in terms of the specific body movements
and positions). Instead, the coach is trying to encourage the athlete’s movement
solution to have a certain form by appealing to an analogy—a metaphor for the
pattern of movement that does not explicitly refer to its specifics. When I tell you
to move “like a rainbow,” the key feature that comes to mind for most people is
an arch in the path. Instead of trying to give you the exact solution to the problem,
we are using an analogy to convey its key features.

Was there any difference between these two groups after six weeks of
training? Using a technique called principal components analysis, the authors
were able to group participants into clusters based on their movements. For
example, some participants used more shoulder motion, while others used more
wrist movement. Before the training, both groups showed four clusters, or, in
other words, they used four different movement solutions for executing a
forehand, After training, the group that was given traditional prescriptive
instructions, not surprisingly, became more homogenous—they now exhibited

27
===== p28 =====
only three different clusters of solutions. The analogy group showed the opposite
result—after training, they exhibited eight clusters. Having more available
movement solutions can be better because it gives more potential for greater
adaptability—the player can still execute a successful forehand despite changes in
the contextual situation and conditions (e.g., the court surface, the height of the
bounce, the speed of the approaching ball, and their level of fatigue).

It has also been demonstrated in a couple of research studies that
prescriptive coaching can result in less creativity. For example, in a 2018 study by
Santos and colleagues, 40 soccer players were split into two training groups: one
involving traditional prescriptive training and a differential /earning group. For the
latter group, random variations in the practice conditions were added, including
changes in the playing surface (e.g., turf vs. natural grass), the shape of the field
(e.g., rectangular vs. circular), and the type of ball (¢.g., a rugby ball vs. a soccer
ball). So, during practice, athletes in the differential learning group never
performed the same action twice in a tow—there were constant changes in
constraints. Creativity was assessed (in matches played before and after training)
using the Creative Behavior Assessment in Team Sports tool, which assesses both
the functionality (e.g., did the pass get to the intended receiver?) and originality
of actions (e.g., % of players that attempted that movement solution). This was
completed by two raters that were blind to what the players were assigned to in
training. What was found? Following five months of training, the prescriptive
coaching group produced actions that were rated as significantly less versatile,
original, and creative. A similar effect was found in a study by Orangi et al.
(2021b). After 12 weeks of training, a prescriptive coaching group (that was
instructed in the ideal techniques for shooting, passing, and dribbling) executed
three times fewer creative actions in a test match as compared to a CLA training

group (who were given no technical instruction and practiced in SSCG with
variability in the number of players, size of the playing area, and rules) . Examples
of creative actions included heel passes, bicycle kicks, and Ronaldo dribbles.

3. Prescriptive coaching can lead to a reduced sense of autonomy & lower intrinsic
motivation

One of the most popular, well-supported theories in sports science is related to
motivation. Specifically, Se/{Determination Theory (SDT), which is a meta-theory
combining a few different ideas, was first put together in a package by Deci &
Ryan in the mid-80s (2012). It proposes that an athlete’s level of intrinsic
motivation (actions driven by internal factors like a desite to succeed rather than
by external rewards like verbal praise and trophies) is driven by three basic human
needs: relatedness, competence, and autonomy. Relatedness concerns the need to
feel connected, involved, and supported and consequently experience satisfying
interpersonal relationships. Competence reflects a belief in one’s abilities and
capacity to control outcomes. Finally, avfonomy represents the desire to express
choice and not to feel controlled or compelled to do something. When these
needs are being met, we act with intrinsic motivation. Meaning, practicing can be

28
===== p29 =====
self-satisfying.

In a paper by Ian Renshaw and colleagues (2012), the authors describe
how ineffective prescriptive, repetition-based coaching is in supporting intrinsic
motivation. Think about the typical drill-based activity, like running around
cones, punching air, or hitting a ball off a tee. For most athletes, these drills can
be boring and monotonous. To get athletes to complete such activities, coaches
must provide several sources of external motivation. We might give our athletes
a pre-practice speech emphasizing the importance of “sacrifice and struggle” in
becoming skillful. During the activity, many coaches resort to yelling things like
“come on, get going” or “keep it up.” Finally, we use the promise of something
more rewarding (“after we finish these drills, we can scrimmage for a few minutes
at the end of practice”). Such coaching methods tend to make athletes externally
motivated. Meaning, the athletes complete the drills to not get yelled at or
punished (e.g., running laps) and receive praise (a “good job” or a high five) or
rewards. There is a lot of research showing the inferiority of external motivation
in comparison to intrinsic motivation and that using a coach-centered,

prescriptive instruction approach can decrease intrinsic motivation (Gillet et al.,
2010).

4. Prescriptive coaching can increase the risk of injury

In 2004, Roger James proposed an interesting twist on the traditional
explanations for sports injuries. The “variability-overuse hypothesis” starts with
the same basic concept as most theories: Repeated application of load eventually
leads to tissue breakdown and injury. Meaning, don’t do it too much. But then it
adds a new twist: this breakdown will occur when there is not enough variability
in movement to allow for adaptation. So, the problem is not that you are not
doing it the one, correct way. In fact, trying to do that—trying to have a highly
consistent, repeatable movement—is likely to increase the chance of injury, not
decrease it. Why might this be the case? Think about making a tackle. If we
performed this movement the same way every time, we would stress the same
muscles, tissues, and bones (and the entire human movement system) in the same
way every time. Allowing for slight variations in the technique used, in terms of
direction, location, magnitude, and frequency of the muscle activity involved,
creates a broader distribution of stressors, which reduces the chance of injury.

To test this idea, Orangi and colleagues (2021a) examined whether
coaching methods that promoted variability helped to reduce risk factors for ACL
injuries in soccer players as compared to traditional, prescriptive coaching. Sixty-
six novice soccer players were split into three groups that trained for 12 weeks. A
traditional, prescriptive instruction group was trained using repetitive, corrective
practice designed to promote the “correct” techniques for shooting and passing.
So, in other words, the coach was trying to minimize the variability in skill
execution. A CLA group was encouraged to explore movement solutions using
constraint manipulations, including the use of small-sided and conditioned
games. Finally, a differential learning group practiced with random perturbations

29
===== p30 =====
to the practice conditions, including things like which side of the foot they had
to kick with, hand positions, and type of ball. To assess the injury tisk, all
participants were asked to perform a change of direction test in which they had
to run at full speed to a marker and then cut at 45 degrees. During this test, the
researchers used motion tracking to measure variables that have been shown to
be risk factors for ACL injuries in previous research (including things like trunk,
hip, and knee flexion angle and peak ground reaction force). What was found?
For both the CLA and differential learning groups, all the measures changed in
the positive direction (and by significantly more than for the traditional training
group). For example, from pre- to post-training, the knee flexion angle increased
and the magnitude of ground reaction force decreased. These results support the
idea that adding variability and exploration to practice serves to reduce the risk
factors for injury.

5. Problems with the shared mental models approach to teamwork,

‘There are some important limitations that have been identified with the shared
mental models approach. First, the typical methods used to develop SMMs (.e.,
drawing a play on a whiteboard or watching video of a play) give the player a
third-person, bird’s-eye view of the action. Thus, the visual information is vastly
different from what is used in the game. The second, even more important issue,
is that (similar to the variability for adjustability issue described above), effective
usage of SMM requires that the coach anticipate all the possible variations in the
events that might happen. What happens if a defender falls down? Or the defense
sends a blitzer from an unusual position? Or you have your back to a defender
that is about to tackle you (¢.g., Saquon Barkley’s incredible reverse hurdle from
the 2024 season). Unless the coach has created an if X, then Y rule for these special
cases, team coordination wil] certainly fail. Simply put, using a SMM approach
results in limited adaptability to changing constraints.

Instead of team cognition being based on shared knowledge in the form
of stored representations and schema, coordination amongst teammates can be
more effectively achieved through shared attunement to perceptual information
(see Chapter 3 for further elaboration) (Silva et al., 2013). The distinction between
shared knowledge and shared attunement can be understood by considering an
example from football. Imagine a QB throws a long pass to a WR at the exact
moment the receiver on an option route chooses to go deep. How did both
players come to execute such coordinated actions without any explicit
communication (about which option would be chosen) beforehand? In the shared
knowledge account, this type of coordination occurs because both players have a
stored schema for the “deep pass play,” and both decide to execute this action
after processing the available perceptual cues (i.¢., the relative positions of the
players). This may also involve an intermediate step of identifying the defensive
strategy that is being played by the opponent (e.g., a cover 3 defense). In this
account, the perceptual cues are non-informative in and of themselves—instead
they have come to be associated with this particular action or play through

30

psd enieetinisnR rine Rieadsicimadedin ns
===== p31 =====
extensive practice and/or a coach’s instruction (e.g., being told that when the
defenders do X, you should do Y). Thus, the keys to team coordination in this
account are that (1) both players have stored a similar set of schema (1.e., they
learned the same set of plays) and (2) these schema are associated with the same
perceptual cues for each player.

The primary distinction with the shared attunement account comes at
the level of the players’ perception. Instead of detecting non-informative
perceptual cues that must be processed and associated with stored knowledge so
that a decision about which action to execute can be reached, the ecological
approach argues that perception involves the pick-up of information sources that
directly specify opportunities for action. For example, in the example described
above, the two teammates might detect a higher-order perceptual variable we
might call Tau Diff, which gives the difference between the time of arrival of the
receiver at the pass landing point and the time of arrival of the DB at the same
location. Tau Diff is visually specified by the ratio of the gap between each player
and the landing location and the rate of change of these gaps. This variable is
informative because it directly specifies whether there is an opportunity for along
pass (Tau Diff is greater than 0) or there is not an opportunity (i.e., Tau Diff is <
0). Coordination between players occurs in this case because both players are

attuned to Tau Diff and thus would simultaneously detect when the environment
affords the opportunity for a lob pass.

The Role of a Skill Acquisition Specialist

To end this chapter, we want to introduce readers to an emerging (but still
relatively uncommon) staff role in Sports organizations that we believe can help
football teams address many of the issues raised above, supporting coaches in
designing and facilitating effective learning and performance environments: the
SAS (Otte et al., 2024). In high-profile collegiate programs and across the
professional level, there is a staff member entrusted with nearly any and every
duty that you can possibly imagine. Yet, even with the recent surge in popularity
of contemporary skill acquisition ideas (e.g., ecological dynamics) in numerous
other sports such as baseball and basketball, many within American football often
continue to operate with a dangerous “this is the way we have always done it”
mentality, employing practices that are outdated and/or not truly supported by
theory and research. In fact, it remains rare to find someone on staff within
professional organizations in American football (e.g., NFL) who possesses a
deeper understanding of skill acquisition concepts and principles. We will admit
that it may be unrealistic to expect every football organization and team to have
a qualified SAS as part of their staff

317	cones, punching air, or hitting a ball off a tee. For most athletes, these drills can
318	be boring and monotonous. To get athletes to complete such activities, coaches
319	must provide several sources of external motivation. We might give our athletes
320	a pre-practice speech emphasizing the importance of “sacrifice and struggle” in
321	becoming skillful. During the activity, many coaches resort to yelling things like
322	“come on, get going” or “keep it up.” Finally, we use the promise of something
323	more rewarding (“after we finish these drills, we can scrimmage for a few minutes
324	at the end of practice”). Such coaching methods tend to make athletes externally
325	motivated. Meaning, the athletes complete the drills to not get yelled at or
326	punished (e.g., running laps) and receive praise (a “good job” or a high five) or
327	rewards. There is a lot of research showing the inferiority of external motivation
328	in comparison to intrinsic motivation and that using a coach-centered,
329	
330	prescriptive instruction approach can decrease intrinsic motivation (Gillet et al.,
331	2010).
332	
333	4. Prescriptive coaching can increase the risk of injury
334	
335	In 2004, Roger James proposed an interesting twist on the traditional
336	explanations for sports injuries. The “variability-overuse hypothesis” starts with
337	the same basic concept as most theories: Repeated application of load eventually
338	leads to tissue breakdown and injury. Meaning, don’t do it too much. But then it
339	adds a new twist: this breakdown will occur when there is not enough variability
340	in movement to allow for adaptation. So, the problem is not that you are not
341	doing it the one, correct way. In fact, trying to do that—trying to have a highly
342	consistent, repeatable movement—is likely to increase the chance of injury, not
343	decrease it. Why might this be the case? Think about making a tackle. If we
344	performed this movement the same way every time, we would stress the same
345	muscles, tissues, and bones (and the entire human movement system) in the same
346	way every time. Allowing for slight variations in the technique used, in terms of
347	direction, location, magnitude, and frequency of the muscle activity involved,
348	creates a broader distribution of stressors, which reduces the chance of injury.
349	
350	To test this idea, Orangi and colleagues (2021a) examined whether
351	coaching methods that promoted variability helped to reduce risk factors for ACL
352	injuries in soccer players as compared to traditional, prescriptive coaching. Sixty-
353	six novice soccer players were split into three groups that trained for 12 weeks. A
354	traditional, prescriptive instruction group was trained using repetitive, corrective
355	practice designed to promote the “correct” techniques for shooting and passing.
356	So, in other words, the coach was trying to minimize the variability in skill
357	execution. A CLA group was encouraged to explore movement solutions using
358	constraint manipulations, including the use of small-sided and conditioned
359	games. Finally, a differential learning group practiced with random perturbations
360	
361	29
362	===== p30 =====
363	to the practice conditions, including things like which side of the foot they had
364	to kick with, hand positions, and type of ball. To assess the injury tisk, all
365	participants were asked to perform a change of direction test in which they had
366	to run at full speed to a marker and then cut at 45 degrees. During this test, the
367	researchers used motion tracking to measure variables that have been shown to
368	be risk factors for ACL injuries in previous research (including things like trunk,
369	hip, and knee flexion angle and peak ground reaction force). What was found?
370	For both the CLA and differential learning groups, all the measures changed in
371	the positive direction (and by significantly more than for the traditional training
372	group). For example, from pre- to post-training, the knee flexion angle increased
373	and the magnitude of ground reaction force decreased. These results support the
374	idea that adding variability and exploration to practice serves to reduce the risk
375	factors for injury.
376	
377	5. Problems with the shared mental models approach to teamwork,
378	
379	‘There are some important limitations that have been identified with the shared
380	mental models approach. First, the typical methods used to develop SMMs (.e.,
381	drawing a play on a whiteboard or watching video of a play) give the player a
382	third-person, bird’s-eye view of the action. Thus, the visual information is vastly
383	different from what is used in the game. The second, even more important issue,
384	is that (similar to the variability for adjustability issue described above), effective
385	usage of SMM requires that the coach anticipate all the possible variations in the
386	events that might happen. What happens if a defender falls down? Or the defense
387	sends a blitzer from an unusual position? Or you have your back to a defender
388	that is about to tackle you (¢.g., Saquon Barkley’s incredible reverse hurdle from
389	the 2024 season). Unless the coach has created an if X, then Y rule for these special
390	cases, team coordination wil] certainly fail. Simply put, using a SMM approach
391	results in limited adaptability to changing constraints.
392	
393	Instead of team cognition being based on shared knowledge in the form
394	of stored representations and schema, coordination amongst teammates can be
395	more effectively achieved through shared attunement to perceptual information
396	(see Chapter 3 for further elaboration) (Silva et al., 2013). The distinction between
397	shared knowledge and shared attunement can be understood by considering an
398	example from football. Imagine a QB throws a long pass to a WR at the exact
399	moment the receiver on an option route chooses to go deep. How did both
400	players come to execute such coordinated actions without any explicit
401	communication (about which option would be chosen) beforehand? In the shared
402	knowledge account, this type of coordination occurs because both players have a
403	stored schema for the “deep pass play,” and both decide to execute this action
404	after processing the available perceptual cues (i.¢., the relative positions of the
405	players). This may also involve an intermediate step of identifying the defensive
406	strategy that is being played by the opponent (e.g., a cover 3 defense). In this
407	account, the perceptual cues are non-informative in and of themselves—instead
408	they have come to be associated with this particular action or play through
409	
410	30
411	
412	psd enieetinisnR rine Rieadsicimadedin ns
413	===== p31 =====
414	extensive practice and/or a coach’s instruction (e.g., being told that when the
415	defenders do X, you should do Y). Thus, the keys to team coordination in this
416	account are that (1) both players have stored a similar set of schema (1.e., they
417	learned the same set of plays) and (2) these schema are associated with the same
418	perceptual cues for each player.
419	
420	The primary distinction with the shared attunement account comes at
421	the level of the players’ perception. Instead of detecting non-informative
422	perceptual cues that must be processed and associated with stored knowledge so
423	that a decision about which action to execute can be reached, the ecological
424	approach argues that perception involves the pick-up of information sources that
425	directly specify opportunities for action. For example, in the example described
426	above, the two teammates might detect a higher-order perceptual variable we
427	might call Tau Diff, which gives the difference between the time of arrival of the
428	receiver at the pass landing point and the time of arrival of the DB at the same
429	location. Tau Diff is visually specified by the ratio of the gap between each player
430	and the landing location and the rate of change of these gaps. This variable is
431	informative because it directly specifies whether there is an opportunity for along
432	pass (Tau Diff is greater than 0) or there is not an opportunity (i.e., Tau Diff is <
433	0). Coordination between players occurs in this case because both players are
434	
435	attuned to Tau Diff and thus would simultaneously detect when the environment
436	affords the opportunity for a lob pass.
437	
438	The Role of a Skill Acquisition Specialist
439	
440	To end this chapter, we want to introduce readers to an emerging (but still
441	relatively uncommon) staff role in Sports organizations that we believe can help
442	football teams address many of the issues raised above, supporting coaches in
443	designing and facilitating effective learning and performance environments: the
444	SAS (Otte et al., 2024). In high-profile collegiate programs and across the
445	professional level, there is a staff member entrusted with nearly any and every
446	duty that you can possibly imagine. Yet, even with the recent surge in popularity
447	of contemporary skill acquisition ideas (e.g., ecological dynamics) in numerous
448	other sports such as baseball and basketball, many within American football often
449	continue to operate with a dangerous “this is the way we have always done it”
450	mentality, employing practices that are outdated and/or not truly supported by
451	theory and research. In fact, it remains rare to find someone on staff within
452	professional organizations in American football (e.g., NFL) who possesses a
453	deeper understanding of skill acquisition concepts and principles. We will admit
454	that it may be unrealistic to expect every football organization and team to have
455	a qualified SAS as part of their staff in the relatively near future. However, at the
456	very least, we believe that the time is now for organizations to begin to prioritize
457	proven skill acquisition ideas that can have both immediate and long-term
458	positive benefits for the players on their team by bringing on staff members who
459	have extensive knowledge, expertise, and experience in skill acquisition.
460	
461	Some in American football may scoff at the claims that anything needs
462	
463	31
464	===== p32 =====
465	to be done to change how practices are conducted or how playets are guided
466	during their skill development and enhancement joutney. After all, there have
467	been some awfully exceptional football players who have emerged throughout
468	the history of the sport. If players like Tom Brady, Reggie White, Walter Payton,
469	and Jerry Rice were able to achieve the level of greatness that they did without
470	SAS support existing in their practice environments, why does anything need to
471	change to include the theory-driven and research-informed practices of SAS now
472	
473	to further develop players of the future? However, we would like to ask: did those —
474	
475	players mentioned above really develop from, and perform because of, the practice
476	methods employed during their time playing? Or could their performance have
477	unfolded i spite of these methods? Furthermore, if there was generally one way
478	that practice was predominantly structured across all teams and levels (e.g., an
479	
480	stb iS pct it gs
481	
482	abundance of isolated and decontextualized drills performed by rote repetition —
483	with an emphasis on technical model adherence), wouldn’t some players still ;
484	
485	succeed and be viewed as the top players in the game? With both theory and
486	research beginning to challenge many of the practices embraced by the traditional
487	sacred cows deeply running through American football, a reconceptualized view
488	of practice environments could begin to take shape where they would be a home
489	for problem-solving, ripe for learning, designed and supported by qualified SAS
490	while underpinned by ideas offered by an ecological dynamics framework.
491	
492	In the chapters to come, we argue that players become more adept at
493	coordinating integrated movement solutions, underpinned by the intertwined processes
494	
495	of perception, cognition, and action, thus leading to more functional, adaptable —
496	
497	problem-solving in football (Myszka et al., 2023b). Furthermore, though these
498	
499	respective processes are always intertwined in our viewpoint, they may not always
500	
501	be as effectively coupled (i.¢., feeding into each other as functionally as needed)
502	if the player is not exposed to the 'right' movement problems that require this \
503	(meaning, the skill has been developed or attacked through the use of dead, sterile —
504	
505	drills), Here, an ecological dynamics approach goes deeper than mere sport-
506	
507	specific tactical or technical frameworks by considering the football player as a —
508	
509	complex adaptive system in constant interaction with their competitive
510	
511	performance environment. On this note, it should be stated that even though
512	
513	position coaches (and other support staff) will certainly play a major role in
514	maximizing the on-field performance and skill development of players, we believe
515	
516	that the inclusion of a SAS will represent the next frontier in the American |
517	
518	football performance landscape, bringing about a paradigm-shifting revolution in
519	the way that practice is designed. Here, players at every level will be the beneficiary
520	of these changes, due to the skillful movement behaviors that will naturally
521	emerge for them on game day.
522	
523	While position coaches in football could potentially share a similar
524	mission and purpose with that of an SAS (e.g., regarding player development, skill
525	execution, and coaching approaches), the SAS role and responsibilities will likely
526	not fully align with those of position coaches, who are typically in possession of
527	more football-specific tactical knowledge. Additionally, though skilled in theit
528	own right, it is likely that most football coaches will not possess the same depth
529	
530	32
531	===== p33 =====
532	of knowledge and understanding pertaining to ideas relevant to skillful movement
533	behavior and creating optimal practice conditions that a SAS does, meaning, there
534	is much more to the SAS role than providing position-specific coaching for
535	individual players. Moreover, instead of possibly viewing SAS as a threat to them
536	and what they do, we hope that position coaches can begin to view SAS as a key
537	integral piece in helping bring athlete development principles and processes to
538	life through the design of more effective practices and enhanced communication
539	methods for player coaching. Here, it will be 2 win-win for all involved!
540	
541	In fact, the benefits of adding SAS to staffs in American football will be
542	multifaceted, providing tremendous supportive value for any football
543	organization at all levels of the game. These could include:
544	
545	¢ SAS may support football organizations in increasing player and team
546	performances by helping athletes become mote skilled and adaptable to
547	changing game environments through the application of contemporary
548	skill acquisition principles
549	
550	¢ SAS may assist the entire coaching staff in co-creating more effective
551	practice designs that maximize chances for learning to transfer from
552	practice to game day
553	
554	¢ SAS may help players to reach their personal career goals, through
555	hitting skill development and execution targets, by guiding them in
556	finding their own authentic ways of solving complex, position-specific
557	problems
558	
559	¢ SAS could help provide opportunities to build bridges across various
560	departments within a football Organization due to their holistic
561	perspective on athlete development and performance, leading to shared
562	development and coaching principles across the entire organization,
563	overcoming potential problems of departments working in isolation.
564	
565	To move further into the real-world application of SAS within football, we will
566	now provide a potential job summary and description that has been adopted from
567	the work of Otte et al., 2024 (which included two of the three co-authors of this
568	book), and modified to specifically address many of the previously highlighted
569	issues that exist across the current American football performance landscape.
570	
571	Title: Skill Acquisition Specialist (e.g., Skill Enhancement Specialist, Director of
572	Skill Acquisition or Enhancement)
573	
574	Summary: The SAS will be tesponsible for assessing and supporting the design
575	of football practice environments where learning, skill evolution, and on-field
576	performance are maximized. By understanding and applying contemporary skill
577	acquisition theory to coaching and training practices (ie., underpinned by an
578	ecological dynamics framework), SAS will partner with various organizational
579	departments to promote a transdisciplinary player development approach
580	throughout the entire football organization. An emphasis will be placed on the
581	SAS assisting in setting "alive movement problems" (see Chapter 5 for more) for
582	
583	33
584	===== p34 =====
585	players to solve in practice in an attempt to facilitate adaptable movement skills
586	that transfer across the situations and conditions present within the game (i.e.,
587	chasing the expression of dexterity for each player). Ultimately, the SAS will
588	spearhead an organizational strategy focused on the skill development and
589	enhancement of the team’s players. This will be achieved through the design of
590	learning environments that incorporate best practices in movement behavior and
591	skill acquisition.
592	
593	Desirable Qualifications and Expertise:
594	
595	1, A strong foundation in kinesiology and sport coaching with an interest or
596	specialty in motor control, skill acquisition, and sports pedagogy
597	
598	2. Proven experience designing learning and practice environments for, or
