Finally, distance refers to the separation between the transfer and criterion task in

terms of the physical and psychological demands. Near transfer of training
involves transfer and criterion tasks that are similar (or often nearly identical) in

terms of the perceptual-motor responses requited, while far transfer involves
transfer and criterion tasks that are relatively dissimilar. In our example, if

practicing the 20-yard shuttle improved your time on the 60-yard shuttle or
running through an agility ladder, that is evidence of near transfer (both tasks

involve avoiding stationary objects placed on the gtound), while if it improved a

Scere see ee
23
===== p24 =====
RB’s average yards per carry (which involves avoiding moving tacklers), that
would be evidence of far transfer.

Researchers have shown that while near transfert is almost always positive
and very large in magnitude, far transfer is much more elusive (Schmidt & Young,
1986). When the criterion task is highly similar to the transfer task (1e., near
transfer), a substantial improvement on the criterion task is observed. Football
decision-makers should take this into consideration when evaluating any new
training technology, equipment, program, or practice activity. The goal is to make
the player better on game day, not better at the training exercise. The reality is
that far transfer of training is much more difficult to produce, as research has
shown that it only occurs for criterion and transfer tasks that are highly similar in
terms of the perceptual-motor demands (see the concept of representativeness
discussed in chapters 2 and 5). This has been borne out in research examining
transfer of training in American football. There have been many studies
demonstrating near transfer of training of action capacity with football players.
For example, strength training (e.g., doing bench presses) improves performance
on the strength tests conducted in the gym (i.e., your 1 rep max for the bench
press). “Agility training” (e.g., practicing changing direction by running through
a course of cones) results in improved times on similar change of direction tests
(e.g., the shuttle tests). But critically, to our knowledge, there have been no
published studies that have demonstrated far transfer of training (1e.,
improvements in performance in the game) for any of these types of training.

Task decomposition and prescriptive instruction are not required to develop “the fundamentals”

As discussed above, a long-held belief in American football (and most other
sports) is that, before an athlete can be skillful in the game, it is necessary that the
basic fundamental skills (¢.g., catching, throwing, running) be mastered first.
Typically, this involves task decomposition (pulling the fundamentals out of the
game) and prescriptive coaching (the coach giving the athlete the ideal solution
through direct instruction and corrective feedback). There is a growing body of
research in other sports providing evidence that is inconsistent with these ideas.
In a study published in 2023, Deuker et al. compared prescriptive
instruction of fundamental passing, shooting, and dribbling skills in soccer to a
constraints-led approach (CLA) that focused on playing small-sided games. In this
study, one group of young soccer players was trained following a traditional,
decontextualized approach (eg., learning to dribble around cones, learning to
pass through cones, and shooting to locations in an empty net). These players
were also given prescriptive instruction about the correct technique (e.g., “pass
on the inside of your foot”) and were given corrective feedback when they
deviated from this. A second group of players learned through playing small-sided
and conditioned games (SSCG). In a SSCG, the number of players and size of
the playing area are deliberately reduced to encourage particular actions (e.g,,
passing the ball). This typically also involves manipulating other task constraints
(e.g., the shape of the playing area, type of ball used) to encourage the player to

24 .

4

ol
===== p25 =====
explore the organization of different movement solutions (note: constraints and
the CLA will be further unpacked in Chapter 5). In the Deuker et al. study,
constraint manipulations included the instructions given to the players (eg.,
“maintain possession” or “play over the defense”), rules (points for scoring or
keeping the ball), the number of players, and the size of the playing area. Before
and after training, players wete given out-of-context tests of dribbling, passing,
and shooting ability on a simple course of cones (analogous to combine tests in
American football).

What was found? Both groups showed similar (and not statistically
different) improvements from pre- to post-training on all the tests. So, in other
words, the CLA group learned these basic skills without having them pulled out
of the game and trained separately. Furthermore, when the authors looked at the
practice data in more detail, they found that the traditional group had a total of
777 touches of the ball, while generating these performance gains while the CLA
group had only 354 touches. So, playing in the small-sided games was more
efficient (and likely more enjoyable!) way to learn the “fundamentals” as
compared to decontextualized, isolated practice. It took fewer repetitions (ie.,
touches) to produce the same overall results.

A similar result was found in another soccer study by Esposito and
colleagues (2024). In this study, 30 players were randomly assigned to either a
CLA group or a prescriptive training group. Before and after training, participants
completed the Loughborough Soccer Passing Test (LSPT). The test involves
players responding to verbal commands to pass the ball in a circuit of cones
within a grid. So, again, the study evaluated how well these two types of training
prepare athletes for a decomposed, out-of-context assessment of technical skill.
Again, there were no significant group differences in pre-post changes in
performance on the LSPT.

Finally, Lindsay et al. (2022) compared prescriptive, linear training with
a nonlinear (CLA) approach to coaching the power clean in weightlifting. Sixteen
novice weightlifters were randomly assigned to either a traditional or CLA
training condition, both of which lasted for four weeks. Both types of training
were designed to address a common flaw seen with novices—looping or
throwing the bar away from the body to get it up in the air. For the traditional
group, the training involved explicit instructions, repetitious practice, and
providing feedback to correct ettots to direct learners toward an ‘ideal’ technique.
This was decomposed into different phases for the action. For example,
instructions for the transition phase were, “When the bar gets just above the
knees, forcefully push the hips forward with a slight bend in the knees. Shift your
body weight onto the middle of the foot; keep your heels on the floor.”

Participants in the CLA group were given no instruction about their
lifting technique. Instead, task constraints were added. These included putting
chalk on the barbell and placing poles in front of the participants. The lifters were
then given the instructions to either “lift so the bar leaves a chalk mark on your
thighs” or “lift to not hit the poles.” As the reader can probably see here, these
constraints encourage the learner to find a movement solution where they keep

25
===== p26 =====
the bar close to their body the entire lift, without telling them exactly how to do
it. The main dependent variable was the forward displacement of the bar during
the lifts. What was found? Both types of training were equally successful at
reducing the forward displacement of the bar, as there were no significant group
differences. The key point here is, again, that in the absence of prescriptive
instructions, well-designed constraints can serve to guide a learner to find “the
fundamentals” and move away from flawed movement solutions on their own.
Along with these studies comparing different training methods, a meta-
analysis of the effects of variability of practice on motor learning has revealed that
there is no evidence to support the idea that novice (and younger athletes) acquire
a skill more effectively with blocked practice (i.e., when one skill is repeated over
and over in a decontextualized practice) as compared to when they practice with

random practice (¢.g., switching between multiple skills in a game setting like a
SSCG)(Ammar et al., 2023).

Problems with a coach-centtic, prescriptive instruction approach

Along with it not being necessary to teach “the fundamentals” of a skill, research
has identified a few other important limitations of adopting a “coach as
instructor’, prescriptive approach to coaching.

7. Prescriptive coaching can encourage an internal focus of attention

As first proposed by Gaby Wulf and colleagues in 1998, there are two broad
categories that can be used to describe the types of instructions used by coaches
to direct an athlete’s attention during the execution of a sports skill. An infernal
focus of attention instruction directs a performer's attention inwards to the
movement or position of their body (e.g., the position of their hands, amount of
flexion in their knee), while an external focus of attention instruction directs it
outwards towards the effect one’s movement has on the environment (¢.g., the
direction the ball goes when it leaves a QB’s hand) or something else in the
external environment, such as the position of the safety (S). From the first study
in 1998 until 2021, there had been a total of 73 studies with 1,824 participants
that demonstrated superior performance for external focus of attention
instructions and 40 studies with 1,274 participants that have shown better motor
learning (Chua et al., 2021), Furthermore, it has been shown that the benefits of
adopting an external focus are both “sticky” (you still see them in retention tests
24 hours after training) and transferable (they result in better performance for
tasks in which the participant was not trained),
Not surprisingly, when a coach is telling you to “bend your knees more,”
“hit the ball with the inside of your foot,” or “snap your wrist when you throw”
(.e., they are using prescriptive coaching), this is highly likely to induce an internal
focus (on the knees, foot, or wrist) in the athlete. As a specific example, Porter
and colleagues compared the effect of different types of attention instruction on
agility performance (2010). In this study, participants were required to run

1

26
===== p27 =====
through an “L”-shaped cone course as quickly as possible. In one condition, they
were given internal focus of attention instructions. Specifically, they were told to
“focus on moving your legs as rapidly as possible” and “focus on planting your
foot as firmly as possible.” In a separate condition, they were given external focus
of attention instructions such as, “Focus on running toward the cone as rapidly
as possible” and “focus on pushing off the ground as forcefully as possible.” Note
the subtle change from focusing on the body (e.g., legs and foot) to focusing on
the external environment (e.g., cone and ground). It was found that, on average,
participants completed the course 350ms faster when given the external focus of
attention instructions. In follow-up questions, it was found that when instructions
referred to their body, participants adopted an internal focus on 76% of the trials,

while when they referred to the external environment, this type of focus occurred
for only 2% of the trials.

2. Prescriptive coaching can lead to less adaptable and less creative athletes

Research has shown that prescriptive coaching can lead to athletes that are less
adaptable, that is, less able to find effective movement solutions in response to
changing constraints. As an example, Lee and colleagues (2014) compared two
types of instruction for coaching the forehand stroke in youth tennis players. The
traditionally coached group was given instructions that prescribed the one correct
technique. One of the instructions given to players in this group was “move the
racquet low to high by turning the shoulders to the side and contacting the ball
in front of the forward foot.” The other group was given an analogy-based
instruction: “hit the ball like the shape of a rainbow.” In the traditional group, the
coach prescribes a movement solution to the athlete by making specific reference
to your body movements and positions (i.e., a specific technique)—“turn your
shoulders” and “in front of your forward foot.” In the analogy group, the coach
is guiding the athlete to find a more authentic solution that has the key
characteristics they are looking for without telling the athlete the specifics of how
that is to be achieved (i.e., the technique in terms of the specific body movements
and positions). Instead, the coach is trying to encourage the athlete’s movement
solution to have a certain form by appealing to an analogy—a metaphor for the
pattern of movement that does not explicitly refer to its specifics. When I tell you
to move “like a rainbow,” the key feature that comes to mind for most people is
an arch in the path. Instead of trying to give you the exact solution to the problem,
we are using an analogy to convey its key features.

Was there any difference between these two groups after six weeks of
training? Using a technique called principal components analysis, the authors
were able to group participants into clusters based on their movements. For
example, some participants used more shoulder motion, while others used more
wrist movement. Before the training, both groups showed four clusters, or, in
other words, they used four different movement solutions for executing a
forehand, After training, the group that was given traditional prescriptive
instructions, not surprisingly, became more homogenous—they now exhibited

27
===== p28 =====
only three different clusters of solutions. The analogy group showed the opposite
result—after training, they exhibited eight clusters. Having more available
movement solutions can be better because it gives more potential for greater
adaptability—the player can still execute a successful forehand despite changes in
the contextual situation and conditions (e.g., the court surface, the height of the
bounce, the speed of the approaching ball, and their level of fatigue).

It has also been demonstrated in a couple of research studies that
prescriptive coaching can result in less creativity. For example, in a 2018 study by
Santos and colleagues, 40 soccer players were split into two training groups: one
involving traditional prescriptive training and a differential /earning group. For the
latter group, random variations in the practice conditions were added, including
changes in the playing surface (e.g., turf vs. natural grass), the shape of the field
(e.g., rectangular vs. circular), and the type of ball (¢.g., a rugby ball vs. a soccer
ball). So, during practice, athletes in the differential learning group never
performed the same action twice in a tow—there were constant changes in
constraints. Creativity was assessed (in matches played before and after training)
using the Creative Behavior Assessment in Team Sports tool, which assesses both
the functionality (e.g., did the pass get to the intended receiver?) and originality
of actions (e.g., % of players that attempted that movement solution). This was
completed by two raters that were blind to what the players were assigned to in
training. What was found? Following five months of training, the prescriptive
coaching group produced actions that were rated as significantly less versatile,
original, and creative. A similar effect was found in a study by Orangi et al.
(2021b). After 12 weeks of training, a prescriptive coaching group (that was
instructed in the ideal techniques for shooting, passing, and dribbling) executed
three times fewer creative actions in a test match as compared to a CLA training

group (who were given no technical instruction and practiced in SSCG with
variability in the number of players, size of the playing area, and rules) . Examples
of creative actions included heel passes, bicycle kicks, and Ronaldo dribbles.

3. Prescriptive coaching can lead to a reduced sense of autonomy & lower intrinsic
motivation

One of the most popular, well-supported theories in sports science is related to
motivation. Specifically, Se/{Determination Theory (SDT), which is a meta-theory
combining a few different ideas, was first put together in a package by Deci &
Ryan in the mid-80s (2012). It proposes that an athlete’s level of intrinsic
motivation (actions driven by internal factors like a desite to succeed rather than
by external rewards like verbal praise and trophies) is driven by three basic human
needs: relatedness, competence, and autonomy. Relatedness concerns the need to
feel connected, involved, and supported and consequently experience satisfying
interpersonal relationships. Competence reflects a belief in one’s abilities and
capacity to control outcomes. Finally, avfonomy represents the desire to express
choice and not to feel controlled or compelled to do something. When these
needs are being met, we act with intrinsic motivation. Meaning, practicing can be

28
===== p29 =====
self-satisfying.

In a paper by Ian Renshaw and colleagues (2012), the authors describe
how ineffective prescriptive, repetition-based coaching is in supporting intrinsic
motivation. Think about the typical drill-based activity, like running around
cones, punching air, or hitting a ball off a tee. For most athletes, these drills can
be boring and monotonous. To get athletes to complete such activities, coaches
must provide several sources of external motivation. We might give our athletes
a pre-practice speech emphasizing the importance of “sacrifice and struggle” in
becoming skillful. During the activity, many coaches resort to yelling things like
“come on, get going” or “keep it up.” Finally, we use the promise of something
more rewarding (“after we finish these drills, we can scrimmage for a few minutes
at the end of practice”). Such coaching methods tend to make athletes externally
motivated. Meaning, the athletes complete the drills to not get yelled at or
punished (e.g., running laps) and receive praise (a “good job” or a high five) or
rewards. There is a lot of research showing the inferiority of external motivation
in comparison to intrinsic motivation and that using a coach-centered,

prescriptive instruction approach can decrease intrinsic motivation (Gillet et al.,
2010).

In 2004, Roger James proposed an interesting twist on the traditional
explanations for sports injuries. The “variability-overuse hypothesis” starts with
the same basic concept as most theories: Repeated application of load eventually
leads to tissue breakdown and injury. Meaning, don’t do it too much. But then it
adds a new twist: this breakdown will occur when there is not enough variability
in movement to allow for adaptation. So, the problem is not that you are not
doing it the one, correct way. In fact, trying to do that—trying to have a highly
consistent, repeatable movement—is likely to increase the chance of injury, not
decrease it. Why might this be the case? Think about making a tackle. If we
performed this movement the same way every time, we would stress the same
muscles, tissues, and bones (and the entire human movement system) in the same
way every time. Allowing for slight variations in the technique used, in terms of
direction, location, magnitude, and frequency of the muscle activity involved,
creates a broader distribution of stressors, which reduces the chance of injury.

To test this idea, Orangi and colleagues (2021a) examined whether
coaching methods that promoted variability helped to reduce risk factors for ACL
injuries in soccer players as compared to traditional, prescriptive coaching. Sixty-
six novice soccer players were split into three groups that trained for 12 weeks. A
traditional, prescriptive instruction group was trained using repetitive, corrective
practice designed to promote the “correct” techniques for shooting and passing.
So, in other words, the coach was trying to minimize the variability in skill
execution. A CLA group was encouraged to explore movement solutions using
constraint manipulations, including the use of small-sided and conditioned
games. Finally, a differential learning group practiced with random perturbations

29
===== p30 =====
to the practice conditions, including things like which side of the foot they had

be risk factors for ACL injuries in previous research (including things like trunk,

the positive direction (and by significantly more than for the traditional training
group). For example, from pre- to post-training, the knee flexion angle increased
and the magnitude of ground reaction force decreased. These results support the
idea that adding variability and exploration to practice serves to reduce the risk
factors for injury.

‘There are some important limitations that have been identified with the shared
mental models approach. First, the typical methods used to develop SMMs (.e.,
drawing a play on a whiteboard or watching video of a play) give the player a
third-person, bird’s-eye view of the action. Thus, the visual information is vastly
different from what is used in the game. The second, even more important issue,

usage of SMM requires that the coach anticipate all the possible variations in the
events that might happen. What happens if a defender falls down? Or the defense
sends a blitzer from an unusual position? Or you have your back to a defender
that is about to tackle you (¢.g., Saquon Barkley’s incredible reverse hurdle from
the 2024 season). Unless the coach has created an if X, then Y rule for these special
cases, team coordination wil] certainly fail. Simply put, using a SMM approach
results in limited adaptability to changing constraints.

Instead of team cognition being based on shared knowledge in the form
of stored representations and schema, coordination amongst teammates can be
more effectively achieved through shared attunement to perceptual information
(see Chapter 3 for further elaboration) (Silva et al., 2013). The distinction between
shared knowledge and shared attunement can be understood by considering an
example from football. Imagine a QB throws a long pass to a WR at the exact
moment the receiver on an option route chooses to go deep. How did both
players come to execute such coordinated actions without any explicit
communication (about which option would be chosen) beforehand? In the shared
knowledge account, this type of coordination occurs because both players have a
stored schema for the “deep pass play,” and both decide to execute this action
after processing the available perceptual cues (i.¢., the relative positions of the
players). This may also involve an intermediate step of identifying the defensive
strategy that is being played by the opponent (e.g., a cover 3 defense). In this
account, the perceptual cues are non-informative in and of themselves—instead
they have come to be associated with this particular action or play through

30

psd enieetinisnR rine Rieadsicimadedin ns
===== p31 =====
extensive practice and/or a coach’s instruction (e.g., being told that when the
defenders do X, you should do Y). Thus, the keys to team coordination in this
account are that (1) both players have stored a similar set of schema (1.e., they
learned the same set of plays) and (2) these schema are associated with the same
perceptual cues for each player.

The primary distinction with the shared attunement account comes at
the level of the players’ perception. Instead of detecting non-informative
perceptual cues that must be processed and associated with stored knowledge so
that a decision about which action to execute can be reached, the ecological
approach argues that perception involves the pick-up of information sources that
directly specify opportunities for action. For example, in the example described
above, the two teammates might detect a higher-order perceptual variable we
might call Tau Diff, which gives the difference between the time of arrival of the
receiver at the pass landing point and the time of arrival of the DB at the same
location. Tau Diff is visually specified by the ratio of the gap between each player

informative because it directly specifies whether there is an opportunity for along

attuned to Tau Diff and thus would simultaneously detect when the environment
affords the opportunity for a lob pass.

abundance of isolated and decontextualized drills performed by rote repetition —

# Action Capacity Is Not Skill

**What it is** — A player's raw action capacities (40-yard dash time, bench-press reps, vertical jump, max throw distance) are *individual constraints*, not skill. Skill is the ability to adapt movement to the information available in the moment. Treating a capacity score as a skill score conflates two different things, and the football industry does it constantly: the NFL Combine is built on the assumption that capacity predicts performance.

**Why it works** — Capacity only widens the set of actions a player *could* take. To convert that into skill, the player must still pick up perceptual information that specifies the relevant action, use it to control the movement in a way that accounts for their own effectivities, and choose among the opportunities actually available. A running back with more raw speed has more affordances open to them — they can string a run wider than a slower player — but they still have to perceive the closing gap and act on it. Speed is potential; skill is realisation.

**When to apply** — Interpreting any isolated physical test. Pushing back on "our fastest guy should be our best back." Explaining why a combine standout underdelivers, or why an unimpressive tester dominates. Framing what a testing battery *can* legitimately tell you (has capacity changed?) versus what it cannot (has skill changed?).

**When NOT to apply** — This is not an argument that capacity is irrelevant. Capacity is a real constraint and expanding it genuinely expands the affordance set; a player who cannot generate force has fewer options available. The claim is narrower: capacity is necessary but not sufficient, and it is a poor *predictor* used alone. Nor does it mean stop testing — capacity tests remain valid for tracking capacity, monitoring load, and screening return-to-play readiness. See [[claim--combine-scores-do-not-predict-nfl-performance]] for the evidence, and [[principle--far-transfer-is-rare]] for why training capacity alone rarely moves game performance.

**Example** — Two running backs run the same 10-yard dash. One consistently finds the crease because they are attuned to how fast the gap between two defenders is closing; the other runs into contact. Identical capacity, different skill. Nothing in the dash distinguishes them.

# NFL Combine Scores Do Not Predict NFL Performance

**What it is** — The empirical case against combine testing as talent identification. Kuzmits & Adams (2008) correlated combine results (10/20/40-yard dash, 20- and 60-yard shuttle, 3-cone, bench-press reps, vertical jump, broad jump) against first-three-year NFL game statistics. For quarterbacks and wide receivers there were **no significant correlations with any game statistic**. For running backs, faster 10/20/40 times correlated with more yards per carry in years one and two — and nothing else reached significance. Rishis et al. (2023) systematically reviewed 12 studies on the question: many reported *a* significant correlation, but **no consistent pattern across studies** — different measures mattered in each, the signature of Type I error from repeated testing rather than a real effect.

**Why it works** — Because skill is not capacity ([[principle--action-capacity-is-not-skill]]). A combine test removes the information a player actually uses to perform: no defenders, no closing gaps, no teammates, no game. It measures what the body can do in a vacuum, and games are not played in a vacuum.

**When to apply** — Any conversation where test scores are being used to project performance, rank players, or justify a training programme. Especially useful with an evidence-oriented audience: this is a clean, citable, negative result from the sport's own flagship testing event.

**When NOT to apply** — This is about *prediction of game performance*, not about whether combine testing has any use at all. Capacity data still informs training prescription, injury-risk screening and return-to-play decisions. Note also the RB finding is real — speed does relate to yards per carry for that position — so "the combine predicts nothing" overstates it. The honest claim is that the relationships are weak, inconsistent, and position-dependent. Finally, this is correlational work on players already selected into the NFL, so range restriction likely attenuates the true relationships.

**Example** — Tom Brady's combine is the folk version of this finding; Vernon Gholston is the mirror image. The systematic review is what turns two anecdotes into an argument a general manager cannot dismiss.

# Near Transfer Is Cheap, Far Transfer Is Rare

**What it is** — Transfer of training is graded by *distance*: how similar the trained task is to the criterion task in perceptual and motor demands. **Near transfer** (20-yard shuttle → 60-yard shuttle, both avoiding stationary objects on the ground) is almost always positive and large. **Far transfer** (20-yard shuttle → yards per carry, which requires avoiding *moving* tacklers) is much harder to produce and, per Schmidt & Young (1986) and the subsequent literature, occurs only when the two tasks are highly similar in their perceptual-motor demands. Myszka, Yearby and Gray state that to their knowledge **no published study has demonstrated far transfer of action-capacity training to in-game American football performance.**

**Why it works** — What gets trained is the whole perception-action coupling, not an abstract "ability" that can be redeployed anywhere. Cone work trains reading stationary objects with self-paced timing; a defender is neither stationary nor self-paced. The information sources differ, so the control law learned in one does not govern the other.

**When to apply** — Evaluating any new drill, device, technology, or programme. The question to ask is not "did they get better at this?" but "does this share perceptual-motor demands with the game?" It is the single most useful filter for a purchasing decision or a practice-plan audit. **The goal is to make the player better on game day, not better at the training exercise.**

**When NOT to apply** — Near transfer is not worthless. When the criterion genuinely *is* the isolated capacity — rehabilitating a specific tissue, restoring a range of motion, rebuilding force production after surgery — near transfer is exactly what you want, and demanding game transfer from a mid-rehab exercise is a category error. The rule bites when an isolated activity is *justified* by a claimed game benefit it has never been shown to produce.

**Example** — A team buys a reactive-lights agility system. Athletes' times on the system improve markedly over eight weeks. That is near transfer and was never in doubt. Whether missed-tackle rate changed is the far-transfer question, and it is the only one that matters for the purchase.

# Near Transfer Is Cheap, Far Transfer Is Rare

**What it is** — Transfer of training is graded by *distance*: how similar the trained task is to the criterion task in perceptual and motor demands. **Near transfer** (20-yard shuttle → 60-yard shuttle, both avoiding stationary objects on the ground) is almost always positive and large. **Far transfer** (20-yard shuttle → yards per carry, which requires avoiding *moving* tacklers) is much harder to produce and, per Schmidt & Young (1986) and the subsequent literature, occurs only when the two tasks are highly similar in their perceptual-motor demands. Myszka, Yearby and Gray state that to their knowledge **no published study has demonstrated far transfer of action-capacity training to in-game American football performance.**

Cone work trains reading stationary objects with self-paced timing; a defender is neither stationary nor self-paced. The information sources differ, so the control law learned in one does not govern the other.

**When to apply** — Evaluating any new drill, device, technology, or programme. The question to ask is not "did they get better at this?" but "does this share perceptual-motor demands with the game?" It is the single most useful filter for a purchasing decision or a practice-plan audit. **The goal is to make the player better on game day, not better at the training exercise.**

**When NOT to apply** — Near transfer is not worthless. When the criterion genuinely *is* the isolated capacity — rehabilitating a specific tissue, restoring a range of motion, rebuilding force production after surgery — near transfer is exactly what you want, and demanding game transfer from a mid-rehab exercise is a category error. The rule bites when an isolated activity is *justified* by a claimed game benefit it has never been shown to produce.

**Example** — A team buys a reactive-lights agility system. Athletes' times on the system improve markedly over eight weeks. That is near transfer and was never in doubt. Whether missed-tackle rate changed is the far-transfer question, and it is the only one that matters for the purchase.

# The Three Types of Task Decomposition

**What it is** — A diagnostic taxonomy for *how* a practice activity has been broken apart. Traditional practice decomposes skills for two reasons: to reduce cognitive load, and because you cannot always assemble a full team. It happens in three distinct ways:

1. **Perception-action decoupling** — severing the link between picking up information and acting on it. A back cutting around cones; a quarterback throwing through a tire; film-room progressions where the only "action" is saying what you would do; screen-based perceptual-cognitive tools where a complex field action is replaced by a tap.
2. **Part-task training** — dividing an action into movement *phases*. Two sub-types (Wickens et al., 2013): **segmentation** separates phases that occur in sequence (drilling the early and late cocking phases of a throw separately), **fractionation** separates phases that normally occur *simultaneously* (footwork drilled apart from throwing).
3. **Scaffolding** — breaking apart at the *task* level rather than the movement level, building sub-skill on sub-skill, each rehearsed to automaticity before the next is added. Teaching a youth tackle as: feet in front → head position → wrap → leg drive.

**Why it works** — As a *diagnostic*, naming the type tells you what has been removed and therefore what is missing. Decoupling removes information. Part-task removes the coordination between phases. Scaffolding reduces the problem space. Each has a different repair.

**When to apply** — Auditing a practice plan or a rehab progression. Ask of each activity: which of the three is this, and what did it strip out? It converts a vague unease ("this drill feels dead") into a specific, fixable diagnosis.

**When NOT to apply** — This is a taxonomy, not a verdict. Decomposition is not automatically wrong — and note that *task simplification* (keeping the whole problem but making it easier) is a different move from decomposition and fares better in head-to-head research. Early rehab in particular may have no choice but to decompose while tissue tolerance is the binding constraint. The framework's value is making the choice conscious and time-limited, not banning it. See [[claim--fundamentals-do-not-require-decomposition]].

**Example** — A return-to-play progression has a receiver catching balls from a machine at a fixed height and speed. Diagnosis: perception-action decoupling — the ball's flight no longer carries information about a thrower, and there is no defender to scale the catch against. The repair is not "stop catching," it is "restore one information source."

# "The Fundamentals" Do Not Require Decomposition or Prescription

**What it is** — The belief that basic skills must be isolated and explicitly taught before a player can use them in the game is not supported by head-to-head evidence. Three studies, cited by Myszka, Yearby and Gray:

- **Deuker et al. (2023), soccer.** Traditional decontextualised practice (dribbling around cones, passing through cones, shooting into an empty net, with prescriptive technical instruction and corrective feedback) versus a constraints-led approach using small-sided and conditioned games. Both groups were tested *on the out-of-context cone tests* — the traditional group's home ground. **No significant difference in improvement.** More striking: the traditional group took **777 ball touches** to produce those gains, the CLA group **354**. Roughly half the repetitions for the same result.
- **Esposito et al. (2024), soccer.** 30 players randomised to CLA or prescriptive training, assessed on the Loughborough Soccer Passing Test — again a decomposed, out-of-context technical test. **No significant group difference.**
- **Lindsay et al. (2022), weightlifting.** Novices learning the power clean, targeting the common fault of looping the bar away from the body. Traditional group: explicit phase-by-phase instruction and corrective feedback. CLA group: **no technique instruction at all** — chalk on the bar ("lift so the bar leaves a chalk mark on your thighs") and poles in front ("lift so you don't hit the poles"). **Both equally reduced forward bar displacement.**

Ammar et al. (2023) add a meta-analysis finding no evidence that novices or younger athletes acquire skills more effectively through blocked, decontextualised practice than through random practice in a game setting.

**Why it works** — A well-chosen constraint makes the desired solution the easiest one to find, without anyone naming it. The chalk and the poles do not describe a bar path; they make a bad bar path fail. The learner still solves the problem, so the solution is theirs and it is coupled to information from the start.

**When to apply** — This is the argument to bring when someone says "they have to master the basics first." It is strong precisely because the CLA groups were tested on the traditionalists' own decontextualised tests and still matched them — while accumulating fewer repetitions.

**When NOT to apply** — These are soccer and weightlifting studies with small samples and short interventions, not American football, and not injured athletes. Do not present them as proof that football fundamentals never need isolation. The defensible claim is the negative one: **there is no evidence that isolation is *required*.** That is enough to shift the burden of proof onto the person demanding it. Also note the Lindsay constraints were carefully designed — "no instruction" only works when the constraint does the teaching.

**Example** — A physician asks why a returning receiver is running routes against a defender instead of drilling hand position. The answer is not preference: matched-group studies show the isolated route produces no better technical outcome, and takes twice the volume to get there — volume being exactly what a healing tissue cannot spend.

# External Focus of Attention Beats Internal

**What it is** — Coaching cues fall into two categories (Wulf et al., 1998). An **internal focus** cue directs attention inward, to the movement or position of the body: "bend your knees more," "snap your wrist," "hit it with the inside of your foot." An **external focus** cue directs attention outward, to the effect the movement has on the environment or to something in it: where the ball goes, the position of the safety, the ground being pushed away. From 1998 to 2021 the literature accumulated **73 studies (1,824 participants) showing superior *performance* under external focus, and 40 studies (1,274 participants) showing better *learning*** (Chua et al., 2021). The benefits are durable — still present in retention tests 24 hours later — and they transfer to untrained tasks.

**Why it works** — Attending to your own body interferes with the self-organising control that produces the movement; attending to the outcome lets it organise itself around the goal. Porter et al. (2010) is the clean demonstration: participants ran an L-shaped cone course. Internal instructions ("focus on moving your legs as rapidly as possible", "plant your foot as firmly as possible") versus external ("focus on running toward the cone as rapidly as possible", "push off the ground as forcefully as possible"). Same task, near-identical wording — **350 ms faster under external focus.** Post-trial questioning confirmed the mechanism: body-referring instructions produced an internal focus on 76% of trials; environment-referring instructions, on 2%.

**When to apply** — Every cue, every session. It is the cheapest available upgrade to coaching practice: no equipment, no schedule change, only different words. It is also the easiest first change to sell to a sceptical coach, because it does not ask them to give up any drill.

**When NOT to apply** — Genuine exceptions exist. Where the body position *is* the outcome — a judged sport, or a clinician cueing a movement away from a healing tissue — an internal reference may be unavoidable, and rehabilitation legitimately uses internal cues to protect structures. The effect is also a group average and somewhat smaller in highly skilled performers. And note this is about *focus*, not about whether to cue at all: an external cue is still prescriptive if it names the one acceptable solution.

**Example** — "Keep your knees over your toes when you cut" versus "drive the ground away from the cone." Same intent, and the second is both faster in the moment and better retained. Rewriting a cue sheet along this line costs nothing and changes every rep that follows.

# Prescriptive Coaching Narrows a Player's Solution Set

**What it is** — Telling athletes the one correct technique measurably reduces the number of movement solutions they can produce, and the creativity of what they do in competition.

- **Lee et al. (2014), youth tennis forehand, six weeks.** Prescriptive group: "move the racquet low to high by turning the shoulders to the side and contacting the ball in front of the forward foot." Analogy group: **"hit the ball like the shape of a rainbow."** Principal components analysis clustered players by how they actually moved. Both groups began with **four** solution clusters. After training, the prescriptive group had **three**; the analogy group had **eight**.
- **Santos et al. (2018), soccer, five months.** Prescriptive training versus differential learning (constant random variation in surface, field shape, ball type — never the same action twice in a row). Creativity was rated in real matches, before and after, by two blinded raters using the Creative Behavior Assessment in Team Sports. The prescriptive group's actions were rated **significantly less versatile, original and creative.**
- **Orangi et al. (2021b), soccer, 12 weeks.** A prescriptive group instructed in ideal shooting, passing and dribbling technique produced **three times fewer creative actions** in a test match than a CLA group that received no technical instruction and practised in small-sided games with varied player numbers, area and rules.

**Why it works** — Prescription rewards convergence on one solution. Convergence is exactly what you do *not* want when conditions change, because a single solution has a single set of conditions in which it works. A larger solution set means the player can still succeed when the surface, the bounce, the closing speed, or their own fatigue is different from practice.

**When to apply** — When someone treats movement consistency as self-evidently good. It reframes the goal from *repeatability* to *adaptability*, and it gives a mechanism for why the technically tidiest player in practice is not always the one who makes the play.

**When NOT to apply** — More solutions is not unconditionally better. The Lee analogy group was still *guided* — "like a rainbow" conveys the key feature (an arched path) without specifying the body. That is not an absence of coaching, it is different coaching, and the distinction matters: unguided variability is not the finding here. Also, all three studies are soccer and tennis with modest samples, and creativity ratings carry some subjectivity even when blinded. Where a specific movement must be avoided for tissue safety, deliberately constraining the solution set is correct.

**Example** — Instead of "turn your shoulders and contact the ball in front of your forward foot," an analogy or a task constraint that makes the arched path the easy answer. The player arrives somewhere similar, and keeps seven other ways of getting there.

# The Variability-Overuse Hypothesis: Repeatability Can Cause Injury

**What it is** — James (2004) reframed overuse injury. The usual account stops at "repeated load eventually breaks tissue down, so don't do it too much." The variability-overuse hypothesis adds the twist: breakdown occurs when **there is not enough variability in movement to allow adaptation**. The problem is not that the athlete is failing to do it the one correct way — *trying* to produce a highly consistent, repeatable movement is itself likely to **increase** injury risk.

**Why it works** — An identical movement loads identical tissue in an identical way, every repetition. Slight variation in the direction, location, magnitude and frequency of muscle activity spreads the stress across a broader distribution of structures, so no single structure accumulates the whole dose.

**Supporting evidence — Orangi et al. (2021a).** Sixty-six novice soccer players, 12 weeks, three groups: traditional prescriptive coaching (repetitive corrective practice toward "correct" shooting and passing technique — that is, deliberately *minimising* variability), a CLA group exploring solutions through constraint manipulation and small-sided games, and a differential-learning group practising with random perturbations (which foot surface, hand position, ball type). Injury risk was assessed with a full-speed run-and-cut-at-45° test under motion capture, measuring established ACL risk factors (trunk, hip and knee flexion angles, peak ground reaction force). **Both the CLA and differential-learning groups improved on all measures, and by significantly more than the traditional group** — knee flexion angle increased, peak ground reaction force decreased.

**When to apply** — This is the entry that answers the safety objection head-on, because it turns it around: the questioner assumes variability is the risk, and the mechanism says rigidity is. Use it when a clinician or coach argues that a returning athlete should be kept to one grooved, controlled pattern. Pair it with [[claim--prescriptive-coaching-narrows-adaptability]] — the same prescription that narrows the solution set is the one that concentrates the load.

**When NOT to apply** — Confidence is **supported**, not proven, and the gap matters. Orangi measured **surrogate risk factors in a cutting test, not injury incidence** — no one has shown that CLA training reduces actual ACL tears. The participants were novice soccer players, not injured athletes returning to American football. Most importantly: this is not licence for unconstrained variability inside a rehabilitation window. Tissue tolerance is a real constraint, and the argument is for varying *within* what the tissue can accept — changing the nuanced parameters of a movement problem without changing its global nature — not for ignoring the limit. Anyone using this to justify uncontrolled exposure has inverted it.

**Example** — A back returning from hamstring injury is drilled through the same cut, at the same angle, on the same surface, a hundred times, because it is "the safe one." Every repetition deposits load in the same place, and none of it prepares them for the angle they will actually face. Varying entry speed, cut angle and surface — inside the tolerated range — distributes the stress and widens what they are ready for.

The problem is not that the athlete is failing to do it the one correct way — *trying* to produce a highly consistent, repeatable movement is itself likely to **increase** injury risk.

**Why it works** — An identical movement loads identical tissue in an identical way, every repetition. Slight variation in the direction, location, magnitude and frequency of muscle activity spreads the stress across a broader distribution of structures, so no single structure accumulates the whole dose.

**Supporting evidence — Orangi et al. (2021a).** Sixty-six novice soccer players, 12 weeks, three groups: traditional prescriptive coaching (repetitive corrective practice toward "correct" shooting and passing technique — that is, deliberately *minimising* variability), a CLA group exploring solutions through constraint manipulation and small-sided games, and a differential-learning group practising with random perturbations (which foot surface, hand position, ball type). Injury risk was assessed with a full-speed run-and-cut-at-45° test under motion capture, measuring established ACL risk factors (trunk, hip and knee flexion angles, peak ground reaction force). **Both the CLA and differential-learning groups improved on all measures, and by significantly more than the traditional group** — knee flexion angle increased, peak ground reaction force decreased.

**When to apply** — This is the entry that answers the safety objection head-on, because it turns it around: the questioner assumes variability is the risk, and the mechanism says rigidity is. Use it when a clinician or coach argues that a returning athlete should be kept to one grooved, controlled pattern. Pair it with [[claim--prescriptive-coaching-narrows-adaptability]] — the same prescription that narrows the solution set is the one that concentrates the load.

**When NOT to apply** — Confidence is **supported**, not proven, and the gap matters. Orangi measured **surrogate risk factors in a cutting test, not injury incidence** — no one has shown that CLA training reduces actual ACL tears. The participants were novice soccer players, not injured athletes returning to American football. Most importantly: this is not licence for unconstrained variability inside a rehabilitation window. Tissue tolerance is a real constraint, and the argument is for varying *within* what the tissue can accept — changing the nuanced parameters of a movement problem without changing its global nature — not for ignoring the limit. Anyone using this to justify uncontrolled exposure has inverted it.

**Example** — A back returning from hamstring injury is drilled through the same cut, at the same angle, on the same surface, a hundred times, because it is "the safe one." Every repetition deposits load in the same place, and none of it prepares them for the angle they will actually face. Varying entry speed, cut angle and surface — inside the tolerated range — distributes the stress and widens what they are ready for.

# Prescriptive, Drill-Based Practice Undercuts Intrinsic Motivation

**What it is** — Self-Determination Theory (Deci & Ryan) holds that intrinsic motivation — acting from an internal drive rather than for external reward — rests on three needs: **relatedness** (feeling connected and supported), **competence** (believing in one's capacity to affect outcomes), and **autonomy** (experiencing choice, not compulsion). Renshaw et al. (2012) argue that prescriptive, repetition-based coaching supports none of them well, and autonomy least of all: the coach holds the solution, transmission runs one way, and the player has no say in how or what they are taught.

**Why it works** — The tell is in what coaches have to add to make drill work happen. Running cones, punching air, hitting off a tee are monotonous, so motivation gets imported from outside: a speech about sacrifice, "come on, keep it up" during, and a bargain afterwards ("finish these and we'll scrimmage"). Each of those is an external motivator, and the literature consistently finds external motivation inferior to intrinsic (Gillet et al., 2010). The scrimmage-as-reward bargain is self-indicting — it concedes that the part the players want is the part being rationed.

**When to apply** — Where adherence, effort quality, or engagement is the problem rather than knowledge. It is also the argument that lands with athletes and with staff who are unmoved by transfer arguments: the constraints-led session is not only better learning, it is the one people want to do. In rehabilitation, where a long solo block is the norm and drop-off is common, autonomy is a lever that costs nothing.

**When NOT to apply** — This is **supported**, not proven, as applied here: SDT itself is well-evidenced, but the specific claim that constraints-led practice raises intrinsic motivation more than drill practice rests largely on argument and the Renshaw analysis rather than on head-to-head trials in football. Do not lead with motivation when talking to a physician — tissue and risk are the currency there. And autonomy is not the absence of structure: giving a player unlimited choice is not the same as designing a task that affords real choices.

**Example** — Two returning athletes with the same restrictions. One works a fixed circuit alone with a rep count. The other is given a small-sided problem with a rule they can vary. Same load, same tissue exposure — but only one of them has any reason to show up early.

# Shared Attunement, Not Shared Mental Models

**What it is** — Two competing accounts of how teammates coordinate without speaking.

**Shared mental models (SMM)** — the traditional account (Filho & Tenenbaum, 2012; DeChurch et al., 2010). Each player stores an internal representation of the system: a 4-3 front, where everyone lines up, where they move once the play is called, and explicit if-X-then-Y rules for their own responsibility. When those representations match across the team, coordination follows. Perceptual cues are treated as **non-informative in themselves** — they matter only because practice or instruction has associated them with a stored response. This account is what justifies the film-room review, the whiteboard walkthrough, and the unopposed rep. It builds what Gibson (1966) called **knowledge *about***: conceptual, indirect, communicated in words and symbols, and scaled in units of physics ("when you are 10 yards from the receiver") rather than to the player's own body.

**Shared attunement** — the ecological account (Silva et al., 2013). Perception picks up information that **directly specifies opportunities for action**; no stored representation is consulted. Teammates coordinate because they are attuned to the *same* information. The worked example: a quarterback throws deep at the exact moment an option receiver breaks deep, with no prior communication. Both are attuned to a higher-order variable — call it **Tau Diff**, the difference between the receiver's and the defensive back's time-of-arrival at the landing point, visually specified by the ratio of each gap to its rate of closure. Tau Diff > 0 affords the pass; Tau Diff < 0 does not. Both players detect the same thing at the same moment, so they act together.

**Why it works** — SMM has two structural limits. First, whiteboards and film give a **third-person, bird's-eye view** — visual information nothing like what the player has on the field. Second, and more damaging, SMM requires the coach to have **anticipated every variation in advance**. What happens when a defender falls, a blitz comes from an unusual position, or a player has their back to a tackler? Without a pre-written if-X-then-Y rule, coordination fails. Attunement has no such requirement, because the information is available in the situation itself, including situations nobody planned for.

**When to apply** — Explaining why a team that knows the playbook cold still breaks down when something unscripted happens; justifying opposed reps over walkthroughs; designing practice so players face the *information* rather than memorising the *answer*.

**When NOT to apply** — Marked **supported**: shared attunement is a well-argued theoretical position with supporting work, not a settled empirical replacement for SMM, and Tau Diff is presented here as illustration rather than as a measured variable in football. Nor does it mean the playbook and film room are worthless — American football is unusually pre-scripted, and players genuinely must know assignments. The claim is that knowledge *about* cannot by itself produce coordination under novelty, not that it is useless.

**Example** — A team spends the week walking through a coverage. On Sunday the safety slips. No rule covers it. The pair who have actually practised reading closing gaps against live bodies adjust; the pair who have only rehearsed the diagram do not.

# The Skill Acquisition Specialist (SAS) Role

**What it is** — A proposed staff role, adapted by the authors from Otte et al. (2024), for someone who assesses and supports the design of practice environments rather than coaching a position. The summary line: the SAS is responsible for practice environments where learning, skill evolution and on-field performance are maximised, applying contemporary skill-acquisition theory (underpinned by ecological dynamics) and partnering across departments for a transdisciplinary player-development approach. The specific emphasis is on **setting "alive movement problems"** for players to solve, so that adaptable skills transfer to the situations actually present in the game.

Claimed organisational benefits: more skilled and adaptable players; co-created practice designs that maximise transfer; helping players hit development targets by finding **their own authentic solutions** to position-specific problems; and bridging departments that otherwise work in isolation, through a holistic view of development.

Desirable qualifications include a foundation in kinesiology and sport coaching with specialty in motor control, skill acquisition and sports pedagogy, plus proven experience designing practice environments for or alongside high-performance football players and coaches.

**Why it works** — It separates two things usually fused in one person. Position coaches hold sport-specific tactical knowledge; the SAS holds knowledge of how skill is acquired and how environments produce it. The authors are explicit that the roles are **not interchangeable** and that the SAS should not be framed as a threat to position coaches — the SAS brings development principles to life through practice design and communication, which is a different job from teaching a position.

**When to apply** — Making the organisational case for such a role, writing a job description, or positioning oneself for one. Also useful defensively: it names a distinct expertise, which is what stops "practice design" being absorbed as an unpaid extra duty.

**When NOT to apply** — Confidence is **untested**, and deliberately so. This is an advocacy position by authors with a direct interest — two of the three co-wrote the Otte et al. paper it is adapted from. Every benefit listed is a claim about what a SAS *may* do; none is an outcome measured in a football organisation. The authors themselves concede the role remains rare and that expecting every organisation to have one soon is unrealistic. Treat it as a well-argued job design, not as evidence that hiring one improves performance.

**Example** — A programme with no budget for a new headcount can still use the description as an audit: of the responsibilities listed, which are currently nobody's job? That gap is usually practice design itself.

===== p37 =====
CHAPTER 2

An Ecological Dynamics Framework to Performance &
Learning

Various conceptual propositions have been advanced to describe how athletes
organize (i.e., coordinate and control) their movements under the challenging
demands of competitive sporting environments (Anson et al., 2005). Traditional
models, rooted in cognitive and experimental psychology, are often utilized,
predominantly adopting an individual/organism-centered perspective by
emphasizing neural processes, including memories, intellectual knowledge, and
the “processing” of information through representations stored in the brain
(Anson et al., 2005; Araujo et al., 2019; Myszka et al., 2023b). However, in this
book, we are adopting an ecological dynamics framework that highlights the
importance of systems thinking and the ongoing relations between an individual
(.e., football player) AND the environment. With this focus on the individual
(player)-environment relationship, coaches and support staff are positioned to
better tell the movement problem-solving story of players within football (and all
other sports). By equally respecting both context (i.e., the problem) and content (i.e.,
the solution), a deeper understanding of the interactions that unfold on a football
field can be developed to determine how to better assist players in moving more

skillfully, ultimately shifting the football performance paradigm to one oriented
around movement behavior as a problem-solving activity.

Introducing an Ecological Dynamics Framework
Weitten by Keith Davids and Duarte Aratijo

The theory of ecological dynamics originated in 2006 when we brought together key
ideas from different areas of science (including ecology, psychology, human
movement science, nonlinear dynamics, and mathematics) to reimagine what skill
performance and skill acquisition might look like. Historically, in the decades
between the 1940s and the 1960s, the study of learning was dominated by the
theory of behaviorism in psychology. Behaviorists focus highly on the dominant
role of the environment, especially the relationship between information GS:
conceived as a stimulus trigger) and a specific response (R), leading learners to
build stronger S-R relationships with skill. Learning motor skills was considered
an issue of building better learning environments in which feedback from coaches
was limited to strengthening the ptobability of specific responses emerging in
performance and the principle of specificity of learning was dominant.

From around 1960 to the new millennium, behaviorist ideas on S-R
learning gave way to a view of skill learning, dominated by a selective intemal focus
on the study of the mind, brain, and central nervous system, operationalized as a
===== p38 =====
J

computer system. This ‘brain as computer’ analogy moved the field of Motor
learning away from the automaticity of a conditioned response in behaviorism,
The new computational metaphor changed how psychologists tried to
understand how stimulus information is received by sensory systems, sometimes
in poor or illusory condition, for example, through opponent deception anq
disguise in football. This new cognitive approach to skill learning proposed thar,
like a computer, information detected by the performer needed to be transformed
and elaborated upon by internal mental processes and stored programs, leading
to outputs in the form of movement skills. In the cognitive approach, feedback
from coaches is used to build better internal movement models.

In fact, in the 1960s to 1970s, there was a rigorous skill acquisition debate
between psychologists who argued for a completely ‘feedback-driven’ theory of
motor performance and learning and those in a camp who argued that becoming
skillful required performers to build better internal motor programs. Regardless,
the conclusion was that skilled athletes are those who were better attuned to the
information surrounding them in their performance envitonment—paying more
attention to relevant stimuli—and who had built more sophisticated motor
programs to contro] their movements ‘automatically,’ without needing to pay too
much attention to micro details.

The essential stages for processing information for movement were
proposed based on:

¢ input (in the form of detecting, through the senses, low-quality
information that needed elaboration and interpretation through internal
processes and memories)

¢ transformation (where the low-grade information was enriched by
internal mental processes such as memories, attention, and decision-
making)

¢ output (where movements were planned and organized with the help of
internal programs, sometimes called schema)

pathways

Figure 2.1 - Schematic of an information processing model of human performance,
showing the transformation of low-quality sensory input by mental processes to
ptoduce outputs.

Skill learning was considered to be dominated by the internal process of
‘writing’ better motor programs and schema, based on improving all three stages
of information processing with practice and experience. In contrast to the heavy

38
===== p39 =====
focus on environmental conditions for S-R bonds, the cognitive computational
approach emphasized internal workings of the brain and CNS during learning.

That was the status quo in the 1990s and into the early 2000s, when ideas
on ecological dynamics started to accelerate as we sought to reimagine skill
learning in a different way. In a nutshell, behaviorist theories were considered to
be too focused on building specific learning environments, and cognitive
psychology was too internally focused on the presence of internal motor

496	cognition), but there are also degrees of freedom befveen these as this LMS and the
497	MPSP becomes organized to fit in with (and relate to!) more relevant movement
498	problems. These underpinning processes will interdependently interact and
499	influence each other with tight, circular causality /o be one, cach guided by one

501	way!
502	
503	Thus, the process of becoming one with, whether captured in an
504	individualized moment in time of movement performance, or over the timescales
505	of learning, can only unfold through a player becoming more attuned, intentional,
506	and adaptable, as they attempt to coordinate a functional, behavioral fit (through
507	their MPSP) to each contextual, performance problem which contains different
508	opportunities and challenges every single time the athlete faces them. However,
509	how does that actually occur and, as importantly, how do we, as coaches, help to
510	facilitate it?
511	
512	Learning to solve football movement problems
513	
514	At its core, learning to more successfully execute a given task in any environment
515	over time will inherently involve problem-solving. Having the functional ability
516	to catch a ball in the chaos of traffic over the middle, beat an offensive tackle
517	around the edge to then pursue a quarterback (QB) moving within the pocket, or
518	leave a wannabe tackler grasping at air via a juke move, is no different. To support
519	===== p56 =====
520	p

522	coaches in designing learning environments that enable players to become Adlepy
523	movement problem solvers, we introduce two concepts embraced by ecologica|
524	dynamics: alive movement problems (Myszka ct al., 2023a; Parry et al., 2025; Yeatby
525	etal., 2022) and repetition without repetition (Bernstein, 1967). We brie fly discuss
526	each here before fully unpacking the utility of the ideas in the applied chapters
527	later in the book (see Chapter 5 and 6), Simply put, through the application of
528	both of these important practical concepts, an athlete will repeat she process of solving
529	problems by changing and adapting the nuances of the movement problem-solving
530	processes (i.e., degrees of freedom of perception, cognition, and action) and how
531	they fit together. It is here where an athlete may be harning to kearn to move (Adolph
532	& Hoch, 2019; Harlow, 1949) as they embark on a nonlinear, motor learning and
533	skill adaptation journey where they /earn to learn to problem solve with, and through,
534	the coordination of their movement.
535	
536	This type of direct earning (Jacobs & Michaels, 2007) that unfolds as a
537	player becomes more skillful over time can be harnessed by coaches and skill
538	acquisition specialists when they design practice and learning environments which
539	are set-up to assist players in developing a direct, functional relationship with their
540	competitive environment. Namely, by solving a diverse range of alive movement
