===== p45 =====
Simulate the key constraints of competitive performance in practice
designs—especially task constraints to channel athlete and team
performance.

e Adding information adds context to practice designs (by infusing variability
into practice contexts).

¢ — Criticisms of traditional skill learning theories in a nutshell:

e S-R bonding in behaviorist approaches is more concerned with the
consequences of training (e.g., reproducing pre-determined patterns of
planned movements), not with what has changed in the individual. The
‘intelligent athlete’ needs to self-regulate and show autonomy on the field
when good opponents create conditions of high uncertainty and
instability. Learning needs athletes to show emotional resilience and
awareness of information, to solve problems, and to make successful
decisions under pressure in cooperation with teammates.

e There is no such thing as ‘muscle memory,’ nor is this phrase a useful
analogy for what goes on during skill learning. The brain is not a
computer. Rather, the body is a highly complex, interconnected
biological system of which the brain has a role to play in forming
memories from interconnections between synapses and neurons. The
brain is simply one important part of the athlete’s deeply integrated
whole movement system. The athlete is, in turn, exquisitely
interconnected with the dynamic, ever-changing performance
environment. The athlete can never be understood, nor meaningfully
considered, without reference to the environment (and vice versa),
leading to the need for an integrated athlete-environment scale of
analysis for understanding skill acquisition.

Skill adaptation helps players to learn how to address the performance

context in a multitude of different ways by reorienting their posture and

body positioning, adapting their stance so that they are poised to move

in different directions and in different ways, as the game changes and
performance context solicits.

(Re)conceptualizing Movement Behavior as Problem-Solving

According to the Merriam-Webster Dictionary, the definition of problem-solving is
simply, “the Process or act of finding a solution to a problem.” Additionally, other
resources may mention the idea of complexity and/or difficulty as it pertains to
the challenges to be addressed within the solving of a problem. Across many
contexts, the use of the term problem-solving, and the contemplation around the
emergence of some sort of unit unfolding to act as a solution, often conjures up
an image of a process which is primatily cognitively-driven. One may initially
think of a mathematician, immersed in deep thought at a chalkboard, working
step-by-step in a linear fashion to find an answer to a puzzling equation. Similarly,
we may envision a group of decision-makers within a business or organization,
sitting around a table contemplating the next move to make after weighing out all

45
===== p46 =====
the available options and comparing them to one another. However, when we ate
investigating ovement solutions, especially in the real-world context of sport
domains like what unfolds on a football field, that which underpins the solution
process, as well as the product that is the solution, could be quite different from
what it would consist of in other domains.

Problems in the context of football

Certainly, like in a math or business example, the goal within the process of
solving a problem in football is oriented around carrying out a solution which
adequately resolves the most pertinent issue(s), facing the player (i.e., as the
solver), at that moment in time. Additionally, the emergence of the most effective
solution will be largely dependent on the unfolding, contextual situation.
However, the interacting problem-solution dynamics (1.e., reciprocally changing states
of organization) within the sport of football will differ significantly from that
which is usually studied, understood, or explained across those other contexts
that may be more cognitively-driven. Instead of relying on intellectual knowledge
or mental processes, players are required to interact with information relevant to
a constantly changing, /ighly alive problem, which will differ (subtly or
significantly) each time it is faced. At a certain level, no two movement problems
in football are ever truly the same and thus, no two movement solutions will truly
be the same either. Additionally, two vastly different movement solutions could
emerge to adequately resolve the issues or challenges present under the
constraints of what appear to be similar problems (at least on the surface while
one is zoomed out far enough).

The movement problem-solving process in football often takes place
under considerably different time constraints than the problems presented in
most other domains. A player rarely has the luxury of identifying, or selecting
from, a list of alternative options to employ in trying to solve any of the problems
they face. There simply isn’t the time, nor even the need, for a player to
thoroughly analyze a movement problem to find out its causes in order to solve
it, in the way one would in many other settings. Words from one of the most
skillful moving football players of all time, Barry Sanders, point to the essence of
this on-field experience. Sanders stated, “I tried to perfect the skill of trying to
make people miss. In a lot of plays where I am doing something impulsive, I had
to turn off the brain in certain ways and just, you know, react” (NFL, 2016). In
most contextual situations in football, problems are constantly changing
moment-to-moment, presenting various opportunities to solve them in authentic,
yet functional, fashions (Orth et al., 2017; Seifert et al., 2013). Thus, to navigate
the resolution of movement problems in the inherently complex and often
challenging environment of a football field, players will need to detect and use
highly specifying information to make decisions from and organize theif
movement actions in connection with (Button et al., 2020; Renshaw et al., 2019).

46
===== p47 =====
Skill according to an ecological dynamics framework

From an ecological dynamics perspective, Araujo and Davids (2011)
reconceptualize ski// acquisition as skill adaptation, ot “the emergence of an adaptive,
functional relationship between an organism and its environment” (p. 7). This
ties in nicely to how Seifert and colleagues (2013) defined expert performance as the
“ongoing co-adaptation of an individual’s behaviors to dynamically changing,
interacting constraints, individually perceived and encountered” (p. 167). Skillful
movement behavior then, when viewed through an ecologically-centered lens,
could be conceived of as the emergence of adaptive movement solutions of an
athlete, which are essentially dynamical products of the player-environment
interactions.

Though many associate the work of Nikolai Bernstein with ideas of
coordination from a motor system perspective (i.e., Bernstein’s degrees of freedom
problem), it’s clear Bernstein felt as though a more appropriate scale of analysis for
movement behavior in real world contexts (e.g., American football) should
extend beyond the motor system to look deeper into the relations and interactions
between systems—connecting movement problems with the movement
solutions coordinated to resolve them. For example, Bernstein’s idea of dexterity
(1996) could be that which captures an individual moving with the highest
expression of coordinated skill. As Bernstein conveyed (1996), “Dexterity is the
ability to find a motor solution for any external situation, that is, to adequately
solve any emerging motor problem” (p. 228).

The work of Bernstein flows seamlessly into that of another giant, James
J. Gibson, who began to shape the narrative around the tight coupling between
not only perception and action but also between a player and their environment
(i.e., signifying the ft between problem and solution). Gibson stated (2015), “The
words animal and environment make an inseparable pair. Each term implies the
other. No animal could exist without an environment surrounding it” (p. 4). In
this way, the two of them will have a constant, mutual and reciprocal relationship
with one another. This idea becomes highly analogous to players and their
movement problem-solving processes within football. Namely, football players
cannot organize a movement solution without first being presented with a
problem, Likewise, sport scientists shouldn’t analyze, or attempt to understand, a
player’s movement solutions in isolation, without paying equal respect to the
dispositional problem which the behavior is organized to meet the needs of.
Additionally, football coaches must begin to ask themselves questions about the
real nature of the problems they present to players in practice (in the form of
practice tasks, drills, and activities), and if they are truly sufficient to bring about
similar solutions (and related problem-solving processes for the mover) as one
would hope to emerge on game day. On these notes, it would be essential to ask,
just how does a player coordinate the proper relations of his movement system
with the problems present within a competitive performance environment?
Furthermore, what individual subsystems, and associated processes, may
underpin this movement problem-solving process?

47
===== p48 =====
ip

The integrated movement problem-solving process

To understand the phenomenon of skillful movement behavior in sport, Seifer
et al. (2013) offered that we should acknowledge that (a) it occurs at the ecologic,
scale of analysis (ie., studied through the ongoing, reciprocal relations between ,
player and their performance environment); (b) perception and action are viewed
as emerging from these interactions; and (c) it emphasizes the circular causality
of the relationship (pp. 168-169). As Gibson stated, “Every animal is, in some
degree at least, a perceiver and a behaver” (2015; p. 4). This means that anima
(e.g., football players!) are perceivers of the environment and behavers i the
environment. That all said, processes of perception and action can be considered
coupled, as perception is needed to adequately regulate our movement actions,
Furthermore, as we act, it allows us to pick up additional information about the
movement problems within the world, which will further serve to guide
subsequent actions in a tightly coupled fashion (Hristovski et al., 2009). As
Gibson famously captured (2015), “We must perceive in order to move, but we
must also move in order to perceive” (p. 213). At a certain level, the organization
of behavior is essentially the same as the interplay between perception and action
processes, where movement is always linked to information.

We must also acknowledge that emerging movement solutions in
football will always be goal-directed. Meaning, they are performed for the sake of
a specific result in the competitive performance environment (e.g., make a
defender miss in an attempt to pick up a first down) and thus cannot be
understood without reference to that functional (i.e. practical, useful) purpose
(Bootsma, 1998; Withagen & Michaels, 2005). Accounts of skillful movement
behavior in any sport must capture the direction of the athlete’s intentional goal(s)
while attempting to characterize how movement solutions are coordinated in
relation to the contextual problems of the environment. The current state of
affairs between the unfolding, interactive problem-solution dynamics can be
assessed by the player through the detection of information or the player’s
perception, which is a dynamic process involving one’s entire human movement
system, not just their senses (Hristovski et al., 2009; Teques et al., 2017). With
increased exposure, players may become more sensitive to (i.¢., perceptual
attunement) which informational variables they should attend to and when to

Chasing Dexterity: To Become One With The Problems

‘No natural phenomenon can be understood without carefully considering how it emerged"
(Bernstein, 1996, p. 45).

No matter the position, football movement problems that players encounter in
the game are highly variable and dynamic, containing numerous opportunities to

player will be different and unique (Bernstein, 1996), and an individualized
approach, investigating player-environment, problem-solution, and context-
content relations, needs to be taken to effectively assess, as well as enhance, the

confined within the movements or actions themselves but is revealed in how these
movements behave in their interaction with the environment, with its unexpectedness and
surprises” (Bernstein, 1996, p. 232).

In this section, we will address how players may learn to problem-solve
through their expressed movement skills more effectively, both in the moment
and over longer periods of time. Through an idea proposed by Jacobs and
Michaels (2007) known as direct learning (i.e., education of attention, education of
intention, and calibration) and a process of exploration, discovery, and

Qualities & Characteristics of Dexterous Movers

When players solve movement problems in the highly emergent fashions outlined
throughout this chapter, coaches and support practitioners may expect to witness
the expression of several signature movement properties (e.g., abundance,
variability, creativity, novelty, authenticity), sometimes viewed as undesirable in
more traditional approaches to football coaching. However, in an ecological
dynamics framework, these respective movement properties are not to be
discouraged, frowned upon, or avoided; instead, they should actually be pursued
as we may be able to recognize them as the key performance indicators of skillful
movement behaviors displayed by dexterous players (Seifert et al., 2013).

Acknowledging that all players (and all humans, actually) have their own
individual constraints, movement history, and form of life, football coaches may
be well served to avoid imposing their own idealized ways of perceiving,
cognizing, and acting upon the athlete (Myszka et al., 2023b). Instead, functional
problem-solving and skill optimization for a player may stem from coaches being
willing to lean into movement qualities like abundance and authenticity when
assisting players in the pursuit of their own personal style of movement skill.
Furthermore, our practice and learning environments should also obviously
reflect this goal (as will be discussed at length in later chapters),

Abundance & Degeneracy

Being that no two movement problems in sport are ever truly the same, and
competitive football environments can present a diverse range of problems to
athletes, we believe that players should have access to a wide range of potenual
movement strategies that can be flexibly adjusted to meet the needs of a peculiar
problem. In other words, degeneracy may precede dexterity (and abundance may precede
adaptability)(Myszka et al., 2023a). The notion of degeneracy, or “the ability of
elements that are structurally different to perform the same function or yield the
same output” (Edelman & Gally, 2001, p. 13763), is pertinent to the discussion
of athletes conceptualized as complex adaptive systems.

To be successful on the field, it is essential that players are not overly

degrees of freedom can provide the opportunity to transition to new, or a larger
variety of, patterns of movement behavior (Gray, 2021). Ultimately, increased
variability of the coordination and control of strategies in a movement system can

# Ecological Dynamics: The Athlete–Environment Scale of Analysis

**What it is** — A theoretical framework, assembled around 2006 by Keith Davids and Duarte Araújo from ecology, psychology, human movement science, nonlinear dynamics and mathematics. Its defining commitment: **the person and the environment are equally important, and neither can be understood without the other.** The unit of analysis is the relationship, not the athlete.

This section of the book is written by Davids and Araújo themselves, and they place it against two predecessors:

- **Behaviourism (1940s–60s)** — learning as strengthening stimulus–response bonds. Coach feedback exists to raise the probability of a specific response. Too focused on engineering the environment, indifferent to what changed inside the learner.
- **Cognitive / computational psychology (1960–2000)** — the brain as a computer. Low-quality sensory **input** is **transformed** and enriched by internal processes (memory, attention, decision-making) into **output** planned by internal programs or schema. Coach feedback exists to build better internal models. Too focused inside the head.

Ecological dynamics rejects the choice between them. The framework's roots run through Kugler & Turvey (1987), whose definition frames ecological science as the study of living systems, their environments, and **the reciprocity that has evolved between the two** — and through James Gibson, who studied how wartime pilots coupled action to information when landing aircraft.

**Why it works** — Two ideas do the work. **Emergence**: behaviour emerges from ongoing *transactions* — the athlete uses information to regulate action, and acts to pick up new information, in a continuous cycle. **Dynamics**: a systems orientation, where person and environment are each highly interconnected systems built of smaller systems, studied as they *change over time* rather than as successive static responses. Athletes are changing at several timescales at once — performing, developing, growing, ageing — and coaches should expect that.

**When to apply** — As the frame underneath everything else in this book. It is also the entry to reach for when someone asks *why* the constraints-led approach works: the CLA is not a bag of drills, it is what follows once you accept that skill lives in the athlete–environment relationship rather than inside the athlete.

**When NOT to apply** — Do not present this as the settled consensus of motor-learning science; the cognitive/representational tradition remains active and productive, and this framework is a live position within a genuine debate, argued here by two of its architects. Also resist the temptation to use "it's all emergent" as an excuse for unplanned practice — emergence is a claim about mechanism, not permission to stop designing.

**Example** — Asked why a player's technique looks worse in games, the cognitive answer looks for a faulty internal program. The ecological answer asks what information was present in practice that is absent in the game, or vice versa — and usually finds it.

# Newell's Model of Interacting Constraints

**What it is** — Karl Newell's (1986) model, the operational heart of the constraints-led approach. Coordination solutions **emerge** under three interacting classes of constraint:

- **Individual (organismic)** — the performer: height, limb length, strength, fatigue, injury status, movement history, intentions, emotional state.
- **Task** — the problem as set: the goal, the rules, the equipment, the space, the number of players, the time available.
- **Environmental** — the surrounding conditions: surface, weather, light, noise, social and cultural context.

**The word means the opposite of what it means in ordinary speech.** In everyday language a constraint is a restriction. In this science, **a constraint is a link — physical or informational — that facilitates, limits, or shapes how a system reorganises over time.** Constraints are not obstacles to be removed; they are the sources of information that shape what emerges. This is the most common point of confusion when the idea is introduced to coaches, and it is worth correcting explicitly every time.

**Why it works** — Because behaviour is emergent rather than prescribed, the practical lever is not the movement but the conditions under which the movement organises itself. A coach cannot install a solution; a coach can change a constraint and let a different solution become the easy one. That is why the CLA is a *design* discipline rather than an instruction discipline.

**When to apply** — Any time you want to change what a player does without telling them what to do. It is also the best available audit grid for an existing practice activity: name the individual, task, and environmental constraints currently in play, then ask which one you would move to make a different solution likely.

**When NOT to apply** — The three classes overlap and the boundaries are argued over — fatigue is an individual constraint that a task constraint produces; a rule is a task constraint that carries social meaning. Do not spend time policing the taxonomy; its value is as a checklist for *what you could change*, not as an ontology. And manipulating a constraint is not automatically good practice: a constraint that produces a solution which does not exist in the game has designed in the wrong thing. Pair with [[principle--representative-design]].

**Example** — A receiver keeps rounding off breaks. Rather than cueing hip position (prescription), narrow the space (task), add a defender at a fixed leverage (task), or run it on a wet surface (environmental) — and let a sharper break become the solution that works.

# Representative Design

**What it is** — How well a practice task reproduces the *relevant conditions* of the competitive environment it prepares for. The term comes from Egon Brunswik; the sporting insight comes from Gibson's wartime work on pilots, who used information from the environment to judge approach speed, direction, descent timing and position in airspace. If practice does not contain that information, it does not prepare the coupling that uses it.

The book gives three tests. A representative practice task should:

**(a)** include appropriate and pertinent **information sources** for players to use;
**(b)** allow players to **act** — move, adapt and think as they would in competition;
**(c)** set **goals and intentions the players can commit to** (defend with speed, exploit a specific area) rather than a set of general instructions and prescribed movements.

**Why it works** — Skill is a coupling between information and action ([[principle--perception-action-coupling]]). A coupling can only be learned against the information it couples to. Remove the defender and you remove the variable that regulates the cut; the player still learns something, but not the thing they need. This is also the mechanism underneath [[principle--far-transfer-is-rare]] — transfer occurs when perceptual-motor demands are shared, and representativeness is the name for sharing them.

**When to apply** — As the first question about any activity: *what information from the game is present here, and what has been removed?* It is the most useful single filter for auditing a practice plan, a rehab progression, or a piece of training technology. The three tests above turn a vague judgement into a checklist.

**When NOT to apply** — Representativeness is a **dimension, not a binary**, and maximising it is not always the goal. Early rehabilitation deliberately reduces representativeness because tissue tolerance is the binding constraint, and that is correct — the error is leaving it reduced once the tissue no longer requires it. Nor does representative mean *identical to the game*: a task can be simplified, slowed, or scaled and remain representative so long as the information that regulates the action survives. Full-scrimmage-or-nothing is a misreading.

**Example** — The authors' own pause-for-thought: picture a practice task in American football high in representative design, then one that lacks it, then ask how you would make the second more representative. A route run against air fails test (a); the same route against a defender at game leverage passes it, without needing eleven-on-eleven.

# Skill Adaptation, Not Skill Acquisition

**What it is** — A deliberate change of term. Araújo and Davids (2011) reconceptualise skill *acquisition* as **skill adaptation**: "the emergence of an adaptive, functional relationship between an organism and its environment." Seifert et al. (2013) define expert performance to match — "the ongoing co-adaptation of an individual's behaviors to dynamically changing, interacting constraints, individually perceived and encountered."

The word "acquisition" smuggles in a theory. It implies skill is a *thing* that gets stored inside the player — acquired, possessed, retrieved. On this account skill is not a possession at all; it is a **relationship**, and relationships are maintained rather than owned.

**Why it works** — If skill were acquired and stored, a player who had it would display it everywhere. They do not. Performance changes with surface, opponent, fatigue, score and stakes, because the relationship changes. Adaptation explains that; acquisition has to treat it as noise or as failure to retrieve.

**When to apply** — Whenever "he has it in practice but loses it in games" comes up. Under acquisition that is a mystery or a character flaw. Under adaptation it is expected: the practice relationship and the game relationship are different, and only the one you built is the one you have. It also reframes the coaching goal — from installing a skill to widening the range of conditions across which a functional relationship can be found.

**When NOT to apply** — This is a conceptual reframe, and it will sound like semantics to a sceptical audience if presented on its own. Lead with the practical consequence, not the vocabulary. Note too that the field's own literature, this book included, still uses "skill acquisition" as the name of the discipline and of the SAS role — the authors are not proposing the term be abolished, only that what it names be understood correctly.

**Example** — A back looks flawless in individual drills and hesitant in team period. The acquisition account says he has not yet automated it and needs more reps. The adaptation account says the drill relationship was never the game relationship, and more reps of the drill will widen the gap rather than close it.

# Perception and Action Are One Cycle, Not Two Stages

**What it is** — Perception and action are **coupled** and mutually causal. Perception regulates movement; movement generates new information that guides the next movement. Gibson's formulation: **"We must perceive in order to move, but we must also move in order to perceive."** And: "Every animal is, in some degree at least, a perceiver and a behaver." Seifert et al. (2013) name the property directly — the relationship shows **circular causality**.

This is the load-bearing claim under the whole framework. It is why perception-action decoupling ([[framework--three-types-of-task-decomposition]]) is the most damaging of the three decompositions: it does not make the task smaller, it breaks the loop the skill is made of.

**Why it works** — Because the information a player needs is not sitting still waiting to be read. A punt returner learns what the two pursuing defenders are committed to *by moving* — the angles and closing rates only become informative as his own path changes them. Standing still and "reading" is not a slower version of the same thing; it is a different, poorer information source.

Perception here is also not "the senses." It is the detection of information through interconnected sensory subsystems — visual, auditory, haptic — combining in varying degrees to give functional contact with the environment (Savelsbergh, 2010), and it involves the whole movement system rather than the eyes alone.

**When to apply** — Diagnosing any activity where the player is acting without the information that normally regulates the action, or receiving information they cannot act on. Cones, tires, bags, ball machines, film-room "what would you do", and screen-based perceptual-cognitive tools all sit on one side or the other of a broken loop. The repair is rarely "make it harder" — it is "restore an information source the player can act against."

**When NOT to apply** — Decoupling is sometimes unavoidable and occasionally correct: a tissue that cannot yet tolerate a live defender is a real constraint, and an early-rehab exercise is legitimately decoupled. The error is treating that as a *skill* exposure rather than a *tissue* exposure, and leaving it in place after the constraint lifts. Also, "coupled" is not a synonym for "chaotic" — a coupled task can be small, slow and simple.

**Example** — Two ways to work a returning back's cutting. A ladder: action with no information. A single defender at a fixed leverage, jogging: the loop is intact, the load is trivially controllable, and the cut is now regulated by something that exists on Saturday.

# Dexterity Is Fit to the Problem, Not Quality of the Movement

**What it is** — Bernstein's (1996) definition: **"Dexterity is the ability to find a motor solution for any external situation, that is, to adequately solve any emerging motor problem."** And, crucially for where it is measured: **"Dexterity is not confined within the movements or actions themselves but is revealed in how these movements behave in their interaction with the environment, with its unexpectedness and surprises."**

The evaluative image is the lock and key: **"A movement is correct when it perfectly fits a motor problem just as a key easily opens a lock."** Correctness is a property of the *fit*, not of the movement's shape.

**Why it works** — It relocates the judgement. A movement cannot be graded in isolation, because the same movement is excellent against one problem and useless against another. To assess a solution you must simultaneously assess the problem it was organised against — the book's repeated demand that context (the problem) and content (the solution) be given equal respect. It follows that dexterity will look **different in every player**, since each faces problems through their own individual constraints, movement history and form of life.

**When to apply** — Any time movement is being evaluated. It is the antidote to technical-model scoring: instead of "how close was that to the ideal pattern?", ask "did that solution fit the problem the player actually faced?" It also sets the standard for film analysis — you cannot grade the solution from a clip that does not show the problem.

# The Integrated Movement Solution and the Movement Problem-Solving Process

**What it is** — The authors' own model (Myszka et al., 2023b), and the conceptual centrepiece of the book. Perception, cognition and action are **not three separate processes** that hand off to one another. They are the constituent, interacting elements of **one** functional unit: an **Integrated Movement Solution (IMS)**, produced by a **Movement Problem-Solving Process (MPSP)**.

Each of the three carries its own **degrees of freedom**, extending Bernstein's degrees-of-freedom problem beyond the motor system:

- **Perceptual DOF** — information detected across interconnected sensory subsystems (visual, auditory, haptic), combining in varying degrees. Highest expressions: *attunement*, then *knowledge of the environment*.
- **Cognitive DOF** — thoughts, intentions, decisions and memories, operating in an **embodied and embedded** fashion. Highest expressions: *intentionality*, *resonance*, *decision-making*.
- **Action DOF** — how limb segments, joints and muscles are continuously reorganised to satisfy the interaction of constraints. Highest expressions: *adaptability*, *calibration*, *creativity*.

Newell (1996) supplies the joining idea: coordination is the function that constrains free variables into a **behavioural unit**. What a player coordinates is therefore not a motor response but a whole functional unit fitted to the problem — and there are degrees of freedom *between* the three levels, not only within each.

**Why it works** — It gives cognition a place without making it a controller. Intentions scaffold what is perceived and shape how action organises, so the brain matters — but as one interconnected part of a whole movement system, not as a computer issuing commands. It also explains why a change at one level propagates: alter *which* information a player picks up, or *when*, and the movement strategy and motor coordination change with it, through tight circular causality.

**When to apply** — As an analysis grid. When a solution fails, ask at which level it broke: did the player not detect the information (perceptual), not intend the right interaction (cognitive), or lack the coordination to execute (action)? Those three failures need three different interventions, and coaching defaults to the third. It also underwrites [[framework--direct-learning-attention-intention-calibration]], which supplies the tools for the first two.

**When NOT to apply** — Marked **supported**: this is the authors' own model, recently published and not yet independently validated, and the "highest levels of expressed skill" listed under each dimension are a synthesis of other people's constructs rather than a measured hierarchy. Treat it as a well-argued organising scheme, not as an established taxonomy. In practice the levels are also hard to separate cleanly — the model's own claim is that they are inseparable, which limits how confidently you can attribute a failure to one of them.

**Example** — A returning safety keeps arriving late. Action-level coaching adds change-of-direction work. The grid asks first whether he is late because he is reading the quarterback's shoulders instead of the release, which is a perceptual problem no amount of footwork will fix.

# Direct Learning: Education of Attention, Education of Intention, Calibration

**What it is** — Jacobs and Michaels' (2007) account of how learning proceeds without internal models, and the most directly usable coaching framework in the chapter. Three levers:

- **Education of attention** — coming to attend to *more useful informational variables*; becoming more sensitive to the information that most specifies the task goal. This is perceptual attunement.
- **Education of intention** — determining *which* informational variable needs detecting, given how the player is aiming to interact with this particular problem. Intention selects what is worth perceiving.
- **Calibration** — the proper scaling of the perceptual-motor system: establishing and updating the mapping between perception and action, so that what is perceived is scaled to what this body can actually do.

**Why it works** — It gives a coach something to do that is neither prescribing a technique nor saying nothing. The coach's job becomes **problem-setter and guide**: leading the player to detect more useful information specifying the relevant affordances, so that a well-fitted solution can emerge. The player still solves the problem, so the solution stays theirs.

**When to apply** — Writing cues. The book's own worked example: a skill player repeatedly gets tackled in space because they act indecisively or let the defender close.

- Educating **attention**: *"On these next reps, I want you to see what you can pick up from the defender's movement actions that could inform you of how, or when, you can or should move."*
- Educating **intention**: *"It's okay to move slower as long as you're using that time to better understand your relationship with the opponent. When you see an opportunity to make him miss, trust what you see and act."*

Neither names a movement. Both change what the player attends to and what they are trying to do. This is the practical difference between constraints-led coaching and simply withholding instruction.

**When NOT to apply** — Calibration is the lever that matters most after injury or a body change, and it is the one most often skipped: an athlete returning at different strength or with different confidence has a **mis-scaled** perception-action mapping, and will misjudge gaps they used to read correctly. Do not treat that as a decision-making fault. Conversely, attention cues assume the information is actually present in the task — cueing a player to read a defender who is not there is empty. Fix the design first ([[principle--representative-design]]), then cue.

**Example** — Rather than "plant and go," a returning back is asked what tells him the defender has committed. He answers with something specific — hips, or the outside foot. That answer *is* the education of attention, and it is now coachable.

# Repetition Without Repetition

**What it is** — Bernstein's (1967) formulation, and the single most portable idea in the book. Ordinary repetition means rehearsing and reproducing a *technique*. **Repetition without repetition means repeatedly solving the same performance problem, challenged differently each time.** What repeats is the problem; what varies is the solution.

The authors are explicit that repetition itself is not the enemy — "while repetition is an important feature of practice, repetition without repetition is even better." And it can be **turbocharged by adding variability**: running the same task at different fatigue levels, or changing the performance context in a way that meaningfully challenges the player.

**Why it works** — Because no two problems on a field are ever the same, so no two solutions will be either. Practising one movement prepares one problem. Practising the *process* of solving prepares the class of problems. The player is, in the authors' phrase, **learning to learn to move** (Adolph & Hoch, 2019; Harlow, 1949) — the degrees of freedom of perception, cognition and action are repeatedly reorganised into different configurations that fit.

**When to apply** — Redesigning any drill that currently runs the same rep twenty times. The conversion is usually small: keep the goal, vary one constraint per rep. It is also the easiest way to raise practice quality without adding volume, which makes it directly useful in rehabilitation, where volume is the scarce resource.

**When NOT to apply** — This is not "make everything different every time." Variability is instrumental — it exists to keep the problem alive, not for its own sake. If the varied element does not change what the player must perceive or decide, it adds noise, not learning. Also mind tissue: varying the problem within a rehabilitation window means changing *the nuanced parameters of a movement problem without changing its global nature*, which is a narrower licence than "add chaos." And a genuinely novel skill may need some stable exposure before variation is useful.

**Example** — Twenty catches from a machine at fixed height and speed is repetition. Twenty catches where the throw, the leverage of a defender, and the space behind all change — same goal, same catch count, same load — is repetition without repetition. The rep count is identical; only one of them prepares Saturday.

# Degeneracy Precedes Dexterity; Abundance Precedes Adaptability

**What it is** — The authors' compact statement of why a wide solution set matters (Myszka et al., 2023a). Two supporting terms:

- **Degeneracy** — "the ability of elements that are structurally different to perform the same function or yield the same output" (Edelman & Gally, 2001). Different configurations, same outcome.
- **Abundance** — having access to more potential ways of coordinating movement-system components to solve problems. More *usable* degrees of freedom.

The claim is directional: you cannot be adaptable to a problem you have only one answer for, so abundance is the precondition. Increased variability in coordination and control strategies is fundamentally linked to skill adaptation (Orth et al., 2017), because it supports the search and exploration through which a fitting solution is found.

**Why it works** — Since no two problems are ever the same, a single grooved solution is a bet that the next problem resembles the last. Having more usable degrees of freedom means the player can transition into a different pattern when it does not (Gray, 2021). Fixation on one prescribed way of behaving is therefore not safety, it is fragility.

**When to apply** — Justifying why practice should widen rather than narrow a player's repertoire, and why a coach should tolerate — actively pursue — movement variability, novelty and unorthodoxy rather than coaching them out. It is the theoretical partner to [[claim--prescriptive-coaching-narrows-adaptability]], which supplies the evidence, and it explains the mechanism behind [[principle--variability-overuse-hypothesis]].

**When NOT to apply** — Marked **supported**: degeneracy is well-established in biology and the reasoning is sound, but "abundance precedes adaptability" is the authors' own formulation and the ordering has not been demonstrated experimentally in football. More options is also not unconditionally better — abundance must be *usable* and *functional*, and a player with many solutions and no attunement to which one fits is not dexterous, only erratic. There is a real question, unresolved here, about whether a beginner needs some stability before abundance helps.

**Example** — The book's illustration is two unrelated Sanders. Barry, described as having "moves on moves," solving apparently unsolvable problems by whatever strategy the moment allowed. Deion, playing shutdown corner, elite punt returner, and roughly half his team's offensive snaps in 1996 — and an NFL and MLB game on the same day. The point is not the highlight reel; it is that both were valuable *because* their toolbox was wide.

# Knowledge Of versus Knowledge About

**What it is** — Gibson's (1966) distinction, and one of the sharpest diagnostic tools in the book.

**Knowledge *about*** is conceptual and indirect. It is demonstrated verbally or through symbols and pictures — a play drawn on a whiteboard, a coverage explained, a film clip discussed. It is **scaled in units of physics** ("when you are 10 yards from the receiver") rather than to the player's own body, because it refers to the typical and the ideal. In terms of action it can only describe *what to perceive* and *what to do*.

**Knowledge *of*** is direct, perceptual contact with the environment. It is body-scaled, available in the moment, and it specifies opportunities for action rather than describing them.

**Why it works** — The two are acquired differently and do different jobs, and confusing them explains a familiar failure. Film rooms, whiteboards and unopposed walkthroughs are efficient producers of knowledge *about* — and they produce almost no knowledge *of*, because they supply a third-person, bird's-eye view of information the player will meet in first person at speed. A player can therefore know the coverage perfectly and still be unable to play against it. See [[framework--shared-attunement-vs-shared-mental-models]].

**When to apply** — Auditing the balance of a training week. Count what actually generates knowledge *of*: opposed reps, live information, real bodies at real leverage. Meetings, install, and walkthroughs all bank into the other account. American football banks heavily into knowledge *about* by tradition, and the imbalance is usually invisible until it is counted.

**When NOT to apply** — This is not an argument that knowledge *about* is worthless — the book is explicit that a skilled player needs **both**. Football is unusually pre-scripted; assignments, checks and situational rules are real requirements, and no amount of attunement substitutes for knowing the call. The claim is that knowledge *about* cannot by itself produce coordinated action under novelty, not that it should be reduced.

**Example** — The authors' case is Tom Brady, who ran 5.28 in the 40 and lacked the traits scouts prize. What made him was both accounts at once: recognising pre-snap how a defence was matching up and changing the call (**knowledge about**), and adapting in the split second once the ball was in his hands (**knowledge of**). Either alone would have been ordinary.

Film rooms, whiteboards and unopposed walkthroughs are efficient producers of knowledge *about* — and they produce almost no knowledge *of*, because they supply a third-person, bird's-eye view of information the player will meet in first person at speed. A player can therefore know the coverage perfectly and still be unable to play against it. See [[framework--shared-attunement-vs-shared-mental-models]].

**When to apply** — Auditing the balance of a training week. Count what actually generates knowledge *of*: opposed reps, live information, real bodies at real leverage. Meetings, install, and walkthroughs all bank into the other account. American football banks heavily into knowledge *about* by tradition, and the imbalance is usually invisible until it is counted.

**When NOT to apply** — This is not an argument that knowledge *about* is worthless — the book is explicit that a skilled player needs **both**. Football is unusually pre-scripted; assignments, checks and situational rules are real requirements, and no amount of attunement substitutes for knowing the call. The claim is that knowledge *about* cannot by itself produce coordinated action under novelty, not that it should be reduced.

**Example** — The authors' case is Tom Brady, who ran 5.28 in the 40 and lacked the traits scouts prize. What made him was both accounts at once: recognising pre-snap how a defence was matching up and changing the call (**knowledge about**), and adapting in the split second once the ball was in his hands (**knowledge of**). Either alone would have been ordinary.

# The Signature Qualities of Dexterous Movers

**What it is** — What to *look for* when a player is solving problems well. The authors group the observable properties into four pairs, and argue these are the key performance indicators of skilful movement behaviour (Seifert et al., 2013):

- **Abundance & degeneracy** — a wide, flexibly adjustable set of potential movement strategies. See [[principle--degeneracy-precedes-dexterity]].
- **Awareness & attunement** — sensitively engaged with the opportunities present, ready for whatever emerges, tracking the changing dispositional state of the problem (opponent behaviour, available space).
- **Aptitude & instinctiveness** — trusting what they see and what is in their toolbox enough to act on it under any circumstances; including intentional strategising, and acting deceptively to draw an opponent into a useful mistake.
- **Authenticity & creativity** — a personal movement style that leverages the player's own individuality rather than an imposed ideal.

**Why it works** — The central move is deliberate: these properties — variability, novelty, unorthodoxy, creativity — are exactly the ones **traditional coaching treats as faults to be trained out**. Reframing them as indicators, not errors, changes what a coach rewards. Since every player has their own individual constraints, movement history and form of life, coaches are warned against imposing their own idealised way of perceiving, cognising and acting.

For the authenticity question the book supplies three usable prompts: **What makes this player different from others? What qualities do they rely on when problems get hard? What brought this player to where they are?** — with the reminder that complete answers require looking off the field as well as on it.

**When to apply** — Building an evaluation rubric, or arguing against one. It is the concrete answer to "so how would you even grade this?" — and it gives a position coach something to watch for that is not adherence to a technical model.

**When NOT to apply** — Confidence is **supported**, and the honest limit is measurement. These are qualitative properties with no validated scoring instrument offered here, so two evaluators can disagree and neither can be shown wrong. That makes the framework useful for *seeing* and risky for *ranking*. There is also a real failure mode: unorthodoxy is not automatically dexterity, and "authenticity" can excuse a player who simply has one bad habit. The properties earn their name only when the solution actually fits the problem.

**Example** — The book's illustrations are players a technical model would have coached differently: Le'Veon Bell waiting like a coiled cobra while coaches shout "just hit it"; Dante Hall reversing field back into pursuit; Troy Polamalu jumping the snap over two lines; Mahomes throwing behind his back when the play breaks. Andy Reid's answer at Kansas City is the coaching version — a period of practice each week for seeing what is possible, so that when a play breaks down Mahomes does not feel handcuffed to established ways.

# There Is No Muscle Memory, and the Brain Is Not a Computer

**What it is** — Davids and Araújo state it flatly: **"There is no such thing as 'muscle memory,' nor is this phrase a useful analogy for what goes on during skill learning. The brain is not a computer."** The body is a highly complex, interconnected biological system in which the brain plays a role in forming memories through synaptic and neuronal interconnections — one important part of a deeply integrated whole movement system, itself interconnected with an ever-changing environment.

The consequence they draw: **the athlete can never be understood, nor meaningfully considered, without reference to the environment, and vice versa.** Hence the need for an integrated athlete–environment scale of analysis.

**Why it works** — "Muscle memory" is not merely imprecise, it carries the cognitive-computational theory inside it: a stored program, written by repetition, that runs off on its own without attention. That picture is what justifies rote drilling, automaticity as the goal, and treating thought during performance as a burden to be lifted. Reject the metaphor and the training rationale attached to it loses its footing.

**When to apply** — When the phrase appears in a staff conversation, a rehab protocol, or a coaching-education document, and is doing argumentative work — "we need more reps to build the muscle memory." That is the moment to ask what is actually being claimed and whether the evidence supports it. Pair with [[framework--ecological-dynamics-athlete-environment]] for the alternative account.

**When NOT to apply** — Marked **supported** rather than proven, and the distinction is worth keeping honest. This is a *theoretical* rejection of a metaphor and of the representational account behind it, argued by proponents of a competing framework — not a demonstrated empirical result, and the representational tradition has not conceded. There is also a genuine physiological phenomenon sometimes given the same name (myonuclear retention after detraining), which is unrelated to this argument. And this is a poor hill to die on socially: correcting a coach's vocabulary mid-conversation rarely changes practice, whereas changing one drill often does.

**Example** — A return-to-play plan justifies 200 unopposed reps as "rebuilding muscle memory." The useful question is not whether the phrase is correct but what the reps are for: if the answer is tissue tolerance, say so and keep them; if the answer is skill, the reps are training a relationship the game will not present.

236	connect to a wider variety of informational variables (i.e., displaying perceptual
237	system degeneracy) that allows them to find a functional fit to the peculiar
238	movement problem at hand. Gibson (2015) captured this idea of more skillful
239	perception when he said, “Perceiving gets wider and finer and longer and richer
240	and fuller as the observer explores the environment" (p. 244). However, just what
241	is it that a player is exploring and searching for? Meaning, what may they find ou
242	there within the information that they can pick up, and what could it mean for
243	
244	them that would allow for more skillful interactions with the problems found on
245	the field?
246	
247	Understanding Affordances
248	
249	Now that we have gotten into the weeds around information in an ecological
250	dynamics framework, the next logical stop on our journey will be to elaborate on
251	the concept of affordances. Simply put, affordances are opportunities for action (Fajen
252	et al., 2009; Gibson, 1979). They could also be viewed as invitations within the
253	performance environment which are essentially beckoning a player to act ina
254	certain way (Withagen et al., 2012). These opportunities will refer to openings
255	within a respective problem which will serve to guide or channel the coordination,
256	control, and organization of the expression of skillful movement behavior for the
257	player. That said though, affordances do not cause the behavior, instead, they just
258	constrain or channel it (i.e., eliminate options or offer up invitations). In this way,
259	they will describe what an individual player can and cannot do under the
260	constraints of that emerging, unfolding movement problem, in that peculiar
261	context within the performance environment.
262	
263	Why Affordances?
264	
265	Importantly, the term affordances refer "to both the environment and the animal
266	in a way that no existing term does. It implies the complementarity of the animal
267	and the environment” (Gibson, 2015, p. 119). Though we have recently
268	introduced this idea, let’s circle back to remind us all once again of one of the key
269	non-negotiable tenants of adhering to an ecological approach: the only
270	appropriate scale of analysis for viewing sport performance is at the player-
271	environment relationship. Just as information links this interdependent system,
272	information will also specify the affordances (again, the behavioral opportunities)
273	present within the interface between the movement problem and the player as
274	the problem solver (and their process of solving). In a seminal paper published
275	in 2009, Fajen and colleagues went as far as stating the following: "We feel that
276	
277	the theory of affordances is ideally suited to capture the behavior of athletes on _ !
278	
279	the playing field, and has great potential to become a guiding principle for
280	research on perception and action in sport" (p, 82). Because they refer to the
281	relation between the player and his environment, as well as between the
282	disposition of the problem and the IMS organized, it is the concept of affordances
283	
284	68
285	===== p69 =====
286	that becomes a key to a deeper understanding in our performance analysis and
287	subsequent practice activity design.
288	
289	Simply put, in sports, the concept of affordances links emerging
290	movement problems and the IMS together because they relate to the unfolding
291	interactions between them (and allow them ‘fo become one with one another).
292	Meaning, affordances capture the reciprocity of the player-environment system.
293	As Turvey and Shaw (1995) said, affordances could be said to provide functional
294	semantics for sport because they are a way of describing what the environment is
295	to the player in terms of how they can personally behave within it (Fajen et al.,
296	2009). Namely, the movement behaviors which emerge (and the integration of
297	perceptions, cognitions, and actions) will be reflected within the selection and
298	realization of the affordances accepted.
299	
300	It’s important to acknowledge that affordances will emerge and decay
301	dynamically; they will come and go, appear and disappear. Here, affordances can
302	give us an understanding about the dynamical changes in the relation between
303	how the problem is unfolding moment-to-moment, while also highlighting the
304	role of the individual player in this constant interaction. In these ways,
305	affordances ate both frame-dependent and individual-dependent. For example,
306	when solving a similar unfolding problem on a football field (e.g., an off-tackle
307	run), one ball carrier may perceive an affordance to cut back between defenders
308	in the middle of the field, while another may perceive an affordance to bounce
309	the ball to the outside, eluding them by outrunning them to the boundary,
310	highlighting the individual-dependent nature of affordances. Furthermore, when
311	interacting with a comparable problem on different occasions, the same ball
312	carrier may detect other opportunities to act—highlighting the frame-dependent
313	nature of affordances—and organize different solutions because of the prevailing
314	constraints (e.g., the movement repertoire of the opposing players, field
315	conditions, their current fatigue level, the down and distance).
316	
317	Landscape of Attordances
318	
319	The tight coupling of a player’s perception, which will be part of that (alongside
320	cognition and action) which underpins the integrated nature of skillful movement
321	behaviors that emerge under constraints, will be oriented around not only the
322	detection of information, but also of affordances themselves. As mentioned
323	earlier, cognitions (e.g., intentions, decisions) cannot be disconnected from this
324	behavioral organization process (the MPSP highlighted in Chapter 2). Namely,
325	ideas around ‘skilled intentionality (Kiverstein & Rietveld, 2015), or the openness
326	and responsiveness to a rich landscape of affordances, will be at play here to allow
327	the player to better link themselves to the range of current possibilities present in
328	
329	the world. Relatedly, actions will be calibrated and organized based on the
330	affordance selected.
331	
332	In this way, the requisite information available for pick-up will also be
333	that which allows for the control and regulation of the movement. For example,
334	to perceive a gap between defenders, a player will need to pick-up information as
335	
336	69
337	===== p70 =====
338	to if the distance between two defenders is pass-through-able for him; and to act
339	accordingly upon that affordance (to execute in an appropriate movement
340	strategy that is coordinated in relation to the gap), one will need to be able to
341	perceive that exact same information. Of course, this brings us to a key discussion
342	point that makes the concept of affordances unique: the tole of action capabilities,
343	ot the effectivities, of the player themselves, in the perception of affordances
344	(related to the possibilities for how that specific player could potentially act).
345	Namely, for an affordance to be deemed as suiting to a player, they must possess
346	the ability to act upon it. For instance, in the emerging gap example mentioned
347	above, the player must have an adequate amount of acceleration, or speed-based
348	action capabilities, to pass through the gap before it closes. This is how
349	affordances will relate to both the opportunities in the environment and to that of
350	the movement characteristics of the player (i.e., affordances point both ways).
351	Furthermore, affordances that can be detected (i.e., perceived) in the first quarter
352	of a game, may be significantly different than those which are picked up in the
353	fourth quarter. This could be due to fatigue and other constraints acting on the
354	system across different situations and conditions, limiting the player’s ability to
355	interact (i.e., perceive, cognize, and act) in the same way in every instance.
356	
357	At any moment in time, there will be both simultaneous and successive
358	affordances being offered to the player. Thus, taking a frame-dependent,
359	moment-to-moment, walk through a play will be important to our movement skill
360	and performance analysis, and subsequent practice activity design too (to be
361	discussed, respectively, in Chapters 4 and 5). Obviously, on any given play, we
362	will never truly be able to fully understand exactly what the player is perceiving
363	(i.e., what information they are detecting as the agent of their movement) or what
364	he is thinking (e.g., truly know how he aims to act), but through the affordances
365	the player accepts and acts upon, we will at least be able to hypothesize around
366	the processes that underpin his movement behavior.
367	
368	As part of the landscape of affordances, and the various opportunities
369	that will be presented to a player simultaneously and successively, lies the idea of
370	nested affordances. Here, we will be investigating and referring to more of the micro
371	problems—or local interactions (e.g., make the defender miss, shed the blocker)—
372	-that will be solved en route to facing macro, global problems, such as attaining a
373	first down or simply limiting the number of yards a ball carrier gains. These nested
374	affordances really begin to speak to the player’s online control of their movement
375	behavior, and how the totality of the contextual circumstances are unfolding
376	moment-by-moment based on the unique behavioral opportunities presented to
377	the player.
378	
379	In a sport like American football, the way one solves an immediate local,
380	movement problem—by perceiving and accepting a nested affordance—can be
381	dependent on what its solving could mean in the resolution of the global, macro
382	problem. Meaning, affordances can be selected and acted upon based on the
383	information available regarding the next potential affordance. This suggests that
384	some players are capable of acting relative to multiple affordances simultaneously
385	(and in a successive manner too), Think of a player like Barry Sanders for a
386	
387	70
388	===== p71 =====
389	moment. Barry was notorious for making opponents miss across a variety of
390	dispositional problems. When closely investigating his movement behaviors,
391	armed with the critical concepts of this chapter, we find that Sanders could often
392	be found accepting affordances (i.e., making X defender miss by going in X
393	direction, at X time, utilizing X movement strategy) based on what was unfolding
394	in other areas within the landscape of affordances (e.g., movement problems
395	behind and/or around the immediate defender).
396	
397	Sharing is Caring
398	
399	Just as an athlete can become attuned to subtle differences in an opponent’s
400	movement behaviors, it’s also important for players to become perceptually
401	connected and sensitive to how their teammates can potentially behave. This
402	concept, known as shared affordances (Fajen et al., 2009; Silva et al., 2013), means
403	affordances perceived for others and of others (e.g., teammates). We have all likely
404	heard the old cliche before, “football is the ultimate team game.” Simply put, the
405	nature of a playet’s interactions with his teammates can be a major determining
406	factor in the movement behavior which emerges for each individual.
407	
408	To illustrate, let’s imagine the following hypothetical interactions, and
409	how the information that a player may perceive, regarding the movement
410	behaviors of a teammate (i.e., interacting in relation to their own unfolding
411	problems), could potentially influence the decisions they make, and how they
412	ultimately act, based on the shared affordances that emerge:
413	
414	e A RB willing to be patient near the line of scrimmage, detecting the
415	posture and kinematics of an OL in front of them (could also potentially
416	combine this information with that which is related to interpersonal
417	distance between them), because they may know that the OL is often late
418	to the point of attack in blocking attempts versus a defensive lineman or
419	LB.
420	
421	e A QB waiting to attempt a deep pass down field, may typically be
422	perceptually attuned to the amount of separation between their wide
423	receivers and the opposing team’s defending cornerbacks. However, let’s
424	say that they have developed tremendous trust in the WR’s
425	understanding and knowledge of the game that the QB looks for the WR
426	to throw up their hand at the moment they believe (and perceive) that
427	they have the corner beat so the QB can subsequently deliver the ball to
428	where that specific WR likes it placed, and simply trusts that the WR can
429	come down with the pass attempt, regardless of how tightly the CB may
430	be playing the WR at the time (think of Tom Brady and Randy Moss for
431	the New England Patriots in the 2007 National Football League season).
432	
433	e A safety (S) playing from inside the box, may take off laterally from the
434	wide side of the field to pursue a quick WR who has taken a handoff on
435	a jet sweep. The WR has a tight end (TE) moving slightly in front of him
436	that the S perceives and momentarily debates slowing his pursuit velocity
437	in relation to. However, the S also has his own outside LB attempting to
438	
439	71
440	===== p72 =====
441	pick up the block attempt from the TE so that the S can subsequently
442	chase with maximum intent and speed. Thus, the S, having played a
443	number of seasons with the LB, knows the backer’s action capabilities
444	and perceives the LB’s speed to reach the TE in time for the S to stay on
445	his own pursuit path and acceleration trajectory to collide with the WR
446	and successfully tackle them.
447	
448	As will be highlighted more in Chapter 6, the activities found within the practice
449	environment should give players ample opportunity to search for, and
450	subsequently explore the use of, this type of information and the affordances they
451	specify, so players are able to better understand their unfolding relationships with
452	teammates.
453	
454	More Affordance Illustrations
455	
456	We must remember that anything that cov/d be an affordance, must be measured
457	or assessed relative to the unique characteristics of the player himself (as
458	affordances are individual and frame-dependent). Meaning, Barry Sanders, Jerry
459	Rice, Ray Lewis, or any other player will perceive entirely different affordances
460	than you or anyone else will.
461	
462	That being said though, investigating the composition and layout of the
463	environment can begin to indicate what specific opportunities for action may be
464	afforded to each individual (again, 7fwe possess the action capabilities to interact
465	with them). Gibson often used examples from everyday life, such as if a surface
466	is walk-on-able (i.e., it affords support for a human for locomotive purposes), or
467	if a tree is climb-up-able (i.e., the branches are sturdy and structured in a way that
468	offers the opportunity for a human to traverse it upwards), or if a chair (or a stool,
469	or a bench, or a tree stump) is sit-on-able (okay, you probably get the picture
470	now).
471	
472	Those Gibson illustrations are just simple examples, existing within the
473	real world, that we should all be able to visualize and understand in reference to
474	our own behavior. Yet, within football, there will be a highly dynamic and
475	complex environment that players exist in where they will continuously interact
476	with emerging and decaying affordances—some of which they will select and act
477	upon, whereas others they will perceive but may ultimately elect to reject. Thus,
478	the identification of affordances that exist on a football field may be less obvious
479	at times. However, one thing remains clear; different layouts of the global
480	problem, along with various emerging local movement problems, will afford
481	different behaviors for different players (or an entirely different landscape of
482	affordances). This, in turn, will equate to different interactions and relations that
483	will inevitably unfold.
484	
485	Of course, in the sport of American football, there are 11 opposing
486	players on the other side of the ball who are operating in a way that contradicts
487	(or attempts to constrain or restrict) the potential behavioral opportunities for
488	every other opponent. In other words, a given player, and his 10 teammates, are
489	
490	72
491	===== p73 =====
492	all potentially (and hopefully) organizing their movement behaviors in a way that
493	affords more advantageous opportunities for one another, and less for their
494	opposing counterparts. Remember, an affordance points both ways; to the player
495	and to the environment, as well as between a player and his adversaries.
496	
497	Figure 3.2 - Investigating the individual and frame-dependent nature of affordances for
498	Lamar Jackson.
499	
500	To illustrate, let’s take a quick look at the third person view snapshot on
501	q P Pp
502	
503	Figure 3.2 of Lamar Jackson, MVP-winning QB of the Baltimore Ravens, on a
504	play versus the Buffalo Bills, as he begins to interact with the landscape of
505	affordances present at this moment in time. Obviously, some of that which will
506	be perceived (throughout the unfolding dynamics of the problem) and the
507	affordances that are offered, and ultimately acted upon, are going to be dependent
508	ona number of constraints such as the particular play-call, the down and distance,
509	the time of the game, and various other potential factors. However, for the sake
510	of thought experimentation, try to put yourself in the human movement system
511	of Lamar Jackson, while amid this static snapshot.
512	
513	Based on what we can see unfolding here, think deeply and ask:
514	
515	What potential affordances could Jackson be perceiving that are all
516	simultaneously available to him?
517	
518	As you work your way through those affordances (and any potential
519	simultaneous and successive opportunities to act also), what
520	informational variables within the problem do you believe he was
521	connecting to in order to tightly couple the subsequent coordination of
522	his movement behavior in relation with?
523	
524	In the interactions of each peculiar local movement problem (and the
525	nested affordance contained within it), how else could Jackson have
526	behaved? What would this be dependent on?
527	
528	What could have changed in the affordances available if it wasn’t Lamar
529	Jackson performing in this problem and instead it was a different player
530	(think of a few players at the QB position and speculate on this by using
531	
532	73
533	===== p74 =====
534	theit individualized movement skill, action capabilities, and form of
535	life)?
536	
537	e How could this information detection potentially be influenced by
538	certain extrinsic factors acting as constraints (e.g., score, quarter and time
539	of the game, down and distance, offensive play call, defensive tactics
540	being played, opponent’s characteristics)?
541	
542	How Information & Affordances affect Skill Acquisition: Constrain
543	to Afford
544	
545	As we explored within Chapter 2, with added exposure and experience to alive
546	movement problems (and /eamning to learn to move/ learning to learn to problem solve),
547	players can become perceptually attuned to the opportunities (1.e., affordances)
548	that are present in the environment and what exactly these offer to the player
549	(based on their action capabilities). As we will discuss at length later in Chapter
550	6, when manipulating constraints to design practice activities we should ensure
551	that:
552	¢ The movement problems that emerge there have a disposition that looks,
553	feels, acts, and unfolds similarly to that of the competitive performance
554	environment
555	e The potential information sources, which could be specifying, are always
556	present whenever possible so players can begin to couple their
557	movement behaviors to and through them (here, as a coach, we may
558	guide a player’s perceptual search so they're able to become more
559	attuned, educating their attention)
560	e As we scale complexity and begin to bring added layers to the movement
561	problems, we should investigate the landscape of affordances available
562	for the players in hopes that it may invite them to perceive and accept a
563	wider range of potential opportunities to interact with on gameday (i.e.,
564	skilled intentionality)
565	
566	Knowing that accumulating repetitions is still a viable way to lead a player into
567	learning, we must place a high priority on the nature of those repetitions. In our
568	viewpoint, these reps can, and should, take place across a wide variety of
569	problematic dispositions (i.e., across diverse situations and conditions). As the
570	player exists there, a critical aspect of the skill adaptation and enhancement
571	process is helping them to change the information that they use to control their
572	movement actions, shifting from perceiving and acting upon less useful
573	information sources to more useful, specifying informational variables. To assist
574	in this process as ecologically minded coaching practitioners, we should constrain
575	to afford (Renshaw et al., 2019) during the movement problem-setting we embark
576	upon in our training and practice environments. To better illustrate this
577	constraining to afford process and exemplify how information and affordances
578	can affect skill adaptation for football players, let’s look at an example from a
579	handful of years ago, in Shawn’s work with a National Football League (NFL)
580	
581	74
582	===== p75 =====
583	player he had in his learning environment.
584	
585	The player was a starting TE who was also required to start on the punt
586	cover unit. Based on this role on special teams, the player was expected to be
587	adept at tackling highly dynamic, elusive players in space; sometimes in what
588	could be viewed upon as a local 1v1 dyadic problem. Obviously, being a TE (as
589	opposed to a LB or S who may possess movement skill nuances where tackling
590	is natural based on previous experience), this was not the type of movement
591	problem that this player had a lot of exposure solving.
592	
593	After going through the practice film, counting all the repetitions the
594	player took during the spring during Organized Team Activities (OTAs) and
595	Minicamp, combined with those repetitions where a problem like this had
596	emerged during Training Camp, it was found that the TE only had three
597	repetitions where he was presented with a problem in a 1v1 situation in the open
598	field with a punt returner (PR) (Note: being that these occurred in practice, he
599	was also only required to tag off on the ball carrier too instead of attempting a
600	real tackle on the returner).
601	
602	However, an NFL game on a Sunday is a very non-forgiving one to
603	play—it does not care what practice environments you’ve been placed within and
604	the problems you’ve been exposed to—as, during the regular season (he played
605	in all 16 games), he actually faced this type of situation on two separate occasions.
606	This may not seem like anything major as it was on/y two times. Right? Yet, within
607	both of those in-game situations, the TE could not coordinate a functional
608	movement solution—meaning he did not make a tackle or bring down the PR. To
609	make matters even worse, the TE’s 10 teammates also did not organize a
610	functional movement solution either! Thus, in both of those situations, the PR
611	scored a touchdown on the play. So, even though this particular type of
612	movement problem didn’t emerge very many times during the course of the
613	season (in practices or games), they did occur at a time of major significance (in
614	a game when a play could’ve been made to save a touchdown) where the player
615	was not able to adequately organize a solution to it mainly based on the lack of
616	representative exposure and experience leading up to that point. We feel as
617	though this illustrates the importance of coaches looking for ways to constrain to
618	afford, which means designing problems for players to interact with that invite
619	(or encourage) them to explore organizing more functional movement solutions
620	to meet the needs of the problems that emerge during games—specifically, those
621	related to the opportunities and gaps in a player’s skill set.
622	
623	In the following offseason, namely in the five weeks leading up to that
624	season’s Training Camp, Shawn frequently set-up this type of unfolding problem
625	in their training environment for this player by designing a specific activity (also
626	see Chapter 6 for the activity listed as ‘High-speed special teams coverage’):
627	
628	1. Having the TE perform a long-distance sprint after getting off an initial block
629	at the line of scrimmage, followed by;
630	
631	2. Tracking the movement actions of a PR (who was catching a punt at an
632	undetermined place on the field), followed by;
633	
634	3). Adaptively pursuing the ball carrying returner in space and attempting to
635	
636	75
637	===== p76 =====
638	organize a functional movement solution to meet the respective needs of the
639	unfolding problem (and subsequently bring the returner down via executing a tag-
640	
641	off on him).
642	To bring added likelihood for positive transfer, different PRs would be
643	
644	rotated in as frequently as possible, all of whom possessed various movement
645	characteristics and tendencies (i¢., theit own problem-solving style), while also
646	manipulating the number of players involved in various positions across the field.
647	This constraint manipulation led to a practice activity design that was more alive
648	and representative, while also playing out in a more variable fashion, with added
649	repetition without repetition.
650	
651	This type of practice activity, and the constraining to afford that ensued
652	with it, was done for 10-12 repetitions on a training day, a total of six times that
653	summer (accumulating approximately 60-72 total exposures to these types of
654	problems). Due to this purposeful constraint manipulation, it allowed the player
655	to become much more accustomed to some of the problem-solution dynamics
656	present in these respective punt cover situations. It was clear to see the sharp
657	increase in the TE’s attunement to the information and affordances present when
658	the player found himself in the midst of these respective situations on gameday
659	in that regular season. Though it would be a small sample size again, as the TE
660	found himself in a 1v1 dyadic situation with a returner only two more times on
661	an NFL Sunday in the following year. However, during both of these instances,
662	the situation (and accompanied movement problem-solving processes) played
663	out differently, and luckily, so did the outcome; on one of the plays, the TE single-
664	handily brought the returner down and, in the other instance, the TE walled the
665	returner off and forced him to run laterally east and west to head out of bounds.
