===== p63 =====
CHAPTER 3

Information & Affordances

As we just learned, at the cote of an ecological dynamics framework exists systems
thinking, where we will study the relationships between component parts of the
system and how they configure together to form a whole, rather than being
examined piece by piece (Clarke & Crossland, 1985). In a tightly coupled unified
system (e.g., the player-environment relationship, the human movement system),
the flow of some resource through that system is its primary integration factor
that allows it to (inter)act as a whole. When it comes to movement problem-
solving in football, the informational variables present in the environment will be
that integration factor as it is what the player will perceptually connect to and
couple their movement actions in relation with. Because of this, we must closely
investigate movement problems and the nature of the information present there
if we expect to subsequently create practice environments that sample and
contain this highly relevant information (in hopes of increasing the potential
likelihood of positive transfer to game day). However, before we begin to closely
examine some of these important relationships, let’s become more familiar with
the concept of information, particularly in this approach and paradigm.

The Nature and Role of Information

To understand the movement problem-solving processes of players on a football
field, we feel it’s important to first deeply examine the information that is
exchanged between the problem and the solver as they interact with one another
in a mutual, reciprocal fashion. Namely, some key questions to ask and attempt
to answer could include:

1. What is the nature, the range, and the bandwidth of information existent in the
problems presented to the player during a specific play?

2. What are the potenual specifying informational variables that could be useful
for the player to perceptually detect in order to functionally regulate their actions?
3. How is the player currently perceiving (Le., picking up and detecting) this
specifying information?

4. How does the player utilize that information he perceived to channel the
coordination of their movement actions?

Ultimately, what we are really trying to answer is, “What is the role of the

information in guiding the coordination and control of players’ movement
behaviors in context?”

Why the need for this ‘information-based’ approach?

63
===== p64 =====
l

From an ecologically-oriented perspective, one of the most important ,
influential contributors to an understanding of the role of information, ang
connection to movement, is undoubtedly, James. J. Gibson. While TEjECting.
traditional perspective on visual perception, offered by information Process,
theories, Gibson felt as though the information present in the environment ;,
the surroundings of organisms that perceive and behave; 1979) was deep, r.
and meaningful, in and of itself. Gibson proposed that information is locate;
the ambient energy atray and optical flows and, as importantly, was din,
perceivable (i.e., with no need for interpretation or ‘processing’) by an organi,
(1.e., a player) and could be utilized to prospectively control one’s movems
actions. As Gibson said, “We perceive in order to move, but we must also mo.
in order to perceive” (1979, p. 223). Meaning, movement generates informati,
which, in turn, supports additional movement, resulting in a cyclical exchan,
between movement and information. This idea will obviously have tremendy
implications as we attempt to study, explain, and address skillful movema
behavior in the real world (Le., a sport setting like American football), and wew
begin to expand upon this in subsequent sections in this chapter and followin
chapters, as well.

Another giant in the skill acquisition space, Michael Turvey, framed;
this way: “Information in the ecological approach refers to specificity between th
structured energy distributions available to a perceptual system and th
environmental and movement properties causally responsible for that structur
(1990, p. 941).” What Turvey is alluding to here is the depth and richness of th
patterns of stimulus energy—both internal, such as that taking place within th
human movement system itself, as well as external, based on the informatio
existing in the outside world—that could be picked up and detected by th
performer (Le., perceived), all of which will directly specify action-relevan
opportunities for the player (i-e., affordances; more to come on this in a bit).

Information-Movement Coupling (Keep ‘em coupled!)

One of the key benefits of adopting an ecological approach to skill execution
and enhancement is the requisite scope of analysis being firmly placed on th
mutual, reciprocal relationship between the player and their environment, as wd
as the emerging movement ptoblems and the coordination of IMS. At the heart
of these important relationships will be the information that is available for
detection that the player could utilize in the organization of movement skill:
Quite simply, the ongoing control of movement is predicated on the role of
information that emerges from the individual-environment system to guide
movement activity (Seifert & Davids, 2017).

Here, we find that the concept of information-movement coupling is quite
useful for coaches and football performance analysts to understand, which is
considered “the development of successful, functional relations betwee!
movement and information in a specific performance context (Anson et al., 2005,
p. 229)." Essentially, information-movement coupling is where an individual i

64
===== p65 =====
able to more effectively utilize useful information present ity a problem to support
the IMS that emetges (reminder: in out view, the merement edutton is a functional
behavioral unit that is composed of, and underpinned by, the intertwined
Processes of perception, cognition, and action).

In the following subsection, we'll take it a step further in our investigation
and explanation of information-movement couplings to help coaches understand
this key idea and better equip them to design effective practice tasks that channel
mote skillful movement behavior for plavers.

How do players connect to this information?

Ultimately, if movement is going to be closely coupled to information, (fad how
an individual connects to the (most specifying and useful) information is vital.
After all, on a football field, there’s a lot of information oat shere pettaining to the
what is: Simply put, the information found in out contextual world is deep and
rich, containing everything we need to interact with the problem without much
need for ‘processing’ in the traditional sense. However, the information can only
be meaningful and relevant if it relates to the perceiver's goals and intentions (ie,
their aims to act in a given way in felation to the problem being faced). Thus,
spotts scientists and coaching practitioners must attempt to understand the
information from the perspective of what the player is aiming to do (as well as in
capturing the various options that exist within and across the landscape of the
opportunities present), Furthermore, the useful information to detect (that will
specify the potential movement actions available), and ultimately utilize, in
guiding the coordination and control of one’s actions, will differ depending on
not only the contextual situation, but also individual player differences. This is
due to a number of contributing, influential factors such as the player's intrinsic
dynamics (i.e., their movement toolbox) and unique affordances (again, more to
come on this shortly!).

Here, we once again begin to lean on the ideas of Gibson, which can
serve to shape our perspective. As Gibson (1979) insinuated, we perceive to act and
we act to perceive. Meaning, perception guides action, and action generates additional
perceptual information; the two are in a relationship of constant circular causality.
It is through this manner that we can start to investigate and assess the nature of
the movement behavioral dynamics as well as the functional fic of the emerging
movement problem-solving process (MPSP) (i.c., how perceptions, cogninons,
and actions are feeding into one another at that moment in time). Under this lens,
we can also begin to gain an understanding regarding whuf information the player
could, and should, be picking up and detecting in his environment to carry Oue
their intended actions.

Because there is so much potential informauon available, and being that
it could be quite overwhelming if a player were to try wo attend to ie all (which
would also be impossible!), it starts to point to the importance of the player's
ability to become highly sensitive to the most specifying information that is
available in any respective movement problem, Known as perceptual attunement
===== p66 =====
(Fajen et al., 2009; Jacobs & Michaels, 2007), this sensitivity will allow the
performer to attend to the most useful information, at the ‘right’ time. When it
comes to perceptual skill (i.e., organization of perceptual DoF), this
characterization of right versus wrong is an undet-discussed and often
misunderstood topic. Often, individuals investigating the coordination of
movement skill will limit their investigation to the link between where a player is
looking, and what the player may be attending to, in attempts to gain an
understanding around the player’s visual perception. However, contrary to
popular belief, the two are not always one in the same. Meaning, the eyes could
be camped, anchored, or fixated somewhere, and the specifying information
needed to optimally couple one’s actions to it is not actually being picked up or
detected. Meaning, the information is not being adequately perceived or utilized
in the unfolding organization of one’s movement actions.

Ultimately, the emergence of functional movement solutions will depend
on the player’s information detection and tight coupling to useful information
sources. Certain informational variables will be useful for successfully carrying
out one’s intended goals and others will not. Though additional research is
definitely needed, related specifically to the sport of Ametican football, some
work in other sports has been carried out that has explored the nature and use of
information in the organization of movement behaviors within sporting
problems that have some similarities to football, such as rugby (Passos et al.,
2008a; Passos et al., 2011; Passos et al., 2013) and basketball (Esteves et al., 2011).
This work could at least offer those within American football a starting point for
applicable hypotheses.

As Gibson stated, “Behavior affords behavior” (1979, p. 135), meaning how
two or more individual players interact will give rise to various emerging
movement behaviors for each party. Namely, in evasion-invasion agility scenarios
in football, such as running back (RB)-linebacker (LB) dyadic relationships, it
would be safe to assume that specifying information detected pertaining to
interpersonal distance, particularly within relationships between immediate
opponents and/or teammates, could help to explain the nature of the
information-movement couplings of successful players. The critical value and
appropriate ranges of this informational variable will be both context and
individual-specific. It can be speculated that interpersonal distance, by itself, will
typically not be sufficient to appropriately coordinate the most functional of
movement solutions, even in these types of problematic situations (Passos et al.,
2011). Meaning, research (Button et al., 2020; Esteves et al., 2011; Passos et al.,
2008a; Passos et al., 2013; Yearby et al., 2022) has shown that skillful players may

need to become perceptually attuned to (i.e., sensitively connected to) additional
information variables related to the following:

e Relative angles between competitors

e Variations in gaps between opponents and/or teammates

e Relative velocity values between competitors

e Kinematics, body orientation, and postural characteristics of a player’s
immediate opponents

66
===== p67 =====
¢ Any combination of these informational variables

Additionally, the perceptual connection to information related to a movement
problem will likely go beyond visual perception. Though a playet’s vision will
likely be the most dominant sensory system responsible for information detection
in many common football situations, truly attuned perception relies on a variety
of interconnected sensory subsystems for its most accurate detection. For
example, a playet’s auditory senses (i.c., the ability to hear) could be at play when
they are being chased ftom behind. Here, they could pick up sound waves due to
the audible heavy breathing and striking of the feet to the ground stemming from
the opponent, informing the player as to the degree of threat based on the
opponent’s pursuit (and relatedly, how fast they will need to move in order to
successfully evade). Similarly, dynamic touch information (Gibson, 1966) can be
highly informative to players when they contact the ground of an object in the
external environment (e.g., a ball or opponent). In these instances, physical
sensations like texture or pressure allow players to respond accordingly, such as
a receiver detecting how hard or fast they may need to clasp their hands when
their fingertips touch the ball, or a LB picking up the direction and speed they
need to move to stay with an offensive lineman (OL) who is running alongside
them while their hands are grabbing onto the jersey on the front of the chest
while immersed in a blocking engagement.

Figure 3.1 - A landscape of affordances; a perspective of the relevant informational
variables present in a movement problem that could specify potential opportunities to
act for Saquon Barkley.

67
===== p68 =====
Theoretically, a dexterous mover (i.e., problem-solver) will be able to
connect to a wider variety of informational variables (i.e., displaying perceptual
system degeneracy) that allows them to find a functional fit to the peculiar
movement problem at hand. Gibson (2015) captured this idea of more skillful
perception when he said, “Perceiving gets wider and finer and longer and richer
and fuller as the observer explores the environment" (p. 244). However, just what
is it that a player is exploring and searching for? Meaning, what may they find ou
there within the information that they can pick up, and what could it mean for

them that would allow for more skillful interactions with the problems found on
the field?

Understanding Affordances

Now that we have gotten into the weeds around information in an ecological
dynamics framework, the next logical stop on our journey will be to elaborate on
the concept of affordances. Simply put, affordances are opportunities for action (Fajen
et al., 2009; Gibson, 1979). They could also be viewed as invitations within the
performance environment which are essentially beckoning a player to act ina
certain way (Withagen et al., 2012). These opportunities will refer to openings
within a respective problem which will serve to guide or channel the coordination,
control, and organization of the expression of skillful movement behavior for the
player. That said though, affordances do not cause the behavior, instead, they just
constrain or channel it (i.e., eliminate options or offer up invitations). In this way,
they will describe what an individual player can and cannot do under the
constraints of that emerging, unfolding movement problem, in that peculiar
context within the performance environment.

Why Affordances?

Importantly, the term affordances refer "to both the environment and the animal
in a way that no existing term does. It implies the complementarity of the animal
and the environment” (Gibson, 2015, p. 119). Though we have recently
introduced this idea, let’s circle back to remind us all once again of one of the key
non-negotiable tenants of adhering to an ecological approach: the only
appropriate scale of analysis for viewing sport performance is at the player-
environment relationship. Just as information links this interdependent system,
information will also specify the affordances (again, the behavioral opportunities)
present within the interface between the movement problem and the player as
the problem solver (and their process of solving). In a seminal paper published
in 2009, Fajen and colleagues went as far as stating the following: "We feel that

the theory of affordances is ideally suited to capture the behavior of athletes on _ !

the playing field, and has great potential to become a guiding principle for
research on perception and action in sport" (p, 82). Because they refer to the
relation between the player and his environment, as well as between the
disposition of the problem and the IMS organized, it is the concept of affordances

68
===== p69 =====
that becomes a key to a deeper understanding in our performance analysis and
subsequent practice activity design.

Simply put, in sports, the concept of affordances links emerging
movement problems and the IMS together because they relate to the unfolding
interactions between them (and allow them ‘fo become one with one another).
Meaning, affordances capture the reciprocity of the player-environment system.
As Turvey and Shaw (1995) said, affordances could be said to provide functional
semantics for sport because they are a way of describing what the environment is
to the player in terms of how they can personally behave within it (Fajen et al.,
2009). Namely, the movement behaviors which emerge (and the integration of
perceptions, cognitions, and actions) will be reflected within the selection and
realization of the affordances accepted.

It’s important to acknowledge that affordances will emerge and decay
dynamically; they will come and go, appear and disappear. Here, affordances can
give us an understanding about the dynamical changes in the relation between
how the problem is unfolding moment-to-moment, while also highlighting the
role of the individual player in this constant interaction. In these ways,
affordances ate both frame-dependent and individual-dependent. For example,
when solving a similar unfolding problem on a football field (e.g., an off-tackle
run), one ball carrier may perceive an affordance to cut back between defenders
in the middle of the field, while another may perceive an affordance to bounce
the ball to the outside, eluding them by outrunning them to the boundary,
highlighting the individual-dependent nature of affordances. Furthermore, when
interacting with a comparable problem on different occasions, the same ball
carrier may detect other opportunities to act—highlighting the frame-dependent
nature of affordances—and organize different solutions because of the prevailing
constraints (e.g., the movement repertoire of the opposing players, field
conditions, their current fatigue level, the down and distance).

Landscape of Attordances

The tight coupling of a player’s perception, which will be part of that (alongside
cognition and action) which underpins the integrated nature of skillful movement
behaviors that emerge under constraints, will be oriented around not only the
detection of information, but also of affordances themselves. As mentioned
earlier, cognitions (e.g., intentions, decisions) cannot be disconnected from this
behavioral organization process (the MPSP highlighted in Chapter 2). Namely,
ideas around ‘skilled intentionality (Kiverstein & Rietveld, 2015), or the openness
and responsiveness to a rich landscape of affordances, will be at play here to allow
the player to better link themselves to the range of current possibilities present in

the world. Relatedly, actions will be calibrated and organized based on the
affordance selected.

In this way, the requisite information available for pick-up will also be
that which allows for the control and regulation of the movement. For example,
to perceive a gap between defenders, a player will need to pick-up information as

69
===== p70 =====
to if the distance between two defenders is pass-through-able for him; and to act
accordingly upon that affordance (to execute in an appropriate movement
strategy that is coordinated in relation to the gap), one will need to be able to
perceive that exact same information. Of course, this brings us to a key discussion
point that makes the concept of affordances unique: the tole of action capabilities,
ot the effectivities, of the player themselves, in the perception of affordances
(related to the possibilities for how that specific player could potentially act).
Namely, for an affordance to be deemed as suiting to a player, they must possess
the ability to act upon it. For instance, in the emerging gap example mentioned
above, the player must have an adequate amount of acceleration, or speed-based
action capabilities, to pass through the gap before it closes. This is how
affordances will relate to both the opportunities in the environment and to that of
the movement characteristics of the player (i.e., affordances point both ways).
Furthermore, affordances that can be detected (i.e., perceived) in the first quarter
of a game, may be significantly different than those which are picked up in the
fourth quarter. This could be due to fatigue and other constraints acting on the
system across different situations and conditions, limiting the player’s ability to
interact (i.e., perceive, cognize, and act) in the same way in every instance.

At any moment in time, there will be both simultaneous and successive
affordances being offered to the player. Thus, taking a frame-dependent,
moment-to-moment, walk through a play will be important to our movement skill
and performance analysis, and subsequent practice activity design too (to be
discussed, respectively, in Chapters 4 and 5). Obviously, on any given play, we
will never truly be able to fully understand exactly what the player is perceiving
(i.e., what information they are detecting as the agent of their movement) or what
he is thinking (e.g., truly know how he aims to act), but through the affordances
the player accepts and acts upon, we will at least be able to hypothesize around
the processes that underpin his movement behavior.

As part of the landscape of affordances, and the various opportunities
that will be presented to a player simultaneously and successively, lies the idea of
nested affordances. Here, we will be investigating and referring to more of the micro
problems—or local interactions (e.g., make the defender miss, shed the blocker)—
-that will be solved en route to facing macro, global problems, such as attaining a
first down or simply limiting the number of yards a ball carrier gains. These nested
affordances really begin to speak to the player’s online control of their movement
behavior, and how the totality of the contextual circumstances are unfolding
moment-by-moment based on the unique behavioral opportunities presented to
the player.

In a sport like American football, the way one solves an immediate local,
movement problem—by perceiving and accepting a nested affordance—can be
dependent on what its solving could mean in the resolution of the global, macro
problem. Meaning, affordances can be selected and acted upon based on the
information available regarding the next potential affordance. This suggests that
some players are capable of acting relative to multiple affordances simultaneously
(and in a successive manner too), Think of a player like Barry Sanders for a

70
===== p71 =====
moment. Barry was notorious for making opponents miss across a variety of
dispositional problems. When closely investigating his movement behaviors,
armed with the critical concepts of this chapter, we find that Sanders could often
be found accepting affordances (i.e., making X defender miss by going in X
direction, at X time, utilizing X movement strategy) based on what was unfolding
in other areas within the landscape of affordances (e.g., movement problems
behind and/or around the immediate defender).

Sharing is Caring

Just as an athlete can become attuned to subtle differences in an opponent’s
movement behaviors, it’s also important for players to become perceptually
connected and sensitive to how their teammates can potentially behave. This
concept, known as shared affordances (Fajen et al., 2009; Silva et al., 2013), means
affordances perceived for others and of others (e.g., teammates). We have all likely
heard the old cliche before, “football is the ultimate team game.” Simply put, the
nature of a playet’s interactions with his teammates can be a major determining
factor in the movement behavior which emerges for each individual.

To illustrate, let’s imagine the following hypothetical interactions, and
how the information that a player may perceive, regarding the movement
behaviors of a teammate (i.e., interacting in relation to their own unfolding
problems), could potentially influence the decisions they make, and how they
ultimately act, based on the shared affordances that emerge:

e A RB willing to be patient near the line of scrimmage, detecting the
posture and kinematics of an OL in front of them (could also potentially
combine this information with that which is related to interpersonal
distance between them), because they may know that the OL is often late
to the point of attack in blocking attempts versus a defensive lineman or
LB.

e A QB waiting to attempt a deep pass down field, may typically be
perceptually attuned to the amount of separation between their wide
receivers and the opposing team’s defending cornerbacks. However, let’s
say that they have developed tremendous trust in the WR’s
understanding and knowledge of the game that the QB looks for the WR
to throw up their hand at the moment they believe (and perceive) that
they have the corner beat so the QB can subsequently deliver the ball to
where that specific WR likes it placed, and simply trusts that the WR can
come down with the pass attempt, regardless of how tightly the CB may
be playing the WR at the time (think of Tom Brady and Randy Moss for
the New England Patriots in the 2007 National Football League season).

e A safety (S) playing from inside the box, may take off laterally from the
wide side of the field to pursue a quick WR who has taken a handoff on
a jet sweep. The WR has a tight end (TE) moving slightly in front of him
that the S perceives and momentarily debates slowing his pursuit velocity
in relation to. However, the S also has his own outside LB attempting to

71
===== p72 =====
pick up the block attempt from the TE so that the S can subsequently
chase with maximum intent and speed. Thus, the S, having played a
number of seasons with the LB, knows the backer’s action capabilities
and perceives the LB’s speed to reach the TE in time for the S to stay on
his own pursuit path and acceleration trajectory to collide with the WR
and successfully tackle them.

As will be highlighted more in Chapter 6, the activities found within the practice
environment should give players ample opportunity to search for, and
subsequently explore the use of, this type of information and the affordances they
specify, so players are able to better understand their unfolding relationships with
teammates.

More Affordance Illustrations

We must remember that anything that cov/d be an affordance, must be measured
or assessed relative to the unique characteristics of the player himself (as
affordances are individual and frame-dependent). Meaning, Barry Sanders, Jerry
Rice, Ray Lewis, or any other player will perceive entirely different affordances
than you or anyone else will.

That being said though, investigating the composition and layout of the
environment can begin to indicate what specific opportunities for action may be
afforded to each individual (again, 7fwe possess the action capabilities to interact
with them). Gibson often used examples from everyday life, such as if a surface
is walk-on-able (i.e., it affords support for a human for locomotive purposes), or
if a tree is climb-up-able (i.e., the branches are sturdy and structured in a way that
offers the opportunity for a human to traverse it upwards), or if a chair (or a stool,
or a bench, or a tree stump) is sit-on-able (okay, you probably get the picture
now).

Those Gibson illustrations are just simple examples, existing within the
real world, that we should all be able to visualize and understand in reference to
our own behavior. Yet, within football, there will be a highly dynamic and
complex environment that players exist in where they will continuously interact
with emerging and decaying affordances—some of which they will select and act
upon, whereas others they will perceive but may ultimately elect to reject. Thus,
the identification of affordances that exist on a football field may be less obvious
at times. However, one thing remains clear; different layouts of the global
problem, along with various emerging local movement problems, will afford
different behaviors for different players (or an entirely different landscape of
affordances). This, in turn, will equate to different interactions and relations that
will inevitably unfold.

Of course, in the sport of American football, there are 11 opposing
players on the other side of the ball who are operating in a way that contradicts
(or attempts to constrain or restrict) the potential behavioral opportunities for
every other opponent. In other words, a given player, and his 10 teammates, are

72
===== p73 =====
all potentially (and hopefully) organizing their movement behaviors in a way that
affords more advantageous opportunities for one another, and less for their
opposing counterparts. Remember, an affordance points both ways; to the player
and to the environment, as well as between a player and his adversaries.

Figure 3.2 - Investigating the individual and frame-dependent nature of affordances for
Lamar Jackson.

To illustrate, let’s take a quick look at the third person view snapshot on
q P Pp

Figure 3.2 of Lamar Jackson, MVP-winning QB of the Baltimore Ravens, on a
play versus the Buffalo Bills, as he begins to interact with the landscape of
affordances present at this moment in time. Obviously, some of that which will
be perceived (throughout the unfolding dynamics of the problem) and the
affordances that are offered, and ultimately acted upon, are going to be dependent
ona number of constraints such as the particular play-call, the down and distance,
the time of the game, and various other potential factors. However, for the sake
of thought experimentation, try to put yourself in the human movement system
of Lamar Jackson, while amid this static snapshot.

Based on what we can see unfolding here, think deeply and ask:

What potential affordances could Jackson be perceiving that are all
simultaneously available to him?

As you work your way through those affordances (and any potential
simultaneous and successive opportunities to act also), what
informational variables within the problem do you believe he was
connecting to in order to tightly couple the subsequent coordination of
his movement behavior in relation with?

In the interactions of each peculiar local movement problem (and the
nested affordance contained within it), how else could Jackson have
behaved? What would this be dependent on?

What could have changed in the affordances available if it wasn’t Lamar
Jackson performing in this problem and instead it was a different player
(think of a few players at the QB position and speculate on this by using

73
===== p74 =====
theit individualized movement skill, action capabilities, and form of
life)?

e How could this information detection potentially be influenced by
certain extrinsic factors acting as constraints (e.g., score, quarter and time
of the game, down and distance, offensive play call, defensive tactics
being played, opponent’s characteristics)?

How Information & Affordances affect Skill Acquisition: Constrain
to Afford

As we explored within Chapter 2, with added exposure and experience to alive
movement problems (and /eamning to learn to move/ learning to learn to problem solve),
players can become perceptually attuned to the opportunities (1.e., affordances)
that are present in the environment and what exactly these offer to the player
(based on their action capabilities). As we will discuss at length later in Chapter
6, when manipulating constraints to design practice activities we should ensure
that:
¢ The movement problems that emerge there have a disposition that looks,
feels, acts, and unfolds similarly to that of the competitive performance
environment
e The potential information sources, which could be specifying, are always
present whenever possible so players can begin to couple their
movement behaviors to and through them (here, as a coach, we may
guide a player’s perceptual search so they're able to become more
attuned, educating their attention)
e As we scale complexity and begin to bring added layers to the movement
problems, we should investigate the landscape of affordances available
for the players in hopes that it may invite them to perceive and accept a
wider range of potential opportunities to interact with on gameday (i.e.,
skilled intentionality)

Knowing that accumulating repetitions is still a viable way to lead a player into
learning, we must place a high priority on the nature of those repetitions. In our
viewpoint, these reps can, and should, take place across a wide variety of
problematic dispositions (i.e., across diverse situations and conditions). As the
player exists there, a critical aspect of the skill adaptation and enhancement
process is helping them to change the information that they use to control their
movement actions, shifting from perceiving and acting upon less useful
information sources to more useful, specifying informational variables. To assist
in this process as ecologically minded coaching practitioners, we should constrain
to afford (Renshaw et al., 2019) during the movement problem-setting we embark
upon in our training and practice environments. To better illustrate this
constraining to afford process and exemplify how information and affordances
can affect skill adaptation for football players, let’s look at an example from a
handful of years ago, in Shawn’s work with a National Football League (NFL)

74
===== p75 =====
player he had in his learning environment.

The player was a starting TE who was also required to start on the punt
cover unit. Based on this role on special teams, the player was expected to be
adept at tackling highly dynamic, elusive players in space; sometimes in what
could be viewed upon as a local 1v1 dyadic problem. Obviously, being a TE (as
opposed to a LB or S who may possess movement skill nuances where tackling
is natural based on previous experience), this was not the type of movement
problem that this player had a lot of exposure solving.

After going through the practice film, counting all the repetitions the
player took during the spring during Organized Team Activities (OTAs) and
Minicamp, combined with those repetitions where a problem like this had
emerged during Training Camp, it was found that the TE only had three
repetitions where he was presented with a problem in a 1v1 situation in the open
field with a punt returner (PR) (Note: being that these occurred in practice, he
was also only required to tag off on the ball carrier too instead of attempting a
real tackle on the returner).

However, an NFL game on a Sunday is a very non-forgiving one to
play—it does not care what practice environments you’ve been placed within and
the problems you’ve been exposed to—as, during the regular season (he played
in all 16 games), he actually faced this type of situation on two separate occasions.
This may not seem like anything major as it was on/y two times. Right? Yet, within
both of those in-game situations, the TE could not coordinate a functional
movement solution—meaning he did not make a tackle or bring down the PR. To
make matters even worse, the TE’s 10 teammates also did not organize a
functional movement solution either! Thus, in both of those situations, the PR
scored a touchdown on the play. So, even though this particular type of
movement problem didn’t emerge very many times during the course of the
season (in practices or games), they did occur at a time of major significance (in
a game when a play could’ve been made to save a touchdown) where the player
was not able to adequately organize a solution to it mainly based on the lack of
representative exposure and experience leading up to that point. We feel as
though this illustrates the importance of coaches looking for ways to constrain to
afford, which means designing problems for players to interact with that invite
(or encourage) them to explore organizing more functional movement solutions
to meet the needs of the problems that emerge during games—specifically, those
related to the opportunities and gaps in a player’s skill set.

In the following offseason, namely in the five weeks leading up to that
season’s Training Camp, Shawn frequently set-up this type of unfolding problem
in their training environment for this player by designing a specific activity (also
see Chapter 6 for the activity listed as ‘High-speed special teams coverage’):

1. Having the TE perform a long-distance sprint after getting off an initial block
at the line of scrimmage, followed by;

2. Tracking the movement actions of a PR (who was catching a punt at an
undetermined place on the field), followed by;

3). Adaptively pursuing the ball carrying returner in space and attempting to

75
===== p76 =====
organize a functional movement solution to meet the respective needs of the
unfolding problem (and subsequently bring the returner down via executing a tag-

off on him).
To bring added likelihood for positive transfer, different PRs would be

rotated in as frequently as possible, all of whom possessed various movement
characteristics and tendencies (i¢., theit own problem-solving style), while also
manipulating the number of players involved in various positions across the field.
This constraint manipulation led to a practice activity design that was more alive
and representative, while also playing out in a more variable fashion, with added
repetition without repetition.

This type of practice activity, and the constraining to afford that ensued
with it, was done for 10-12 repetitions on a training day, a total of six times that
summer (accumulating approximately 60-72 total exposures to these types of
problems). Due to this purposeful constraint manipulation, it allowed the player
to become much more accustomed to some of the problem-solution dynamics
present in these respective punt cover situations. It was clear to see the sharp
increase in the TE’s attunement to the information and affordances present when
the player found himself in the midst of these respective situations on gameday
in that regular season. Though it would be a small sample size again, as the TE
found himself in a 1v1 dyadic situation with a returner only two more times on
an NFL Sunday in the following year. However, during both of these instances,
the situation (and accompanied movement problem-solving processes) played
out differently, and luckily, so did the outcome; on one of the plays, the TE single-
handily brought the returner down and, in the other instance, the TE walled the
returner off and forced him to run laterally east and west to head out of bounds.

# Affordances Are Opportunities for Action

**What it is** — An **affordance** is an opportunity for action (Gibson, 1979; Fajen et al., 2009) — or, in Withagen et al.'s (2012) framing, an **invitation** in the environment beckoning a player to act in a certain way. Affordances are the openings within a problem that guide and channel how a movement solution organises.

One qualification matters and is routinely lost: **affordances do not cause behaviour.** They constrain or channel it — eliminating options, offering invitations. They describe what this player *can and cannot do* under the constraints of this unfolding problem, in this context.

Gibson's own everyday examples make the shape of the concept clear: a surface that is walk-on-able, a tree that is climb-up-able, a chair that is sit-on-able. On a football field the affordances are less obvious but no less real — a gap that is pass-through-able, a defender that is beat-outside-able.

**Why it works** — Affordances are the concept that links problem and solution, because they refer to the *relation* between them. Turvey and Shaw (1995) call them the **functional semantics** of sport: a way of describing what the environment *is* to this player, in terms of how they can personally behave in it. Fajen et al. (2009) went so far as to say the theory of affordances "is ideally suited to capture the behavior of athletes on the playing field, and has great potential to become a guiding principle for research on perception and action in sport."

**When to apply** — Analysing film, and designing practice. In analysis, the affordances a player *accepts* are your best window into what they perceived and intended — you can never know directly, but acceptance is observable and lets you hypothesise. In design, the question becomes what opportunities a task makes available, rather than what movements it rehearses.

**When NOT to apply** — Do not treat "affordance" as a synonym for "option" or "cue." The word carries the specific claim that the opportunity is *directly perceivable* and *relational*, and using it loosely empties it. Also beware the just-so trap: because affordances cannot be observed directly, it is always possible to explain any action after the fact by positing the affordance that produced it. That is a description, not an explanation, unless it makes a prediction about what changes when you change the environment.

**Example** — Two backs face the same off-tackle run. One perceives an affordance to cut back between defenders; the other perceives one to bounce outside. Neither is wrong. The environment did not dictate either action — it offered both, and each player took the one that fit them.

# Affordances Point Both Ways: Effectivities Scale What Is Available

**What it is** — An affordance belongs to the player *and* to the environment at once. Gibson: the term "implies the complementarity of the animal and the environment." For an opportunity to exist for a given player, **that player must possess the ability to act on it** — their **effectivities**, or action capabilities.

The gap example makes it concrete. To perceive a gap between two defenders, a player must pick up whether that distance is **pass-through-able for him** — and to act on it, he must have enough acceleration to get through before it closes. Same physical gap, two players, two different landscapes: for one it is an affordance, for the other it does not exist.

**Why it works** — This is the precise sense in which affordances are **individual-dependent**. It also makes them **frame-dependent**: affordances available in the first quarter may be genuinely different from those in the fourth, because fatigue and other constraints have changed what the player can do. The environment did not change; the complementarity did.

**When to apply** — This is the entry that matters most for return to play, and it is worth stating plainly to a medical audience: **an athlete returning with altered action capabilities is facing a genuinely different landscape of affordances.** The gap they used to take is no longer take-able. If their perception has not rescaled to match — the calibration problem in [[framework--direct-learning-attention-intention-calibration]] — they will accept affordances they can no longer realise. That is a mechanism for re-injury that has nothing to do with tissue strength and will not appear on a strength test.

It also closes off a common shortcut: you cannot design one practice task and assume it presents the same problem to every player on the roster.

**When NOT to apply** — This is not an argument that capacity is what matters — see [[principle--action-capacity-is-not-skill]]. Capacity sets the boundary of the landscape; it does not determine what the player does inside it. Nor is the relationship simple enough to compute: knowing a player's 10-yard split does not tell you which gaps they will perceive, because perception of an affordance is learned and calibrated, not derived.

**Example** — A back six months from ACL reconstruction, cleared on strength testing, still reads gaps the way he did at full speed. He is not being reckless and he is not weak. His perception is calibrated to a body he no longer has, and nobody has designed the exposures that would recalibrate it.

# The Landscape of Affordances

**What it is** — At any moment a player faces not one opportunity but a **landscape** of them, offered **simultaneously and successively**. Affordances **emerge and decay dynamically** — they come and go, appear and disappear — so the landscape is not a menu but a shifting terrain.

Two properties define it:

- **Frame-dependent** — the same player meeting a comparable problem on a different occasion detects different opportunities, because the prevailing constraints differ (the opposing players' repertoire, field conditions, fatigue, down and distance).
- **Individual-dependent** — different players facing the identical layout face different landscapes. See [[principle--affordances-point-both-ways]].

The cognitive side has a name: **skilled intentionality** (Kiverstein & Rietveld, 2015) — openness and responsiveness to a rich landscape of affordances, letting the player stay linked to the range of possibilities actually present.

**Why it works** — It supplies the right unit for analysis. Because a landscape changes moment to moment, a **frame-dependent, moment-by-moment walk through a play** becomes the appropriate method for movement-skill and performance analysis — and the basis for designing the practice activity that follows.

The book is honest about the epistemic limit: on any given play **we will never truly know what the player is perceiving or what he is thinking**. But through the affordances he *accepts and acts upon*, we can at least hypothesise about the processes underneath. Acceptance is the observable; perception is the inference.

**When to apply** — Film study, done properly. The book's own exercise, on a still of Lamar Jackson against Buffalo, is a usable protocol for any clip:

1. What affordances could the player be perceiving, all simultaneously available?
2. What informational variables was he coupling to?
3. How else could he have behaved, and what would that depend on?
4. What would change if a *different* player were in this problem — given their movement skill, action capabilities and form of life?
5. How is information detection shaped by extrinsic constraints — score, quarter, down and distance, play call, opponent tendencies?

**When NOT to apply** — Marked **supported**: the landscape is a well-developed theoretical construct with no established measurement, and the analysis above produces hypotheses rather than findings. Two analysts will list different affordances for the same frame and there is no procedure here to adjudicate. Treat it as a disciplined way to *look*, not as a scoring method — and resist reporting an inferred affordance as though it were the player's actual experience.

**Example** — A coach grades a clip "wrong read." The landscape method asks what else was available, and what would have had to be true for the player's choice to have been the fitting one. Often the answer is that it *was* fitting for the affordances his body made available, and the coaching problem is elsewhere.

# Nested Affordances: Local Problems Inside Global Ones

**What it is** — Affordances sit inside one another. **Nested affordances** are the **micro, local** problems — make this defender miss, shed this blocker — solved en route to the **macro, global** problem: attain the first down, or limit the yards gained.

The consequential claim: **how a player solves the immediate local problem can depend on what solving it means for the global one.** An affordance is selected and acted on partly on the basis of information about the *next* potential affordance. Which implies some players are acting relative to **multiple affordances at once**, simultaneously and successively.

**Why it works** — It explains behaviour that looks like a mistake at the local scale and is correct at the global one. It also captures a real feature of football: one movement problem never exists in isolation. It is surrounded by successive problems and shaped by what came before it — **context-conditioned variability** — so the boundaries between one solution and the next are not cleanly locatable.

**When to apply** — Grading film, and setting practice problems. In analysis it stops you scoring a local decision without asking what it bought globally. In design it warns against a task that presents only one isolated local problem: solving a 1v1 with nothing behind it trains a different thing from solving the same 1v1 with a second defender arriving and a sideline to use.

**When NOT to apply** — Marked **supported**. That players act relative to multiple simultaneous affordances is an interpretation of observed behaviour, not a measured finding, and it is very hard to distinguish from a simpler account — a sequence of fast local decisions — using film alone. Be careful, too, not to use nesting to retro-justify every poor local decision as globally clever. And there is a practical limit: nesting makes analysis expensive, since you cannot grade a frame without the frames around it.

**Example** — Barry Sanders is the book's illustration: he can be found accepting an affordance — making *this* defender miss, in *this* direction, at *this* moment, with *this* strategy — on the basis of what was unfolding elsewhere in the landscape, including problems behind and around the immediate defender. The local move only makes sense given the global one.

# Shared Affordances: Reading What Teammates Afford

**What it is** — **Shared affordances** (Fajen et al., 2009; Silva et al., 2013) are affordances perceived **for others and of others.** A player becomes attuned not only to what opponents afford but to how *teammates* can behave — and what their behaviour opens or closes.

This is the ecological account of teamwork, and it does the job that shared mental models cannot ([[framework--shared-attunement-vs-shared-mental-models]]): coordination without prior communication, in situations nobody scripted.

**Why it works** — Because a teammate's action capabilities and tendencies are themselves information. Knowing what your teammate affords changes what you afford. The book's three illustrations:

- A **running back** willing to be patient at the line, reading the posture and kinematics of the offensive lineman in front of him — combined with interpersonal distance — *because he knows this lineman is often late to the point of attack.*
- A **quarterback** normally attuned to separation between receiver and cornerback, who has developed enough trust in one receiver's reading of the game that he throws on the receiver's raised hand and places the ball where that receiver likes it — regardless of how tight the coverage is. Brady and Moss in 2007.
- A **safety** from inside the box pursuing a jet sweep, momentarily debating whether to slow for a tight end moving across — until he perceives that *his own outside linebacker* will reach the tight end in time. Having played several seasons with that linebacker, he knows the backer's action capabilities, keeps his pursuit path and speed, and makes the tackle.

**When to apply** — Designing team practice, and defending it. Shared affordances only develop through repeated exposure to *these* teammates solving *live* problems together, which is an argument for opposed reps and against walkthroughs. It also gives a mechanism for why continuity of personnel matters — the safety's read is not transferable to a new linebacker.

**When NOT to apply** — Marked **supported**: the illustrations are anecdotal and constructed, not measured, and each could be redescribed in shared-mental-model terms by someone unpersuaded by the framework. Note also the failure mode: trust built on a teammate's tendencies becomes a liability when the teammate changes, is injured, or is substituted, and this account has nothing to say about how quickly attunement transfers to a replacement.

**Example** — For a returning athlete this reframes the last phase of rehab. Practising alone against a coach restores individual coupling but rebuilds none of the shared attunement, which is a distinct thing and takes reps with the actual unit.

# The Specifying Variables in 1v1 Evasion Problems

**What it is** — The candidate list of informational variables a player couples to in evasion-invasion situations — the running back versus linebacker dyad and its relatives. Drawn from work in rugby (Passos et al., 2008a, 2011, 2013) and basketball (Esteves et al., 2011), plus Button et al. (2020) and Yearby et al. (2022):

- **Relative angles** between competitors
- **Variations in gaps** between opponents and/or teammates
- **Relative velocity** values between competitors
- **Kinematics, body orientation and postural characteristics** of immediate opponents
- **Any combination** of these

The important negative result: **interpersonal distance alone is typically not sufficient** to coordinate a functional solution, even in these dyadic situations (Passos et al., 2011). Distance is the obvious variable and the one a coach reaches for first, and on its own it does not do the job. The critical values and useful ranges of any of these are **both context- and individual-specific.**

Gibson's compact statement of why the dyad is the right unit: **"Behavior affords behavior."** How two players interact gives rise to the emerging behaviours of each.

**Why it works** — Naming candidate variables converts "read the defender" from a platitude into something coachable. You can direct attention to relative angle or to body orientation; you cannot direct attention to "reading."

**When to apply** — Writing attention cues ([[framework--direct-learning-attention-intention-calibration]]), and designing tasks that make a particular variable available or salient. Also useful in analysis: when a player consistently mistimes evasion, hypothesise *which* variable they are coupling to and which they are missing.

**When NOT to apply** — Marked **supported**, and the authors are explicit about why: **this work is in rugby and basketball, not American football**, and they say directly that research specific to football is needed and that these findings offer "a starting point for applicable hypotheses." Treat the list as hypotheses to test with your own athletes, not as established football variables. Also, because critical values are individual-specific, no threshold from these studies transfers as a number.

**Example** — A defender consistently arrives a step late in space. Rather than more change-of-direction work, test the hypothesis that he is coupling to interpersonal distance alone. Set a task where distance is uninformative — the ball carrier varies velocity without varying distance — and see whether he adapts.

# The Specifying Variables in 1v1 Evasion Problems

**What it is** — The candidate list of informational variables a player couples to in evasion-invasion situations — the running back versus linebacker dyad and its relatives. Drawn from work in rugby (Passos et al., 2008a, 2011, 2013) and basketball (Esteves et al., 2011), plus Button et al. (2020) and Yearby et al. (2022):

- **Relative angles** between competitors
- **Variations in gaps** between opponents and/or teammates
- **Relative velocity** values between competitors
- **Kinematics, body orientation and postural characteristics** of immediate opponents
- **Any combination** of these

The important negative result: **interpersonal distance alone is typically not sufficient** to coordinate a functional solution, even in these dyadic situations (Passos et al., 2011). Distance is the obvious variable and the one a coach reaches for first, and on its own it does not do the job. The critical values and useful ranges of any of these are **both context- and individual-specific.**

Gibson's compact statement of why the dyad is the right unit: **"Behavior affords behavior."** How two players interact gives rise to the emerging behaviours of each.

**Why it works** — Naming candidate variables converts "read the defender" from a platitude into something coachable. You can direct attention to relative angle or to body orientation; you cannot direct attention to "reading."

**When to apply** — Writing attention cues ([[framework--direct-learning-attention-intention-calibration]]), and designing tasks that make a particular variable available or salient. Also useful in analysis: when a player consistently mistimes evasion, hypothesise *which* variable they are coupling to and which they are missing.

**When NOT to apply** — Marked **supported**, and the authors are explicit about why: **this work is in rugby and basketball, not American football**, and they say directly that research specific to football is needed and that these findings offer "a starting point for applicable hypotheses." Treat the list as hypotheses to test with your own athletes, not as established football variables. Also, because critical values are individual-specific, no threshold from these studies transfers as a number.

**Example** — A defender consistently arrives a step late in space. Rather than more change-of-direction work, test the hypothesis that he is coupling to interpersonal distance alone. Set a task where distance is uninformative — the ball carrier varies velocity without varying distance — and see whether he adapts.

# Where the Eyes Are Pointed Is Not What Is Being Perceived

**What it is** — A direct warning against the standard shortcut in perceptual assessment. Investigations of movement skill routinely reduce perception to the link between **where a player is looking** and what they are therefore assumed to be attending to. The authors call this out: **the two are not the same.** The eyes can be "camped, anchored, or fixated" somewhere while the specifying information needed to couple the action is **not actually being picked up**, and so is not being used to organise the movement.

A second, related point: perception is **not vision**. Though vision dominates in many football situations, attuned perception uses interconnected sensory subsystems:

- **Auditory** — a ball carrier chased from behind picks up audible breathing and foot strike, informing him of the degree of threat and how fast he must move to evade.
- **Dynamic touch** (Gibson, 1966) — texture and pressure on contact. A receiver detecting from fingertip contact how hard and fast to clasp; a linebacker reading direction and speed from his hands on an offensive lineman's chest while engaged in a block.

**Why it works** — Gaze is a proxy that measures the aiming of one sensor, and attunement is a property of the whole perceptual system's relation to the task. A proxy can be right on average and wrong in the individual case, which is exactly where assessment decisions get made.

**When to apply** — Evaluating any eye-tracking product, gaze-based assessment, or "visual training" claim. Also when interpreting a player's own report: "I was looking right at him" is not evidence that the relevant information was detected. And in contact positions, remember the haptic channel is doing real work that no visual measure will capture.

**When NOT to apply** — Marked **supported**: this is a well-reasoned caution, argued rather than demonstrated here, and it is not a claim that gaze data is worthless. Gaze research has produced genuine findings about expert-novice differences, and eye tracking remains one of the few objective windows onto perception available. The claim is narrower — gaze is not equivalent to attunement, so a gaze measure should not be read as a perception score.

**Example** — A screen-based perceptual-cognitive tool reports a player's "processing speed" from where they look and how fast they tap. It has measured neither the information that regulates a cut nor the action that couples to it. Whatever it is tracking, it is not the perceptual skill in question.

# Constrain to Afford

**What it is** — Renshaw et al.'s (2019) design heuristic, and the operating instruction that Chapters 2 and 3 build toward. **Design problems that invite the player to explore organising more functional solutions — specifically aimed at the opportunities and gaps in that player's skill set.** You do not add a constraint to restrict; you add it to *make an opportunity available* that was not there before.

The book's three design requirements for the practice activities that result:

- The movement problems that emerge should have a disposition that **looks, feels, acts, and unfolds similarly** to the competitive environment.
- The potential **specifying information sources should always be present** wherever possible, so players can couple to them — and the coach can guide perceptual search, educating attention.
- As complexity is scaled and layers are added, examine the **landscape of affordances** the task makes available, so it invites players to perceive and accept a **wider range** of opportunities on game day.

On repetitions the authors are pragmatic rather than purist: accumulating reps **is still a viable way to lead a player into learning** — the priority is on the *nature* of those reps, taken across a wide variety of problematic dispositions. The mechanism of improvement is stated crisply: help the player **change the information they use to control their actions**, shifting from less useful to more useful specifying variables.

**Why it works** — Because skill gaps are usually exposure gaps. A player who has never faced a problem has had no chance to become attuned to the information it presents. Constraining to afford is how you manufacture that exposure deliberately rather than waiting for it to occur.

**When to apply** — Whenever analysis has identified a specific gap. The sequence is: find the problem the player cannot yet solve → design a task that reliably produces that problem → vary it so the solving repeats without the solution repeating. See [[case-study--tight-end-punt-coverage-exposure-gap]] for a full worked instance.

For return to play the audit question is direct: **which problems will this athlete face on their first game back, and how many representative exposures to each have they actually had?**

**When NOT to apply** — Marked **supported**: this is a design principle with a strong rationale and a single illustrative case, not an intervention with a controlled trial behind it. Two cautions. First, a constraint that produces a solution not present in the game has designed in the wrong thing — constrain to afford *what the game affords*. Second, in rehabilitation the tissue is a real constraint, and inviting a solution the athlete cannot yet safely produce is the failure mode of this heuristic, not an aggressive application of it.

**Example** — A player who never gets 1v1 open-field tackling reps in team practice will not develop the attunement it requires, no matter how much tackling circuit work he does. The fix is not more tackling; it is a task that reliably generates *that* problem.

# Case Study: The Tight End Who Had Three Reps

**What it is** — Shawn Myszka's own account of an NFL tight end, and the most directly usable example in the first third of the book because it is an **exposure audit followed by a designed intervention followed by an observed change.**

**The situation.** A starting tight end also started on the punt-cover unit, where he was expected to tackle elusive players in space — often a 1v1 dyadic problem in the open field. As a tight end, rather than a linebacker or safety with tackling embedded in his movement history, this was not a problem he had much experience solving.

**The audit.** Myszka counted the reps. Across spring OTAs, minicamp and training camp, the player had faced a 1v1 open-field problem against a punt returner **three times** — and because these were practice, he was only required to tag off rather than tackle.

**The consequence.** In a 16-game regular season he faced that exact situation **twice**. Twice sounds negligible. In both, he could not coordinate a functional solution — no tackle. In both, his ten teammates did not either. **Both plays were returned for touchdowns.** The problem was rare and decisive at once.

**The intervention.** Over five weeks before the following training camp, Myszka built the problem deliberately (listed in Chapter 6 as *High-speed special teams coverage*):

1. A long-distance sprint after getting off an initial block at the line of scrimmage, then
2. tracking a punt returner catching the ball at an **undetermined** place on the field, then
3. adaptively pursuing in space and organising a solution to bring him down by tag-off.

Variation was built in: **different punt returners rotated in as often as possible**, each with their own movement characteristics, tendencies and problem-solving style, plus manipulation of how many players were involved and where. That made the activity alive, representative, and variable — repetition without repetition.

**The dose.** 10–12 reps per training day, six times that summer: roughly **60–72 exposures**, against three the year before.

**The outcome.** The following season he again met the 1v1 punt-return problem twice. This time both played out differently: on one he brought the returner down single-handedly; on the other he walled the returner off and forced him laterally out of bounds.

**Why it works** — It demonstrates the whole chain: gaps in skill are gaps in **representative exposure**; exposure is countable; and once counted it can be manufactured on purpose. See [[heuristic--constrain-to-afford]].

**When to apply** — As the template for a return-to-play audit. Count the problems the athlete will actually face and the representative exposures they have had to each. The count is usually far lower than anyone assumes, and the rare-but-decisive problems are the ones missed.

**When NOT to apply** — Marked **supported**, and the honest limit is the sample: **n = 1, with two game instances before and two after.** Two-of-two failure and two-of-two success is a compelling story and statistically almost nothing. The player also had a further year of general development and the reps were tag-off rather than live tackling. Use it as a demonstration of the *method* — audit, design, dose, re-check — not as evidence of an effect size.

**Example** — The transferable move is the arithmetic. Three practice exposures against two season occurrences is a ratio anyone can compute from practice film, and it makes an argument no amount of theory will.

234	Context shapes content
235	
236	As you can see, and as Shawn learned the hard way (on two related occasions), in
237	the world of complex adaptive systems in sports, context shapes content. We are
238	confident that performance analysis underpinned and informed by ideas within
239	ecological dynamics can represent the way forward for many within football
240	coaching, sports science, and talent evaluation. However, with the nonlinearity
241	present within skill execution and development, coupled with the highly diverse
242	nature of the dynamic problems found within the game, how do we really begin
243	to capture and understand the movement skills that emerge for players? Namely,
244	when a performance analysis is enlightened by ecological dynamics, what does
245	this look like?
246	
247	For starters, as you have learned by this point in the book, in an
248	ecological approach, the only relevant scope of analysis is one that is placed on
249	the player-environment relationship and the mutual, reciprocal nature of it
250	(Button et al., 2020). Meaning, we must closely investigate the movement
251	
252	81
253	===== p82 =====
254	problems that players are facing equally as much as the movement solutions that
255	are organized in attempts to resolve them. In Shawn’s story shared above, this is
256	looking at the finger avd the moon, together in unison. By shifting our attention
257	here, we can attempt to focus on ow the player is able to functionally adapt to
258	the specific constraints present within the game (as explored in Chapter 2 when
259	unpacking both skill and dexterity).
260	
261	Let’s recall that in this player-environment interaction, we will
262	conceptualize movement behavior as emerging from the intertwined processes
263	of perceptions, cognitions, and actions that underpin the problem-solving of
264	athletes. We propose that it is this holistic movement problem-solving process
265	(MPSP) that we must capture and attempt to explain when we are investigating
266	players. So, by adopting an ecological approach, one would study the interactive
267	processes involved in movement problem-solving in football; understanding how
268	playets coordinate their behaviors in dynamic performance environments
269	through the continuous, interconnected processes of perception (i.e., information
270	detection of affordances), cognition (e.g., intentions and decision-making), and
271	action (i.e., adjusting and adapting motor system degrees of freedom) to
272	functionally fit the needs, opportunities, and challenges of the problems
273	encountered in competition (the latter which we must begin to capture and
274	explain also).

276	The notion of gamespeed (aka football speed)
277	
278	Unfortunately, all too often, we find that both coaches and performance analysts
279	alike continue to place too much emphasis on performances happening well
280	outside of the context of the game—valuing the display of some performance
281	metric, no matter how it may come to be expressed (i.e., vot during the solving of
282	real-world football problems). One of the most obvious areas that we see this
283	outright decontextualization and misguided extrapolation of a_ specific
284	characteristic’s impact on performance is in the quantification of acceleration and
285	speed, captured in places like the NFL Scouting Combine, camps, or showcases.
286	We will acknowledge that these types of events likely aren’t going anywhere
287	anytime soon, nor are they likely to be modified in any major way to better respect
288	the problem-solution dynamics present in the game. Additionally, there may be
289	instances where we can glean something of value from these types of events and
290	the performance of players within them. However, all too often, we find very
291	well-intentioned football professionals continue to make erroneous assumptions
292	about how players may execute on the field simply stemming from their
293	misguided analyses.
294	
295	Luckily, it would seem as though some high performers within the sport
296	recognize the massive limitations of measuring speed in these ways, pushing our
297	need to go much beyond it in our analysis, as well as in the importance placed on
298	it in training. For example, in 2016, the Head Coach with the most Super Bowl
299	appearances and victories, Bill Belichick, stated:

365	Out of context measures of perception and cognition
366	
367	Speaking of problems to be solved that do not resemble those found on a football
368	field, we felt it was necessary to briefly address some newly popular methods of
369	assessing (or developing drills with the information gleaned from these
370	assessments) an athlete’s problem-solving qualities, namely those related to
371	various perceptual and cognitive functions. Recently, many football teams,
372	especially those at the higher levels, have begun to use tests targeting perception
373	and cognition in their scouting and talent identification process, such as the 52
374	Cognition, in attempts to determine weaknesses related to highly important
375	problem-solving characteristics needed to perform at the highest levels at given
376	positions on a football field (Clinton, 2025). S2 Cognition is a digital evaluation
377	test that is proclaimed to measure skills related to cognition, such as an array of
378	perceptual (e.g., search efficiency, tracking capacity) and decision-making
379	capabilities (e.g., improvisation, timing control) (https://www.s2cognition.com/).
380	Quite simply, empirical evidence on this testing method and the potential transfer
381	to the field is very limited at the time of this writing (Simons et al., 2016).
382	However, we would have serious doubts as to the level of its efficacy, at least if it
383	is being used for anything more than a general measure. Why do we make a claim
384	as bold as this? Well, these tests are quantifying reactions related to responding
385	to visual stimuli on a screen (using a specialized laptop and response pad) in an
386	attempt to subsequently predict how on-field processes unfold and the potential
387	results of performance. As we have already addressed in the pages leading up to
388	this point, the further a problem (or assessment) gets from that which actually
389	takes place on the field, the less relevance and practicality (i.e., functionality) the
390	behaviors found there will have to the context that really matters—in this case,
391	game day. See Renshaw et al. (2019) for a detailed critique.

393	How to watch film
394	
395	To be frank, the complexities of the game’s problems (and associated solution
396	dynamics organized by players in response to them) make it next to impossible
397	to sufficiently assess them live, in real-time (at least to get the most accurate
398	
399	84
400	===== p85 =====
401	analysis and draw any relevant hypotheses). Thus, much of our analysis process
402	likely needs to unfold while closely dissecting video and film (whether it’s from
403	practice or games). The realities of the human movement system, even of athletes
404	at the highest of levels, make this whole process even more challenging. Those
405	realities, namely oriented around the nonlinear nature of both motor learning and
406	skill execution, are those that we constantly must account for. For example, one
407	day, a player may be extremely sensitive in perceiving the information in their
408	environment (i.e., exhibiting perceptual attunement), and the very next day,
409	because of any number of contributing factors, they could be overwhelmed by
410	similar movement problems or missing opportunities that they seemed to be
411	adept at seizing before.
412	
413	Furthermore, minor changes to the movement problem being faced may
414	equate to the player coordinating dramatic changes to the movement solution
415	which emerges (and vice versa). Theoretically, the more film a coach can analyze
416	of a player, the more exposure to a wider range of complex movement problems
417	they should see the player attempting to solve in their own authentic fashion.
418	However, we should also remind ourselves that no two movement problems are
419	the same and there will simply be some problems that the player has never faced
420	as of yet. Thus, do not fret if, at the end of your analysis, you feel as though you
421	haven’t seen sufficient evidence to make a proclamation (for good or bad) as to
422	what a player may be capable of under certain constraints or when presented with
423	certain problems.
424	
425	That being said, it is helpful to find and analyze as much film as possible
426	to learn how players solve movement problems as it makes it more likely that you
427	will see a wider breadth of interactions for a player. For example, when first
428	starting with a new NFL player, using NFL+ or NFL Rewind (or other resources
429	like them), Shawn performs a deep movement skill analysis of the player by
430	watching every single snap the player has taken within the league. Additionally,
431	depending on the age and status of the player, he will also go back to any college
432	game film he may have access to (even if it is just highlights or clips). Finally, one
433	could even look at highlights from the player’s high school days. When you begin
434	to look at the movement behavior emerging on a field through the ecological lens
435	around context-content, you would be shocked at some of the trends in a player’s
436	skill you can see unfolding over the course of their development. We understand
437	that this can all sound quite daunting and may seem like overkill, but we feel that
438	it is essential to unpack how the current phenomena that is the player’s movement
439	skill has come to be over time if we are to adequately determine where the player
440	may need to go in the future (and how we can best assist him in doing so for his
441	skill development).

444	or if you work as an individual trainer or coach) may determine the nature of the
