===== p77 =====
CHAPTER 4

Analyzing the Player-Environment Relationship

It’s time for us to move our discussion from more theoretical and philosophical
to being much mote practically driven. Meaning, it’s time to dive into how the
important concepts discussed in the earlier chapters can directly change how
you're viewing the game and the organization of movement behaviors of the
players within it. Namely, we are going to unpack how being armed with an
ecological dynamics framework will allow you to more effectively understand the
ways that players are solving movement problems on the field, the challenges they
face, the gaps and limitations they display, and where (and how) we may need to
spend time in the individualized development of their skill. To conclude this
chapter, we will bring things full circle by analyzing one of the most dexterous
movers the sport has witnessed in recent years, carrying out a Strengths,
Weaknesses, Opportunities, and Threats (SWOT) analysis on his skill, and
offering a number of general suggestions as to how his movement behavior could
be improved through the use of contemporary skill acquisition practice
principles.

Keeping Player-Environment Relations Intact Within Analysis

As discussed in Chapter 1, tradition has seemed to repeatedly set the tone
throughout various practices within the sport of football. The ‘this is the way we
have always done it’ attitude that is highly prevalent, as already highlighted, leads
to coaches within practice environments clinging tightly to breaking down the
technical actions of players in detail and then repeating them (in practice) until
the players theoretically cannot get it wrong (in games). However, not to be
outdone by practice design and the guidance of players’ skill execution by
coaches, the practical approach of those carrying out performance analysis duties
(e.g., general managers, scouts, sports scientists) and other player support roles
(e.g., Sports medicine, physical preparation) can also be found grasping at straws
laid out by many of the traditional customs of the sport.

Repeatedly across football citcles, like a dog chasing its own tail, we hear
the questions being asked: How fast does the player run? How quickly can they
change direction? How high do they jump? How effortless or fluid do they look
when they complete the position drills? Are they currently executing the right
technique(s)?

Truth is, across these circles, we find one underlying theme that can be
threaded throughout: an adoption of reductionism that seems to give
practitioners added comfort and control, even if it fails to adequately capture the
complex nature of the game and the roles within it. This leads to talent evaluators
paying close attention to the execution of players in an environment devoid of

77
===== p78 =====
contextual information, such as the National Football League (NFL) Scouting
Combine. This focus may then trickle down to the priorities of many strength &
conditioning coaches who chase the enhancement of physical qualities and
measurables, sometimes forgetting to look at how these abilities are being applied
and expressed out on the field. We may see the same thing unfolding in the
practices of those within sports medicine (e.g., athletic trainers, rehabilitation
specialists, physiotherapists), who may chase repeatability and the isolation of
positions and patterns being coordinated by the rehabilitating athlete, during
exercises that are purported to be foundational to other more complex movement
skills found in the game. Last, but certainly not least, we find position coaches
during ‘individual’ (Indy) drills, installation periods, and other practice periods,
emphasizing the importance of detailed technical execution and idealistic ways of
behaving in practice tasks (e.g., unopposed drills) that do not always look, feel, or
unfold anything like competitive football problems will demand.

Now, we are certainly not beyond falling guilty of adopting such an
approach depicted above. In fact, we have all actually learned the hard way of the
significant repercussions that can come if we are not careful and look to consider
more of the context-content relationship (e.g., player-environment, problem-
solution) which should begin to drive more of the practical approaches
undertaken in the field across the sport. To illustrate, let’s join Shawn for two
quick stories (told in the next two sections) as we collectively take a quick walk
down memory lane before expanding upon where we suggest more in football
should consider standing.

Two toads diverged

The year was 2008. Besides a brief stint in the Strength & Conditioning
department with the Chicago Bears in 2003, most of my athlete training time up
to that point was with lower-level movers and developmental athletes
(predominantly high school) at my training facility in Eden Prairie, Minnesota.
Yes, we had an occasional professional athlete come through the facility, namely
from the National Basketball Association (NBA), Major League Baseball (MLB),
and Association of Tennis Professionals (ATP) tennis tour. However, working
with, and alongside, high-level professional American football players was what I
had ahvays aspired to be doing. Thus, “sis situation that awaited me was my shot
at proving what I could do!

A starter in the NFL (a player who shall remain anonymous based on the
nature of this story) had gotten my contact information from a Sports
Rehabilitation Specialist that I had partnered with prior to that point working
with a number of those aforementioned other professional athletes. The fellow
professional insisted to the athlete: “Shawn is a different type of trainer and will
certainly take your game to the next level based on how he attacks an athlete’s
weaknesses!” I appreciated the good Doctor’s recommendation because, at least
in my mind too, he was not wrong! This sentiment was about to be tried and
tested though.

78
===== p79 =====
Like any self-respecting strength & conditioning professional, before I
could ever even begin to fathom working with the player, I ran him through a
gamut of athlete testing measures that I had access to and that I strongly believed
to be important. Looking back at it now, that testing session at the facility
probably closely resembled a late February day in Indianapolis at the annual NFL
Scouting Combine, both in the level of the seriousness that I approached this
testing with, and the specific tests and drills I subjected the player to. In fact, even
though some time has now passed since that initial interaction, I can still
remember the player explicitly saying to me, “what is this, the Combine?!” In
retrospect, that should have been my first indication that I was nof exactly on the
right track with what I was asking him to perform.

Yet, when the smoke had cleared on the day, and I began to compare the
player’s performance versus his Combine testing just a few years prior when he
first entered the NFL, I realized just how far off his performance currently was.
In fact, both the player and I were shocked to find out how much he had
diminished in many of the areas that are deemed to be important by so many
across football (including me at that moment in time). For example, his standing
countermovement vertical jump had decreased by just over five inches while his
40-yard dash time was two tenths of a second (0.20) slower.

Of course, I set out to change this! I thought to myself, ‘how could he
even be playing at a starter level these last three seasons?!’ Thus, I had big
aspirations to not only get his physical prowess back up to par, but far exceed
those past performance numbers as I believed that when I would be able to do
that (in my mind, it wasn’t a matter of 7), I would also be able to send him back
to his team in such a superior state that he was sure to go dominate in the
upcoming season.

You may be able to see the writing on the wall as to what unfolded from
here. Due to the work the player and I put in over the course of the next 12
weeks, the player did increase his performance in each of these key testing
measures. I am talking about significant improvements here, especially for a
professional athlete. For example, he increased his vertical jump by over seven
inches, his broad jump by 14 inches, and his 40-yard dash and pro-agility shuttle
times both improved by 0.25 seconds! However, when he went back to his team
for NFL Training Camp that July, and he performed on the practice field, he
reported to me each day, “things just feel okay.” Day-to-day, the time passed each
week during Camp, and I| anxiously awaited the preseason games ahead, thinking
that the player was just being modest and showing humility, and was, in fact,
actually dominating in everything he was being asked to do on the field. However,
the preseason games arrived (and later the regular season too), and he was spot-
on in his affective analysis: not only did it just feel okay, it also only looked okay
(to my subjective analysis). Now, on-field, he didn’t look horrible but he also
didn’t look to be behaving any differently than he was in the past.

As a relatively young strength and conditioning (S&C) coach, I was
beyond flabbergasted and puzzled: how could this be?! With all the improvements
made, how was there no change to what was emerging on the field for the player?

79
===== p80 =====
At this point, there seemed to be two roads diverged in the trail, and it was clear
that I needed to take the road less traveled. Meaning, instead of doing what I had
always done (or what tradition would indicate across the football performance
community), in terms of supporting players in chasing performance metrics, |
needed to more closely investigate the movement behaviors of players on the
field and center the focus there in my coaching, aiming to impact athletes in
becoming more masterful at executing these behaviors when and where it counts:
on gameday. This all led to a transformation of me and my craft, and ultimately,
changed the trajectory of my career. Instead of being justa personal performance
coach (or S&C professional if you’d prefer), I began to consider myself to be a
Movement Coach (from 2008 to 2012).

The next road

Being a Movement Coach, I began to really dive into the study of the way(s) that
players moved on the field much more intimately. In fact, this ‘movement
analysis’ began to drive my entire approach and the related programming within
it. For example, any of the ways that the game was routinely asking players to
move on the field (e.g., highlighted by the motor patterns, positions, shapes, and
actions an outside observer would witness), quickly became my religious focus
where players and I would attempt to perfect every minute detail of those
movement patterns, with the expectation that they would then automatically
unfold on game day. We collectively lived and breathed the old cliche that perfect
practice makes perfect. 1 would then go back through the film with a fine-tooth comb,
zooming in on the movements to determine if they were, in fact, getting closer to
perfection. If they weren’t, I almost always chalked it up to the expectation that
players simply needed more repetitions, of more perfect execution, unfolding in
a more deliberate and intentional fashion.

At the end of the season in 2012, I was at the Metrodome in Minneapolis,
MN for the final game of the regular season for the Minnesota Vikings as they
faced off against the Green Bay Packers in hopes of finding themselves in the
playoffs the following weekend. This game just so happened to be the same one
where Adrian Peterson was attempting to break the single season rushing record
(ultimately coming up 8 yards short of Eric Dickerson’s 2,105 yard total from
1984). Though the Vikings won the game, and a number of the players I had
partnered with on that roster seemed to be thriving (on the field), I watched from
the lower level of the Metrodome with an overwhelming feeling that there was
still something major missing. It was like an out-of-body experience of sorts,
honestly, as I could see so clearly that many of these very players were actually
performing én spite of me and the work we were doing rather than because of me
and the work we did together. I’ve said many times over my career that the NFL’s
best players are simply the world’s best compensators. Well, as I thought back to
the countless (near perfect!) repetitions performed in our training facility over the
course of that calendar year, and as I analyzed the game film, comparing our
training drills to how players were actually executing within their movement on

80

|
===== p81 =====
the field when the time(s) for it arose, 1 found that the players were doing that
which they knew how to do best. Meaning, they were compensating and adapting
in any way that they could to swim in the deep waters of complexity on-field.

It was duting this experience outlined above, and what I learned there
about my work with players, that I began to view my role very differently and this
included what I would need to see within the performance analyses I carried out.
A Bruce Lee quote from one of my favorite all-time movies, Enter the Dragon,
began to speak loudly to me. He said, “It’s like a finger pointing away to the
moon. Don’t concentrate on the finger or you will miss all that heavenly glory.”
It all hit me! I was so busy focusing on the finer, minute details of the player and
their movement (i.e., the finger), without paying equal respect to the problems
truly found within the environment (ie., all the heavenly glory), and the
interactive relationship between these two. This is why I felt, that despite some
success on-field for the players I worked with, there was still something major
missing that I needed to address to more effectively prepare the players. As 2013
kicked off, I began to deeply explore ideas from an ecological dynamics
framework, and both my performance analysis (¢.g., now unpacking the problem-
solving interactions in a mutual relationship with the dynamic environment) and
my training environments (e.g., now containing aliveness, constantly changing
problems, and repetition without repetition) began to see tremendous changes
emerge. Along with it, the essence of me and my role also began to
metamorphosize from that of the Movement Coach that I had come to be in
2008, to the Skill Acquisition Specialist (SAS) that I now stand in front of the
community as. It is my hope that by sharing both of these stories, it can serve as
anecdotal evidence for all out there as to the importance of investigating the right
things, in order to paint the most complete picture around not only who a player

might be, but also how we may attempt to influence their performance on the
field.

Context shapes content

As you can see, and as Shawn learned the hard way (on two related occasions), in
the world of complex adaptive systems in sports, context shapes content. We are
confident that performance analysis underpinned and informed by ideas within
ecological dynamics can represent the way forward for many within football
coaching, sports science, and talent evaluation. However, with the nonlinearity
present within skill execution and development, coupled with the highly diverse
nature of the dynamic problems found within the game, how do we really begin
to capture and understand the movement skills that emerge for players? Namely,
when a performance analysis is enlightened by ecological dynamics, what does
this look like?

For starters, as you have learned by this point in the book, in an
ecological approach, the only relevant scope of analysis is one that is placed on
the player-environment relationship and the mutual, reciprocal nature of it
(Button et al., 2020). Meaning, we must closely investigate the movement

81
===== p82 =====
problems that players are facing equally as much as the movement solutions that
are organized in attempts to resolve them. In Shawn’s story shared above, this is
looking at the finger avd the moon, together in unison. By shifting our attention
here, we can attempt to focus on ow the player is able to functionally adapt to
the specific constraints present within the game (as explored in Chapter 2 when
unpacking both skill and dexterity).

Let’s recall that in this player-environment interaction, we will
conceptualize movement behavior as emerging from the intertwined processes
of perceptions, cognitions, and actions that underpin the problem-solving of
athletes. We propose that it is this holistic movement problem-solving process
(MPSP) that we must capture and attempt to explain when we are investigating
players. So, by adopting an ecological approach, one would study the interactive
processes involved in movement problem-solving in football; understanding how
playets coordinate their behaviors in dynamic performance environments
through the continuous, interconnected processes of perception (i.e., information
detection of affordances), cognition (e.g., intentions and decision-making), and
action (i.e., adjusting and adapting motor system degrees of freedom) to
functionally fit the needs, opportunities, and challenges of the problems
encountered in competition (the latter which we must begin to capture and
explain also).

The notion of gamespeed (aka football speed)

Unfortunately, all too often, we find that both coaches and performance analysts
alike continue to place too much emphasis on performances happening well
outside of the context of the game—valuing the display of some performance
metric, no matter how it may come to be expressed (i.e., vot during the solving of
real-world football problems). One of the most obvious areas that we see this
outright decontextualization and misguided extrapolation of a_ specific
characteristic’s impact on performance is in the quantification of acceleration and
speed, captured in places like the NFL Scouting Combine, camps, or showcases.
We will acknowledge that these types of events likely aren’t going anywhere
anytime soon, nor are they likely to be modified in any major way to better respect
the problem-solution dynamics present in the game. Additionally, there may be
instances where we can glean something of value from these types of events and
the performance of players within them. However, all too often, we find very
well-intentioned football professionals continue to make erroneous assumptions
about how players may execute on the field simply stemming from their
misguided analyses.

Luckily, it would seem as though some high performers within the sport
recognize the massive limitations of measuring speed in these ways, pushing our
need to go much beyond it in our analysis, as well as in the importance placed on
it in training. For example, in 2016, the Head Coach with the most Super Bowl
appearances and victories, Bill Belichick, stated:

“The time-speed is always a tricky thing because time-speed isn’t football speed ... So a
player's running a ball or running full speed covering a kick or running the ball and there is
people in front of him and people trying to tackle him, it’s a little different speed than running
a sprint on the stopwatch" (Florio, 2016).

Additionally, the most productive wide receiver (WR) to have ever played the
game, Jerry Rice, routinely talked about the differences between being fast and
displaying football speed. In fact, Rice reportedly ran relatively slow times in the
40-yard dash coming out of college at Mississippi Valley State, with some
observers in attendance at his pro day recording his speed as slow as 4.71 seconds.
Rice’s 40-yard performance obviously leaves a great deal to be desired under most
people’s standards at the position. However, very few WRs could ever play the
game as skillfully as Rice. He stated: “You’ve got to separate yourself from the
DB [defensive back]. That’s all it is. And I don’t really know where the extra speed
comes from that makes me do it (Oates, 1987).” Teammate and fellow Hall of
Fame player, Ronnie Lott, said about Rice: “Fifi [Rice's nickname] has deceptive
speed. He may be 4.6 [seconds over 40 yards] on Tuesday and Wednesday, but
he’s 4.2 on Sundays.” These types of anecdotes suggest that many well-meaning
coaches and analysts may have been slightly misguided in how they seek to
identify and develop prospective players.

If we begin to draw upon the ideas that form ecological dynamics and
use this to shape our perspective, the notion of speed could be (re)conceptualized
as gamespeed, or, following the quote offered by Belichick, football speed. Football
speed would transcend the traditional ways of viewing speed and acceleration,
emphasizing the mutual nature of the player-environment relationship, centering
a player’s Anowledge of (Gibson, 1966) the game as a key performance indicator in
how they move while solving problems on the field. Thus, enhancing one’s
knowledge of the environment is an integral part of skill acquisition methods
utilized in football as well as in steps taken in assessing a playet’s skill through the
ways they solve problems. Namely, this distinctive conceptualization of
knowledge and problem-solving may also imply that the game’s fastest players are
those who can operate at “optimal” speeds while interacting with alive problems
of the competitive environment, and not always those who register the fastest
times On a stopwatch while running a set distance outside of game contexts (e.g.,
like as seen within the NFL Combine during the execution of decontextualized
tests and drills).

This idea of football speed could begin to help us explain why many of
the names we might see near the top of the fastest times ever recorded at the
NFL Combine never made a distinctive mark on the field while playing in the
NFL. Though some players may register fast 40-yard dash times AND also
execute at a high level on the field under the problematic demands of their
position (e.g., Chris Johnson, Champ Bailey), there are countless others where
there seemed to be a large disparity between their performance on the field
(possessing gamespeed/football speed) and the fast times they recorded running
in nothing but their underwear in Indianapolis (e.g., Dri Archer, John Ross). Of

Out of context measures of perception and cognition

Speaking of problems to be solved that do not resemble those found on a football
field, we felt it was necessary to briefly address some newly popular methods of
assessing (or developing drills with the information gleaned from these
assessments) an athlete’s problem-solving qualities, namely those related to
various perceptual and cognitive functions. Recently, many football teams,
especially those at the higher levels, have begun to use tests targeting perception
and cognition in their scouting and talent identification process, such as the 52
Cognition, in attempts to determine weaknesses related to highly important
problem-solving characteristics needed to perform at the highest levels at given
positions on a football field (Clinton, 2025). S2 Cognition is a digital evaluation
test that is proclaimed to measure skills related to cognition, such as an array of
perceptual (e.g., search efficiency, tracking capacity) and decision-making
capabilities (e.g., improvisation, timing control) (https://www.s2cognition.com/).
Quite simply, empirical evidence on this testing method and the potential transfer
to the field is very limited at the time of this writing (Simons et al., 2016).
However, we would have serious doubts as to the level of its efficacy, at least if it
is being used for anything more than a general measure. Why do we make a claim
as bold as this? Well, these tests are quantifying reactions related to responding
to visual stimuli on a screen (using a specialized laptop and response pad) in an
attempt to subsequently predict how on-field processes unfold and the potential
results of performance. As we have already addressed in the pages leading up to
this point, the further a problem (or assessment) gets from that which actually
takes place on the field, the less relevance and practicality (i.e., functionality) the
behaviors found there will have to the context that really matters—in this case,
game day. See Renshaw et al. (2019) for a detailed critique.

How to watch film

To be frank, the complexities of the game’s problems (and associated solution
dynamics organized by players in response to them) make it next to impossible
to sufficiently assess them live, in real-time (at least to get the most accurate

84
===== p85 =====
analysis and draw any relevant hypotheses). Thus, much of our analysis process
likely needs to unfold while closely dissecting video and film (whether it’s from
practice or games). The realities of the human movement system, even of athletes
at the highest of levels, make this whole process even more challenging. Those
realities, namely oriented around the nonlinear nature of both motor learning and
skill execution, are those that we constantly must account for. For example, one
day, a player may be extremely sensitive in perceiving the information in their
environment (i.e., exhibiting perceptual attunement), and the very next day,
because of any number of contributing factors, they could be overwhelmed by
similar movement problems or missing opportunities that they seemed to be
adept at seizing before.

Furthermore, minor changes to the movement problem being faced may
equate to the player coordinating dramatic changes to the movement solution
which emerges (and vice versa). Theoretically, the more film a coach can analyze
of a player, the more exposure to a wider range of complex movement problems
they should see the player attempting to solve in their own authentic fashion.
However, we should also remind ourselves that no two movement problems are
the same and there will simply be some problems that the player has never faced
as of yet. Thus, do not fret if, at the end of your analysis, you feel as though you
haven’t seen sufficient evidence to make a proclamation (for good or bad) as to
what a player may be capable of under certain constraints or when presented with
certain problems.

That being said, it is helpful to find and analyze as much film as possible
to learn how players solve movement problems as it makes it more likely that you
will see a wider breadth of interactions for a player. For example, when first
starting with a new NFL player, using NFL+ or NFL Rewind (or other resources
like them), Shawn performs a deep movement skill analysis of the player by
watching every single snap the player has taken within the league. Additionally,
depending on the age and status of the player, he will also go back to any college
game film he may have access to (even if it is just highlights or clips). Finally, one
could even look at highlights from the player’s high school days. When you begin
to look at the movement behavior emerging on a field through the ecological lens
around context-content, you would be shocked at some of the trends in a player’s
skill you can see unfolding over the course of their development. We understand
that this can all sound quite daunting and may seem like overkill, but we feel that
it is essential to unpack how the current phenomena that is the player’s movement
skill has come to be over time if we are to adequately determine where the player
may need to go in the future (and how we can best assist him in doing so for his
skill development).

The specific role that you have (e.g., whether you work directly for a team
or if you work as an individual trainer or coach) may determine the nature of the
specific film you have access to (e.g., practice or game film, various views).
However, as a general rule, we would recommend watching each play from as
many vantage points as possible (e.g., sideline view, endzone view, all-22) and
across various speeds (e.g., full speed, half speed, super slow motion). This will

help to ensure that you are able to crosscheck the details of your analysis across
conditions to offer a more complete glimpse into a playet’s interactions within

A Player’s Form of Life

Just as no two movement problems will ever be the same (if investigated at a deep
enough level anyway), no two athletes ever move or behave in the exact same
manner. The player and their movement solution is like a fingerprint or a
snowflake—each one is different from every other that exists. Not only is this
the way it should be, but we, as coaches, should attempt to harness this
authenticity and also use this understanding of who someone is, to better inform
our performance analysis and attempt to understand the player’s unique MPSP.
You see, the differing styles of solving problems—and using one’s own

way—is made possible by, and is also progressively shaped from, one’s form of life
and how it may evolve over a player’s lifetime. What could be categorized as a
player’s form of life, according to Vaughan and colleagues (2019), can begin to
capture an individual’s ways of being, acting, and behaving. In other words, this
form of life could be best described by the unique personality, essence, or style
witnessed when a player moves and performs on a football field—it is what is
displayed within the authentic movement behavior that the player expresses
himself through. As Bruce Lee famously said on the Pierre Burton Show in 1971,
“To honestly express oneself ... now that, my friend, is very hard to do.”
Practically speaking, for us in our performance analysis and evaluation process,
we must remember that one’s form of life could facilitate (or also limit) one’s
perception, selection, and actualization of the affordances present on a football
field while the integrated MPSP unfolds. The player’s form of life could be shaped
by things such as the following:

e where they are from

e how they grew up

¢ previous sports they played

¢ activities they like to do

¢ quirky tendencies of their personality

Overall, what we witness as a player solves problems on the field can be
somewhat thought of as a cumulative product, one that is impacted by a long list
of potential influencing factors from an athlete’s past. Their experiences all flow
into a peculiar movement skillset, coalescing at that moment in time to help bring
about this specific, emerging movement solution. In summary, the following
questions are pertinent for us to explore in our performance analysis:
e How has the player’s upbringing, as well as the unique interests they
have, impacted what we witness from them?
e What movement experiences have potentially influenced them in the way
they uniquely see the world?
e What qualities make them different from other players who play their
position when involved in "these types" of movement problems?

better understand the phenomenon of the movement behavior we see unfolding.

form of life. For instance, imagine we are witnessing a player like Kyler Murray
(QB, Arizona Cardinals), making a side-arm throw, executed while on the run or

What are they ‘attuning to’ & ‘adapting around’?

To help players organize movement solutions with an enhanced functional fit,
coaches must attempt to assess what their current movement problem-solving
processes consist of (see Chapter 2 for more). In doing so, and while qualitatively
assessing how the player interacts with the unfolding problems (i.e., how they are
acting, cognizing, and perceiving), coaches should ask themselves, "What are they
attuning to and adapting around?

While watching plays unfold, coaches should be attempting to adequately
and accurately tell the movement problem-solving story for each player—trying
to get into their human movement system and the organization of their integrated
movement solutions (IMS). Doing so can help coaches to understand more about
the information players could be detecting (i.e., perceiving), what the information
and its opportunities could mean to them (i.e., the affordances), and how they are
flexibly adapting their actions to take advantage of opportunities to get closer to
their goal at the moment (i.e., their cognitive degrees of freedom in terms of their
intentions and strategies for resolving the problems).

To help illustrate, imagine investigating the movement skills of a RB.

Along with analyzing the context of the emerging movement problem—
highlighting its peculiar disposition—coaches and performance analysts should
speculate as to how the RB is coordinating and controlling an IMS to functionally
fit the problem. In this case, the information that the RB is perceiving related to
the behavior of the opponent(s) may be scrutinized, such as the number of
opponents in a given space, their speed, and their posture and/or kinematics,
Next, think about how the information detection feeds into, with tight circular
causality (note: remember it goes both ways), what the RB intends to do moment-
by-moment and the decisions they are making (or the potential affordances
they’re rejecting too). Finally, these more qualitative speculations will perpetually
feed into the observable movement strategies they are carrying out (i.e., how they
are acting) and how these actions are being adapted based on the unfolding nature
of the problem. In short, if coaches can gain an informed understanding regarding
what a player is attuned to and adapting around, it can help to identify potential
areas of improvement and problematic slices of the game where players can be
immersed within to help them develop their movement skills in relevant ways.

Using the illustration unpacked above, but going beyond the RB
position, some examples of key events that could unfold on a given play for other
positions, that we may elect to investigate deeper, could include:

e A DE and OL relationship in the ongoing interaction as the rusher
attempts to get past the OL in an attempt to sack the QB or bring down

a RB

e A WR and DB interaction at the moment a passed ball is reaching the
target and the ball is either received (by the WR) or broken up (by the

DB)

e A LB looking to find the right time and location for a gap to shoot

through the line of scrimmage in an attempt to bring a ball carrier down
in the backfield

Semi-structured interviews with players

An often-overlooked method of analyzing is that which can be performed when
we lean into the experience of the player in attempting to understand how they
were approaching the MPSP in situ. After all, players can be the coach or SAS’s
most important collaboration partner. Here, semi-structured interviews could be
used to gain a first-person, post-performance account of players’ lived experience
relating to their movement problem-solving processes (i.e., what they perceived,
intended to do, remember feeling in the moment). These types of interviews
could allow for both rigor and flexibility in the exchange between the
performance analyst and the player. In particular, when watching video of the
player in action, interview questions can focus on informational variables the
player believes they detected during the solving of each problem, and how they
subsequently adapted their movement actions in relation to these perceptions.
Though these types of interactions will unfold retrospectively, and the player may
not be able to explicitly state or vividly recall exactly how they went about their
process of solving each problem we see on film, they can also bring added insight
not accessible in the rest of the analysis. At the very least, involving the athletes
in your performance analysis can create added buy-in, trust, and ownership
between the player and subsequent direction of skill enhancement efforts. A
number of questions to be asked could include:
e What information do you remember picking up about the unfolding
problem?
e What were you aiming to do here, and what led to the decision you made?
e Are there any practice activities that you have utilized in the past that you
feel positively contributed to how you acted in this play?
e How else do you feel you could have acted in response to solving this
type of problem successfully?

93
===== p94 =====
What about measurables and metrics?

Of course, in today’s football performance landscape, many programs are now
utilizing various forms of technology and devices for player tracking to try to
analyze team or individual performance and/or gain insight regarding (some)
aspects of a player’s movement behaviors on the field. The most common
methods employed here are GPS trackers worn in a vest under one’s jersey or
RFID tags within one’s shoulder pads. Typically, sports scientists or performance
analysts will utilize these systems to determine a variety of metrics, usually related
to speeds (e.g., peak speed at different times of the game), distances covered, load,
and analysis of key biomechanical events, such as acceleration and deceleration
or other explosive efforts.

Though this type of quantitative data and associated analysis could prove
to be useful in supporting a thorough and well-rounded performance analysis,
coaches and support staff must be careful not to overprioritize the data collected
without attempting to add context to what the numbers depict. In a perfect world,
it would be desirable for coaches and support staff to adopt a more integrated
approach with systems thinking when analyzing data. Embracing this approach
would entail attempting to quantify the environment as a place for problem-
solving (e.g., measuring locations of players forming the disposition of a
problem), allowing more to move beyond capturing numbers that solely describe
some aspect of an individual player’s movement qualities (e.g., top speed reached
during a play).

That said, a mixed-methods approach, utilizing these types of existing
quantitative measures alongside our detailed qualitative film analysis discussed
earlier, could prove to be highly beneficial if coaches want to draw comprehensive
conclusions around the level of the player’s movement skill. Simply put, we feel
that a mixed-methods approach supports a more holistic analysis of sport
movement behaviors by accounting for the complex and dynamic nature of
various relationships at several levels (Anguera et al., 2012).

Identification of Gaps & Weaknesses

Of course, the purpose of any detailed performance analysis is to adequately and
accurately understand the movement problem-solving nature of the players
you’re entrusted with coaching and helping to develop. When looking at a singular
play (the system at a local level), or across a longer timescale like an entire season
(the system at a more global level), our focus should be on maintaining a healthy
balance between the strengths and weaknesses of the player’s movement skill.
This initiative may be most important when reporting one’s findings of the
performance analysis to the player themselves. After all, who wants to hear a list
consisting of nothing but areas in which they aren’t quite so good at?

However, we also should not lose sight of our responsibilities and
purpose as a coach and SAS around identifying the gaps and weaknesses the
player possesses. It is here that our ideas around the direction of the training,

===== p102 =====
Designing Practice Environments Informed by One’s Analysis

All of the deep diving analyses in the world, no matter how comprehensive and
accurate we can make them in capturing the movement skill and performance
behaviors of a player, will be of very little value unless the information and details
within the analysis can be utilized in informing our design of the practice
environment and the movement problems presented for the player to encounter
there. Through detailed film analysis, one will be able to determine the gaps and
weaknesses of players (as discussed in earlier sections in this Chapter), while also
allowing us to pay close attention to certain issues and challenges that have arisen
within games for them, so we are then able to design practice activities that better
represent the slices and scenarios that resemble these problems. This should help
players to further connect the dots between practice and competition while also
creating buy-in and intentionality within the practice environment. Ultimately, we
feel that this is what the main purpose of any performance analysis should be: to
change how (and what!) the player practices so we can have a greater impact as
to how skillfully the player can eventually solve problems on game day.

Putting it all together

Similar to the earlier worksheet provided in assessing and analyzing a singular
play, we want to provide another worksheet to assist the performance analyst in
their journey into a player’s skill and movement problem-solving story. Again,
this worksheet was adapted and adopted from the S&é/led Movement Analysis course
released by Emergence (Myszka & Yearby, 2022), and it can be used as a template
to summarize one’s thoughts throughout performing their analysis on the film
watched. Once again, this is just a sample only, and coaches, performance
analysts, talent evaluators, and other support staff should adjust it to best align
with their own unique role and perspective.

Longitudinal Player Worksheet
Individual Player: Self-explanatory
Season: This should be self-explanatory for the most part, however, there will be
times that multiple seasons could be investigated for this type of longitudinal
performance analysis

Date completed: Self-explanatory

Film assessed to support analysis: What film did you have access to that
informed your investigation?

# of games: How many games did you look at? Which ones were they?

102
===== p104 =====
Opportunities: This category is oriented around prognosticating as to the areas
(e.g., movement qualities or skill execution nuances) that could represent a
potential chance for individualized growth that a coach or SAS could aim to
address in their work with the player. Typically, the opportunities a performance
analysis will highlight will build upon the weaknesses, but not always. For
example, one may find that a player is a highly creative mover but is only
displaying this trait in certain, or relatively limited, situations. Thus, this may not
be considered a weakness per se in the traditional sense, but could be utilized as

an area of focus (e.g., to educate the player’s intentions) in future training and
practice activities.

Threats: Though each aspect of the movement skill SWOT analysis may require
a great amount of subjectivity and speculation, the shreats portion will often
demand that the individual doing the analysis put themselves out on a limb to an

extent to make claims around what could keep the player from progressing to the
next level.

Training & learning environment Rx ideas to evolve the movement skill-
set from here: Leaning into the strengths within a player’s movement skillset
while revolving around the weaknesses, sports scientists, coaches, and SAS alike
should use the performance analysis as a chance to speculate and hypothesize as
to the practical interventions that could be leveraged to assist in the enhancement
of the player’s skill. These ideas could be global (e.g., X player needs to exist
within more alive movement problems that maintain representativeness) or
specific (e.g., X player needs to cover more receivers with larger frames that can
highpoint balls proficiently), depending on the individual's unique role and their
comfort making recommendations.

Sample Movement Skill SWOT Analysis - Saquon Barkley

To offer a tangible and practical example of what this type of analysis could look
like when fully built out, we have included one that was created by the lead author
of this book (Shawn), and provided to a specific player, Saquon Barkley, at the
end of the 2019 NFL season. It should be noted that depending on the nature of
the relationship between the analyst and the player, as well as the way that the
analysis itself would be used (e.g., internal in an organization, given to a player,
for public use), it may change the exact verbiage and nomenclature utilized
throughout the analysis. For example, this one was written from the
SAS/performance analyst and directed individually to the player in an attempt to
get him thinking differently about the way he was solving movement problems in
situ and his subsequent training methods he could employ for enhancing his skill.
As such, it was assumed that the player himself would be relatively unfamiliar
with thoughts and ideas housed within contemporary skill acquisition so care was
taken to strike a balance in how concepts were articulated within the analysis.

104
===== p105 =====
Though Saquon Barkley did not end up working together directly with any of us
in his skill enhancement journey, he has personally begun to fill in some of the
specific gaps in his skill that were highlighted within the SWOT analysis provided
below. Whether this was purely coincidental or it had any correlation whatsoever
is completely unknown. However, at the time of this writing, Saquon Barkley has
gone on to record a 2,000 yard season with the Philadelphia Eagles in the 2024-
2025 NFL season, en route to winning the Offensive Player of the Year award in
that given year.

Individual Player: Saquon Barkley

Season: 2019-2020 NFL season

Date completed: At the end of the 2019 NFL season (1/1/20)

Film assessed to support analysis: NFL game film accessed through NFL+
(sideline, end zone, and all-22 views)

# of games: 13

Significant influential injuries: Right ankle (week 3 vs. TB) that sidelined him
from mid-way through the 3 game through week 6 vs. NE)

Additional considerations: Saquon Barkley was named the Mover of the Year
in 2018 at Football Beyond the Stats (see:
https:/ /footballbeyondthestats.wordpress.com/2019/01/16/2018-mover-of-
the-year-saquon-barkley/). More performance analysis and findings setting the
tone for this investigation can be found there.

Short summaty regarding Individual’s Form of Life: Saquon Barkley is a
dynamic RB that is a potentially generational mover who thrives off being able to
make opponents miss in a variety of ways. Saquon is a super ball of energy and,
when he solves movement problems on the field, it is easy to see a tremendous
lasting influence from players who have come before him (e.g., Barry Sanders,
Adrian Peterson) that he has obviously modeled his game after and blended into
his own authentic style of movement skill. From afar, he seems to be a
connoisseur of the game, highly respecting the RB position, who aspires to be a

true professional, tirelessly working on the intricacies of his craft to ultimately be
considered one of the best to ever do it.

Strengths:

e Your wide-open movement toolbox is the calling card to your immediate
success as well as in you achieving what you have the potential to be
(transcendent movement skill). Simply put, a player must have an
abundance of movement strategies before they can ever solve the wide

105
===== p106 =====
range of problems which they may face on field...especially at your
position. Very few players ever have access to such a wide range of
positions and movement patterns to execute from. Thus, this platform
will give you a plethora of strategies to select from. And the best part of
it is, if and when you gain the experience of the right fit of how you
should use each ‘tool’ and why, then it will equate to enhanced
movement skill that will stand the test of time no matter what you face
and what occurs over time (think of the diverse style of Barry Sandets).
e When you're feeling it, nothing is off limits for your movement skill and
what will emerge. You have the ability to put yourself in a special zone
where you just trust that you can get out of any position, in any way, at
any time. Don’t lose this rare feeling because you can use this type

of energy to ultimately define and channel your own unique, authentic
movement style.

e Due to your age and your current state of being, your movement skill-
set is in a ripe place for growth and you compensate quickly if exposed
to the requisite conditions for change and positive transfer (there’s a
catch with this though: you could likely just as easily and quickly can learn
sub-optimal nuances of your movement skill execution too if you’re not
careful).

e You obviously have a special gas pedal. This allows you to exploit
random gaps as opportunities for immediate acceleration differently than
your peers. You should aim to let other characteristics of movement
skills build onto this rare quality. For example, it can allow you to be both
mote patient as well as more deceptive in various ways as with it (i.e., the
acceleration and ability to trust yourself when you see a small gap) you
are able to get yourself out of certain binds and challenges. Additionally,
small gaps which are able to be exploited, which open and close quickly,
you can still accept those and trust that you can make it through them.

Weaknesses:

e The holes within your movement skill-set that were present and
prevalent last season (see the Mover of the Year analysis from 2018),
namely in regards to how your perception was being organized (i.e., what
you were picking up in the world versus what was being missed — all
of which would serve to inform you of the problem you were facing)
actually became magnified this season.

o Your visual gaze appears to be anchored too often and too long
on the nearest/immediate defender in front of you as if every
problem were a 1v1 problem

o Because of this, you sometimes miss opportunities to act that
exist across your field of vision, specifically within your
peripheral vision (to your right, most often)

© In most contextual situations, it would be advised that your eyes
should continue to scan to take in information about both

106
===== p107 =====
defenders and teammates in the petiphery as well to pick-up
information that exists beyond/behind as well as around the
nearest defender (if you are able to take steps with this, it will
relate to a whole new, rich and meaningful experience of the
world that you have yet to really see!)

o It seems that you don’t always have an accurate understanding
of the amount of distance between you and the nearest obstacle
(opponent or teammate). Then the subsequent controlling of
the distance between yourself and the nearest obstacle while you
try to move (execute an action coupled to the unfolding
problem) is hampered. You are also sometimes in too much of
a hurry in these situations because you’re rushing to eat up yards,
get yourself out of trouble, or just because you aren’t in adequate
control here.

o Your head/shoulders sometimes become too fixed. However, I
feel that you can and should allow your head to turn to allow the
eyes to take quick glances to gather information your brain and
movement system may need to understand the problem
disposition at-hand.

Because of the above points regarding your perception, there are times
that I believe that your cognitive decision-making (e.g., thoughts going
on in your head, your intentions and aims to act) then becomes ‘frozen’
to a certain degree. In this, you end up slightly a step behind in detecting
the information in the world you need, understanding what the
information means for you, and making the most accurate decision off
of it. Think of it as a form of paralysis by analysis. It’s also why there are
times that immediately after the play is over, you may find yourself
second guessing the decision that you made because you know you
missed an opportunity to make something bigger happen.

At times, it certainly felt as though you were trying too hard to show the
world that you can be a very physical back along with a very elusive one.

o Certainly coaching, tactical strategy, and play-calling dictated
that this would be the case throughout the season (these things
are obviously outside of your control). However, it sometimes
appeated that you were overly eager to lower your
shoulder/head and get the dirty yards between the tackles (even
at times when there were definite opportunities to bounce it to
open space which fits more in your forte).

Opportunities:

Perceptual sensitivity! If exposed to the right movement problems in
training and practice (see below), and you ate given the chance to go
explore them, searching your movement toolbox, you can and will
ultimately exploit those problems and become more connected to them.

o Devote yourself here. Train your perception (especially your

107
===== p108 =====
eyes). Your perception can hold a key to you solving a wider
variety of more complex movement problems!
Your creativity is certainly an opportunity. It just needs to be harnessed
by being tested to be ‘activated’ in the right ways under the right
circumstances (e.g., when to spin, when to hurdle, when to Walter high-
step). For this to occur, your movement system likely needs more
exposure beyond it taking place in actual games.
By continuing to be creative with your movement and by exploring a
wide range of movement execution strategies (i.e. attempting a wide
variety of cutting actions), you will actually make your entire movement
system (and the body) more robust to handle your style of skill. This
could decrease injury likelihood and make you more resilient to taking
certain shots on the field.
Think a little more about what you’re thinking! And by this, I mean, when
seeing yourself on film, where were your thoughts? What were you
intending to do? Were you over-thinking? Maybe trying too hard to act
in a certain way? Or would you say that your brain was just reacting?

Threats:

Coaching! Many across the NFL landscape will try to shape your skills to
be what they want or think they need to be. I would advise that you fight
to stay authentic and individually unique to who you feel you were created
to be. You should be honestly expressing yourself at all times.
The more elite you become, the less representative NFL practice settings
will likely be for you. Meaning, coaches and organizations will continue
to treat you with ‘kid gloves.’ As this happens, your movement skill-set
evolution could become stagnant if you are not careful because the
information present within those problems at practice won’t behave
accordingly to the way you need it to for further enhancement of your
skill. Even as it stands now, the only time that problems likely take you
to where you need them to (where your movement skill set can be
challenged to evolve the way you specifically need) is on Sundays when
you face it in the actual game itself. But, the game is likely too chaotic a
place for the system to get the necessary education and experience.
Closed, sterile learning environments; meaning, training activities which
are not alive and non-changing such as traditional speed, change of
direction, and “agility” drills
o Many of these will likely give you too many false assumptions
that your movement is getting more fluid. However, they are
void of any of the specifying information that is present in real
football problems. Thus, too much exposure in these types of
activities will only make you less sensitive to perceiving the

information that is needed for you to solve problems on the
field!

108
===== p109 =====
Training/ Learning Environment Rx to evolve the movement skill set from

here:

Quite simply, I believe that what is needed is a training and learning environment
which is ALIVE and one that allows you to gain full ownership of your entire

skill set! Meaning:

°

Drills and activities should be representative of that which you will face
during a real game situation. There should be active problem-solving
required from you that looks, acts, feels, and behaves like it will on an
NFL Sunday. The problem should be completely unpredictable so you
have to solve it! This will allow you to search your existing toolbox, and
to understand how the problem relates to your. — most optimal
methods for solving it.
Of course, I am not implying that you should be getting tackled
frequently in training. However, I am suggesting that each on-field
activity that you perform in training should have at least one (if not many
more) defenders in it to be able to become more connected to picking
up and detecting information from opponents. This opponent(s) can and
should be attempting to tag off but it’s important that his movement
behaviors resemble closely enough to how they would if he were trying
to tackle you in space. This will allow you to become sensitive to, and be
able to accurately detect:
o Opponent’s space and time relationship to yourself (how much
time exists between the two of you interacting?)
Opponent’s speed (can he catch me?)
Opponent’s angles (where will he meet me?)
Opponent’s body position (what movement options does he personally
have at the moment?)
Get thrown into the deep waters and go solve any problem.
o Deep waters will equate to facing problems where you’re at a
severe disadvantage within it
o —_ Lots of small-sided situations; 1v2, 1v3, 1v4, 2v3, 2v4, 2v5
o This should also be done facing a wide variety of opponents
(with varying skills and characteristics)
© The use of teammates to help you solve problems is vital and
something that many players often miss
© Specifically, for you, I encourage you to perform lots of tight
space work; do more when you have less green grass to work
with due to more obstacles surrounding you
Repetition to repetition, you should face a different problem (this idea
aligns with a concept mentioned earlier known as repetition without

Designing Practice Environments Informed by One’s Analysis

All of the deep diving analyses in the world, no matter how comprehensive and
accurate we can make them in capturing the movement skill and performance
behaviors of a player, will be of very little value unless the information and details
within the analysis can be utilized in informing our design of the practice
environment and the movement problems presented for the player to encounter
there. Through detailed film analysis, one will be able to determine the gaps and
weaknesses of players (as discussed in earlier sections in this Chapter), while also
allowing us to pay close attention to certain issues and challenges that have arisen
within games for them, so we are then able to design practice activities that better
represent the slices and scenarios that resemble these problems. This should help
players to further connect the dots between practice and competition while also
creating buy-in and intentionality within the practice environment. Ultimately, we
feel that this is what the main purpose of any performance analysis should be: to
change how (and what!) the player practices so we can have a greater impact as
to how skillfully the player can eventually solve problems on game day.

play, we want to provide another worksheet to assist the performance analyst in
their journey into a player’s skill and movement problem-solving story. Again,
this worksheet was adapted and adopted from the S&é/led Movement Analysis course

performance analysis

# Context Shapes Content

**What it is** — The organising claim of the analysis chapter, and Myszka tells it as two failures of his own.

**2008.** A starting NFL player came to him. He ran a full combine-style battery, and found the player had declined badly since entering the league — vertical jump down over five inches, 40-yard dash 0.20 slower. Twelve weeks of work produced large gains: **vertical up over seven inches, broad jump up 14 inches, 40 and pro-agility both improved 0.25 seconds.** The player went to training camp and reported, every day, that "things just feel okay." Preseason and regular season confirmed it. **Every metric moved; nothing on the field did.**

**2012.** Now working as a "Movement Coach," he had shifted to perfecting the movement patterns themselves, filming and grading them toward an ideal. Watching from the Metrodome at the end of that season, he saw that players he worked with were performing **in spite of** the work rather than because of it — compensating and adapting their way through complexity. His line: **"the NFL's best players are simply the world's best compensators."**

The resolution came from a Bruce Lee quote: *"It's like a finger pointing away to the moon. Don't concentrate on the finger or you will miss all that heavenly glory."* He had been studying the finger — the player and their movement — without equal respect for the moon: the problems in the environment, and the relationship between the two.

**Why it works** — In complex adaptive systems, **context shapes content.** A solution cannot be improved in isolation from the problem it is organised against, because the solution only exists in relation to it. Improving the isolated capacity or the isolated pattern changes neither the problem nor the relationship.

**When to apply** — Whenever an intervention produced clean test gains and no observable change on the field. That pattern is not a failure of dose or of effort; it is a category error about what was being trained. Also as a caution against the reductionism the chapter identifies across every department — scouts at the combine, S&C chasing measurables, sports medicine chasing repeatability and isolated positions, position coaches chasing technical detail in unopposed drills.

**When NOT to apply** — Marked **supported**: these are two candid anecdotes from one practitioner, not controlled evidence, and both are retold by the person whose framework they now justify. There is no counterfactual — we do not know how the 2008 player would have performed without the twelve weeks. Do not deploy this as proof that physical preparation does not transfer; deploy it as a warning that test gains are not evidence of transfer, which is the narrower and defensible point ([[principle--far-transfer-is-rare]]).

**Example** — The honest version of the 2008 story for any performance report: "every number improved and we have no evidence anything on the field did." Saying that out loud is what starts the useful conversation.

# Gamespeed Is Not Stopwatch Speed

**What it is** — A reconceptualisation of speed as **gamespeed** (or, following Belichick, **football speed**): the speed a player operates at while solving alive problems, which centres their **knowledge of** the game as a key performance indicator rather than a time over a set distance.

Belichick, 2016: *"The time-speed is always a tricky thing because time-speed isn't football speed... So a player's running a ball or running full speed covering a kick or running the ball and there is people in front of him and people trying to tackle him, it's a little different speed than running a sprint on the stopwatch."*

Jerry Rice is the standing counterexample — reportedly as slow as **4.71** at his pro day, and arguably the most productive receiver ever. Rice: *"You've got to separate yourself from the DB. That's all it is. And I don't really know where the extra speed comes from that makes me do it."* Ronnie Lott on Rice: *"He may be 4.6 on Tuesday and Wednesday, but he's 4.2 on Sundays."*

**Why it works** — The implication is precise: **the game's fastest players are those who can operate at optimal speeds while interacting with alive problems** — not those who register the fastest times outside game contexts. Optimal is not maximal. The same logic extends to jumping and change of direction: jumping high from a pre-planned countermovement is not high-pointing a ball before a defender; cutting quickly at a predetermined location is not making someone miss in the open field.

**When to apply** — Interpreting GPS peak-speed data, combine numbers, or any timed test, and especially when someone infers on-field ability from them. It gives a name to the thing a coach means when they say a player "plays faster than he times," and a mechanism for it rather than a shrug.

**When NOT to apply** — Marked **supported**: the argument rests on quotes and named examples rather than a measure. There is no operational definition of gamespeed offered here and no instrument for it, which means it currently cannot be assessed, only asserted — a real limitation when the alternative at least produces a number. The authors also concede that some players time fast *and* play fast (they name Chris Johnson, Champ Bailey), so the two are not opposed, merely weakly related. And speed testing retains legitimate uses in load monitoring and return-to-play.

**Example** — The book's contrast: players near the top of all-time combine 40 times who never made a mark (Dri Archer, John Ross) against players whose gamespeed was never in doubt. The stopwatch was accurate; it was just measuring something else.

# Screen-Based Perceptual-Cognitive Tests Are Weak Evidence About On-Field Problem-Solving

**What it is** — A direct challenge to the growing use of digital perceptual-cognitive assessments in football scouting and talent identification. **S2 Cognition** is the named example (Clinton, 2025) — a digital evaluation using a specialised laptop and response pad, claiming to measure perceptual capabilities (search efficiency, tracking capacity) and decision-making capabilities (improvisation, timing control).

The authors' position, stated plainly: **empirical evidence on this testing method and its transfer to the field is very limited** (they cite Simons et al., 2016), and they have "serious doubts as to the level of its efficacy, at least if it is being used for anything more than a general measure." They point to Renshaw et al. (2019) for a detailed critique.

**Why it works** — The reasoning follows from everything before it. These tests quantify **reactions to visual stimuli on a screen**, then use them to predict how on-field processes unfold. But the further an assessment gets from what actually happens on the field, the less functional relevance its behaviours have to the context that matters. The action is a tap; the perception is of a screen; the information is not the information that regulates football movement. # How to Watch Film

**What it is** — The practical method for ecologically-informed performance analysis.

**Live analysis is not enough.** The complexity of the problems, and of the solutions organised against them, makes real-time assessment next to impossible if you want an accurate reading. Analysis happens on video.

**Watch widely.** Myszka's practice with a new NFL player is to watch **every single snap the player has taken in the league** (via NFL+ or NFL Rewind), then, depending on age and status, college film — even highlights — and sometimes high school. The rationale: you cannot determine where a player should go without unpacking how their movement skill came to be. Trends across a career are visible through the context-content lens that are invisible in a season.

**Watch each play from as many vantage points as possible** — sideline, endzone, all-22 — and **at various speeds** — full, half, super slow motion. Cross-checking across conditions is what keeps a detail from being an artefact of one angle.

**Two honesty rules the chapter insists on:**

1. **Nonlinearity is real.** A player highly attuned one day can be overwhelmed by similar problems the next, for any number of reasons. Minor changes in the problem can produce dramatic changes in the solution, and vice versa.
2. **Absence of evidence is not evidence.** No two problems are the same and some problems the player has simply never faced. **Do not fret if you finish an analysis without enough to make a proclamation, good or bad.** Saying "I have not seen this player solve that problem" is a legitimate finding — and it is often the most actionable one, because it names an exposure gap ([[case-study--tight-end-punt-coverage-exposure-gap]]).

**Why it works** — Breadth substitutes for the experiment you cannot run. You cannot present a player with a controlled problem set, so you find the range of problems they have already met.

**When to apply** — Any serious individual analysis. The volume prescription is the part most people skip and the part that produces the trend.

**When NOT to apply** — Marked **supported**: this is one practitioner's method, offered without validation, and the authors concede it "can all sound quite daunting and may seem like overkill." Watching every career snap is not feasible for most staff at most levels, and there is no guidance here on what a reduced version preserves. Access also constrains it — what film you can get depends on your role. Treat the *principles* (multiple angles, multiple speeds, breadth over depth, comfort with an inconclusive verdict) as the transferable part.

**Example** — A staff with two hours per player should spend them on twelve plays from three angles rather than one play frame by frame. The trend is the finding; the frame is the illustration.

# Position-by-Position Problem Inventory

**What it is** — The book's starting list of the situations, and their problem-solution dynamics, that a complete analysis of each position should cover. It is offered as a starting point to be adjusted for level and scheme, not a fixed standard. Condensed:

- **QB** — every route on the tree with placement and timing; different receiver types; touch versus velocity; pocket navigation (clean and collapsing); throwing on the run; making plays with his feet.
- **RB** — between the tackles; off tackle; zone versus gap scheme; making someone miss in tight space ("agility in a phone booth"); beating the first defender *while* perceiving the next layer of threat; open field; receiving out of the backfield.
- **WR** — every route against coverage types and against different DB styles (speedsters, physical) and strategies (press, off); strategies to manipulate or deceive at release, in the stem, at the break; catching balls thrown in various ways; skills after the catch; blocking.
- **TE** — blocking in space, in-line, at the second level; route running; catching in traffic, high-pointing, boxing out; after the catch.
- **OL** — step blocks; pass protection against speed and power rushers; blocks on the move (pulling, second level); physicality when the problem calls for it.
- **DE / DL** — tackling in space across situations and opponent styles; pass rush variety; double teams; engagement and release; pursuit in a phone booth and in open space; turnover situations.
- **LB** — tackling at the line, in the open field, in pursuit from various angles; taking on blocks; coverage of RBs and TEs.
- **CB / S** — coverage across contexts and styles; planting, change of direction and turning at the break point; pass break-ups; skills near the line; pursuit and tackling; recovery when beat; creating turnovers; playing in the box; being a field general.
- **Returners** — tracking and receiving under pressure and chaos; deciding to return or fair catch and choosing an initial path; beating the first man while reading the next; open field.
- **Specialists** — pooch punts under imminent pressure; slow or off-target snaps; kicking with defenders closing and a poor hold; botched snaps requiring evasion or a throw; working with the coverage unit.

Alongside the position list, the chapter says to record **location on the field** (red zone, middle of field), **direction of the play**, and **specific conditions** (weather, time of game, surface, home or away).

**Why it works** — It converts "assess the player" into a coverage checklist, which is what makes gaps visible. A problem never sampled is a gap you will not otherwise notice.

**When to apply** — This is the most immediately usable page in the chapter for return to play. Take the athlete's position row, and for each item ask: **has this athlete faced this problem since injury, and how many times?** The answer produces the reintegration plan.

**When NOT to apply** — Marked **supported**: it is an expert-generated list, not a validated taxonomy, and the authors say so — a starting point to adjust for level and scheme. It is also not exhaustive, and some items a player is never asked to do, either because of a genuine skill limitation (worth noting as an opportunity) or because the scheme protects them (not a gap at all). Distinguishing those two requires knowing the scheme.

**Example** — A returning linebacker is cleared on the strength of tackling circuit work. Run the row: tackling at the line, in the open field, in pursuit from various angles, taking on blocks, covering a back, covering a tight end. Most return protocols cover the first item and none of the others.

# A Player's Form of Life

**What it is** — Vaughan et al.'s (2019) term for an individual's ways of being, acting and behaving — the unique personality, essence or style visible when a player moves. It is what the authentic movement behaviour expresses. Bruce Lee, on the Pierre Berton Show in 1971: *"To honestly express oneself… now that, my friend, is very hard to do."*

The practically important claim: **a player's form of life can facilitate — or limit — their perception, selection and actualisation of the affordances present on the field.** It is not decoration around the analysis; it is inside the mechanism.

It is shaped by where they are from, how they grew up, previous sports played, activities they like, and quirky tendencies of personality.

**Why it works** — What you see a player do is a **cumulative product** of a long list of influences from their past, coalescing into this movement solution at this moment. The book's illustrations make the causal path visible:

- **Kyler Murray's** side-arm throws on the run, off one leg — traceable to a lifetime of baseball (he was the ninth overall MLB draft pick in 2018 and the first overall NFL pick in 2019).
- **Justin Jefferson's** flair, and The Griddy, carried from his college days at LSU.
- **Jerry Rice's** sure hands — growing up in Mississippi working alongside his bricklayer father, snagging bricks out of the air in every conceivable way, all day.

**When to apply** — Before prescribing anything. The three questions the chapter offers: **How has the player's upbringing and their unique interests shaped what we see? What movement experiences have influenced the way they see the world? What makes them different from others at their position in these types of problems?**

It also supplies the strongest argument against imposing a technical model: a solution that conflicts with a player's form of life is not merely different, it is fighting the history that produced their perception.

**When NOT to apply** — Marked **supported**: the illustrations are plausible narrative reconstructions, not demonstrated causal links — nobody has shown that brick-catching produced Rice's hands, and the story is exactly the kind that survives because it is satisfying. Treat form of life as a lens that generates hypotheses about a player, not as an explanation you can assert. It can also become an excuse — "that's just who he is" is not analysis, and a genuine gap does not stop being a gap because it is characterful.

**Example** — Two backs both hesitate at the line. One is a converted receiver reading the second level the way he used to read a safety; the other is simply late. The coaching is different, and only the biography distinguishes them.

category: [analysis, film-study, perception, method]

# "What Are They Attuning To, and Adapting Around?"

**What it is** — The single question the chapter puts at the centre of qualitative analysis. Watching a play, the analyst's job is to **tell the movement problem-solving story** for that player — to get inside their movement system and the organisation of their integrated movement solution.

Answering it means working the three levels of [[framework--integrated-movement-solution]] in order:

1. **Perception** — what information is the player detecting? For a back: the number of opponents in a given space, their speed, their posture and kinematics.
2. **Cognition** — how does that detection feed, with circular causality, into what they intend moment by moment and the decisions they make — including **the affordances they reject**?
3. **Action** — how do those feed into the observable movement strategies, and how are those adapted as the problem unfolds?

**Why it works** — Because it forces the analyst past the only level that is directly visible. Actions are what an outside observer can see, so untrained analysis stops there and prescribes action-level fixes. This question makes perception and intention explicit as candidate explanations, which is where a large share of the real causes sit.

The payoff is stated directly: **if you can gain an informed understanding of what a player is attuned to and adapting around, it identifies areas of improvement and the problematic slices of the game they should be immersed in.** Analysis exists to change practice design, not to produce a grade.

**When to apply** — Every play you analyse seriously, and every time a coach's diagnosis is a movement fault. It is also the right question to ask *about a rehabilitating athlete*: what are they now attuning to, and what are they adapting around that they did not have to before — pain, apprehension, a brace, a slower first step?

**When NOT to apply** — Marked **supported**, and the chapter is honest that the answers are **speculations**. You cannot observe perception or intention; you infer them from accepted affordances. Two analysts will tell different stories about the same play and there is no adjudication procedure here. Guard against the confident narrative: the story that explains everything smoothly is the one most likely to be your own construction. Where possible, check it against the player ([[heuristic--semi-structured-player-interviews]]).

**Example** — A safety consistently arrives a half-step late. Action-level answer: more change of direction. This question asks instead what he is attuning to — and if the answer is the quarterback's shoulders rather than the release, no amount of footwork will fix it.

# Key Events and Notational Analysis

**What it is** — The method for turning a landscape of affordances into something you can actually work with, and eventually count.

**Key events** are the moments in a play where analysis should concentrate — chosen because they are where the important informational variables specify the important affordances. Selection is acknowledged as **subjective and individualised**, but it should be grounded in the ecological scope (perception-action coupling) and in what prior research suggests matters: gaps and distances between players, relative speeds and angles, opponent orientation ([[framework--specifying-variables-in-dyadic-problems]]).

A workable definition: a key event is where **a transition in action occurs for both players** — e.g. a back meets a defensive back in the open field and executes a cutting strategy to evade him. Success and failure then have a clear criterion: the solution is functional when the back forces a missed tackle, unsuccessful when the defender makes it.
