===== p181 =====
CHAPTER 7

Skill Acquisition Periodization in Football

Planning across the calendar year, with an emphasis on the development and
enhancement of players’ skill, is an important part of being a football coach.
Coaches are entrusted with ensuring that they can help the player advance their
craft, get the most out of their developed gifts and talents, and put them in the
best positions to excel in the immediate season ahead as well as in the future.
Ultimately, we want and need the players to be performing their best and
executing in their most skillful manner when the season rolls around and games
are on the line (i.e., so they are best able to express their own movement skill
across situations and conditions).

The need for a periodized plan around skill enhancement

For decades, performance coaches, strength and conditioning (S&C) coaches,
and sport-specific coaches have all utilized ideas related to periodization in an
attempt to split training programs up into phases (e.g., microcycle, mesocycle),
each having highly specific goals, with a hope of maximizing development and
performance over time in a strategic’ way in reap long-term rewards (ie.,
macrocycle). In fact, it is not far-fetched to say that a considerable amount of
energy and thought has gone into theorizing and researching the various ways of
organizing these developmental plans in the most effective ways, leading to the
emergence of very different approaches (e.g., undulating periodization, linear
periodization, block periodization) towards the manipulation of training and
programming variables in line with that specific approach.

In recent years, some experts have begun to offer a way forward for
periodization oriented around skill acquisition, in a similar manner to more
physically oriented training, considering the evolution of movement skill and
placing its enhancement at the heart of the entire training process and calendar
year. Namely, Farrow and Robertson (2017) put forth a framework embracing
the acronym SPORT, centering the approach around relevant principles (ie.,
specificity, progression, overload, reversibility, and tedium) usually focused on
more traditionally, but now with a skill acquisition spin. Later, Otte and colleagues
(2019) took aim at their own attempt at this concept, proposing the ‘Periodization
for Skill Training’ framework to try to offer more proven insights as to how a
specialist coach or a skill acquisition specialist (SAS) can support sport coaches
in the development and enhancement of skills relevant to the athlete’s
individualized needs and stage of learning to positively influence training transfer
for competitive sport performance through an ecological lens.

Our chapter provided here is written by using anecdotal evidence and
the experience of the lead author (Shawn) and his personal work with individual,

181
===== p182 =====
professional National Football Players, from 2008 to present. This is obviously a
unique context, and all coaches should put the following content through this
respective filter. However, this approach has been tweaked and adjusted over the
years while Shawn’s own understanding evolved to be more ecologically oriented
on the adaptation of skill. We respect the fact that this entire situation could differ
quite significantly from a coach’s own in the team sector at the organizational
level. Thus, readers are encouraged to use it as an opportunity to absorb, discard,
and add to what they are already doing in the planning and periodizing of their
own annual approach. That said though, we do feel as though the content here
could offer some useful food for thought that coaching practitioners can modify
and apply across levels and timescales of learning. Depending on the hat you wear
and the role you find yourself within (e.g., position coach, S&C coach), the timing
of the phases will likely need to be adjusted accordingly to fit your own contextual
situation.

What does our annual approach look like?

A couple of quick notes here before we go further: in a sport as physically
demanding, grueling, and risky as football, it probably doesn’t make sense to plan
out too many training variables, in too great of detail, too far out in advance.
Meaning, we should expect that each day’s training and practice activities will
likely have to change considerably based on certain individual constraints that are
relatively dynamic (i.e. fluctuations in player state like their readiness, emotions,
soreness) as well as learning trends of each individual’s movement system. As we
have elaborated upon earlier, the human movement system, and the learning
process as a whole, is nonlinear. Additionally, this is a 30,000 foot global view of
how things look used for illustrative purposes to highlight performance and
learning trends from over the last 16 plus years of locking arms with National
Football League (NFL) players. Every situation is unique though and this means
it doesn’t always fit cleanly within the model discussed below. The annual training
approach and its details, on either a micro (on the day) or macro level (across the
year), will always be a fluid, dynamic, individualized, and complex process that
has more gray than it does black and white. Just like with the athletes’ skill,
adaptability is the only constant.

Phase 1: Post-season (End of the season until approximately two to six
weeks after the last game)

Main Objectives:
e Rest and recover—get the entire system back to ‘neutral’
© ‘Get a life and keep one’s mind off football
e Physically get right: surgeries (if needed) and any required rehabilitation,
extended regeneration, and active recovery

For players who are professional NFL veterans, this period usually lasts anywhere

182
===== p183 =====
from two to six weeks. As a rule, the older and more experienced a player is, the
more time they should be encouraged to stay away from thinking about football,
training for football, and being around all that playing football at the highest-level
demands. An additional elephant in the room here is that when it comes to
professionals, this is also the time that players should do any requisite soul-
searching regarding their desires to continue playing. This is something we should
nudge every player to do at the end of every competitive season regardless of
one’s beliefs as to how long they think the player wants to play or the goals and
aspirations that they once set out to achieve. Obviously, playing professional
football is too difficult of an endeavor to do unless your entire heart and soul are
all-in on it. Thus, it’s important to ensure that a player’s intentions are still in the
appropriate space heading into that next calendar year.

No matter the player’s status, this period is the perfect time to hit the
reset button and to attempt to recharge from the previous grueling season. Most
players go on vacation(s) with their family in this period to start the NFL off-
season. However, if given too much autonomy, some players—especially the
younger ones—could allow this period to drag on too long, indulging in a little
too much of what they really were not allowed to during the course of the
previous four to five months (e.g., alcohol consumption, inconsistent sleep
patterns).

Various factors can drastically change the length of time spent here in
this post-season phase. For instance, the wear and tear of that previous NFL
season makes the duration of this phase very fluid depending on the individual
player. For example, some individuals were depth players (e.g., back-ups, practice
squad) and didn’t see much playing time so it may be appropriate that this phase
is shorter and these players can (and should!) get back to work sooner (as they
likely will be fighting for a job in that following year). Other players, such as NFL
starters, may need to take the entire six weeks before they really get back to
intense training because their minds and bodies (and maybe their spirits too) are
likely pretty beat up.

There are a few general recommendations to give players regarding their
behavior, though:

e The player should not forget that they are still a brand even if the season
is complete (it’s never really over!).

e Be more relaxed about nutritional habits (a few buffets or the occasional
drink(s) never hurt anyone), but don’t let things get too out of hand. The
player should be honest about one’s behaviors as they go along (or have
someone close to them help to keep them accountable). With very few
exceptions, players should never fluctuate more than approximately
five(ish) pounds from their previous season playing weight.

e Find some balance! Now is the time to catch-up on things that the player
could not prioritize at other times of the year—taking the kids to school
every day, going to lunch with their significant other, and hanging out
playing video games with the boys.

183
===== p184 =====
Somewhere throughout this post-season period, players should be encouraged to
begin participating in activities where they can get moving again in very general
fashions. For some players, that could be an entirely different sport like tennis,
basketball (almost every NFL skill player secretly believes they can hoop), or golf
(the older the player gets, the more likely golf becomes the activity of choice). For
some others, this could take shape in the form of active recovery and regeneration
modalities that they believe have some performance efficacy, as well, such as
Yoga or Pilates. Finally, for other players, this bucket could be filled through the
incorporation of more general and/or natural movement patterns that they know
we will be starting our Early off-season with in the coming weeks.

Adjusting this to apply in your setting:

The recommendations here likely still apply quite closely to the college
level but with one major exception in that the duration of the phase itself will
likely be shorter (e., approximately two to three weeks maximum though any
holiday breaks could affect this in some way). At the high school or
developmental level, the football player may be moving into the participation of
another sport (if they play others) so the recommendations may only have limited
application.

Phase 2: Early offseason (lasting four to six weeks; early/mid-February
until mid/late March)

Main Objectives:
¢ Enhance coordination (1st sub-phase) and control (2°4 sub-phase)
e Increase upon effectivities and begin to address determined rate limiters

e Begin to open degrees of freedom across the system (perceptual,
cognitive, and action)

It happens like clockwork, the day after the Super Bowl, things seem to start anew
for all! Without fail, every year on Super Bowl weekend, text messages and phone
calls start pouring in from players who are starting to seriously think about
football again and where their craft should head in the coming year. Personally,
we need to try to place tremendous trust in the players themselves and leave it to
them to determine when they are ready to start that off-season training phase
(though they may need to get ‘nudged’ in certain ways). Of course, if you are
employed with a team, this type of laxity likely won’t work to the same degree.

When a player gets started in this phase, we should attempt to ‘slow cook’
things. For the first two to three weeks (the first sub-phase of the early offseason),
the player will only be doing formalized training on three days per week on
average. And in the second block of two to three weeks (the second sub-phase of
the early offseason), we will usually have the player bump up to four times per
week.

In the first sub-phase, we just want to get the player back to moving
fluidly and with some semblance of freedom again. Here, we incorporate a large

184
===== p185 =====
dosage of more general and ‘natural’ movement activities. Meaning, these are
movements that must be coordinated and controlled to perform better as a
human being first and foremost instead of being entirely focused on being an
NFL football player and the specific problems you must solve there. In this phase,
we could include activities from individuals like Erwan LeCorre (Natural
Movement), Ido Portal (Movement Culture), Rafe Kelley (Evolve Move Play),
and Moshe Feldenkrais (The Feldenkrais Method).

Even though the time a player spends moving in this phase may be of a
more general nature, we still believe that all movement should be an expression
of the highly integrated problem-solving process of perception, cognition, and
action. Meaning, we still present alive movement problems for the athlete to solve
at this time of the year; it’s just that these problematic activities will actually lack
specificity and representativeness. During this phase of the early offseason, we
are simply trying to allow the player to open degrees of freedom and coordinate
their perceptions, cognitions, and actions in various fashions. The activities we
require players to perform within here should give them the opportunity to add
to the abundance of their movement toolbox (i.e. degeneracy) that potentially
could (or might not) contribute later on in the further refinement of their
contextual movement skill execution that is more specific to the problems they
may face on Sundays.

As we get into the second sub-phase of the early offseason, we will now
get the player back into a cleat on the field to start solving some movement
problems that are more indicative of those that may be found in the competitive
arena (albeit considerably less complex). Meaning, we will ‘progress’ from the
more general movement skills found in the last phase, to begin coordinating and
controlling movement skill in more specific fashions now such as acceleration,
change of direction, multi-directional cutting, and high-speed sprinting. To do
this in line with our overarching beliefs articulated in previous chapters, we want
to have as many of these movement activities be performed in highly
contextualized fashions (i.e., with opponents present, through problem-oriented
scenarios). However, this is the only time of the year where we may have to have
a small amount of decontextualized work with more isolated, repetitive execution
for those movement skills (i.e. such as linear sprinting without an opponent). We
will admit, this application violates our ecologically-oriented beliefs and
preferences to a great degree but there are simply less players present in our
groups at this time of the year (or more inconsistency in their schedules anyway).
That said, if we worked in a team setting (as you might), this would not be the
way it would be done as a high number of athletes would likely always be present
(and it is a blessing, not a curse!).

In these early phases, we are looking for the players to gradually become
more connected to all the information in the world around them and begin to get
back to coordinating and controlling their actions in tighter responses to
movement problems in that dynamic context (the task and environment). This
early in the year though, we need to scale the information present and greatly
decrease the problem’s complexity and intensity (in comparison to how the

185
===== p186 =====
problem-solution dynamics may unfold later in the annual plan). For example,
the movement activities that the players face will usually contain less individuals
(both opponents and teammates) so the player himself will have the opportunity
to actively search the information space and become more attuned to specifying
information that is present in these less overwhelming movement problems.
Here, we will do a great deal of 1v1 activities, of lower complexity, while
potentially progressing to 1v2 and 2v2 activities (at maximum in this phase). At
all times during any unfolding movement problems containing a smaller number
of players, close attention should be paid to the interactions between each of the
players to ensure they unfold similarly, or at least close enough to, how they con/d
during competition (ie., the full 11v11 game). This can be a challenging endeavor;
however, it is of critical importance to establish that the emerging movement
solutions—the movement problem-solving process (MPSP), consisting of the
relationships formed between the perceptions, cognitions, and actions—could
still be functional in the competitive arena.

Of course, from repetition to repetition, we will always aim for
“repetition without repetition” (i.e., where no two problems or solutions will be
the same), but this will be done across a smaller bandwidth of situations or
conditions. However, as Bernstein told us long ago, dexterity in movement skill
is about being able to solve any emergent movement problem, in any situation
and in any condition (Bernstein, 1996). Thus, everything within our programming
(and the problem-setting and activity design) must start heading in that direction
as time passes and players get closer to facing more dynamic and unpredictable
problems to solve with higher numbers of players on the field.

Adjusting this to apply in your setting:

The main difference in the recommendations offered here for this phase,
if applied to the college, high school, or developmental level, may be in the
amount of focus placed on the enhancement of general motor abilities that will
be inherently less important for higher level players (i.e., NFL players). Though
that change could potentially apply across the whole annual plan itself for these
levels (as the increase of general motor abilities will lead to greater positive
transfer to competition for these lower levels), this phase will likely set the tone
for the entire year to come.

Phase 3: Late offseason (lasting approximately four weeks; mid/late
March until the third week in April)

Main Objectives:
e Tightly couple perception, cognition, and action to the specifying
information present in more representative tasks
e Explore the landscape of affordances present throughout contextual
slices of the game

¢ Get more comfortable being wore uncomfortable

# Skill Acquisition Periodization: The Seven-Phase Annual Model

**What it is** — Myszka's annual plan for skill, built from working with individual NFL players from 2008 onward. It sits alongside two published attempts at the same problem: Farrow and Robertson's (2017) **SPORT** framework (specificity, progression, overload, reversibility, tedium, given a skill-acquisition spin) and Otte et al.'s (2019) **Periodization for Skill Training**.

**Phase 1 — Post-season** (end of season to ~2–6 weeks after the last game). Rest and recover, get the system back to neutral; **"get a life and keep one's mind off football"**; surgeries, rehabilitation, regeneration. Duration is individual: depth players should return sooner (they are fighting for a job), starters may need the full six weeks. Veterans should be encouraged to stay away longest.

**Phase 2 — Early offseason** (4–6 weeks, ~February to mid/late March). Enhance **coordination** (first sub-phase), then **control** (second). Increase effectivities and address identified rate limiters. **Begin to open degrees of freedom** across perception, cognition and action. Sub-phase one is general, "natural" movement — the traditions named are Erwan Le Corre, Ido Portal, Rafe Kelley, Feldenkrais — still presented as **alive problems**, just lacking specificity. Sub-phase two returns to cleats and to acceleration, change of direction, cutting and high-speed sprinting, mostly contextualised, at 1v1 progressing to 1v2 and 2v2.

**Phase 3 — Late offseason** (~4 weeks, mid/late March to third week of April). **Tightly couple** perception, cognition and action to specifying information in more representative tasks. Explore the landscape of affordances across contextual slices. **"Get more comfortable being more uncomfortable."**

**Phase 4 — OTAs / minicamp** (9–10 weeks, late April to mid-June). Begin to **test the movement system** across more contextual situations and conditions. **Educate attention and intention.** Possibly target specific strength qualities for the individual and the position.

**Phase 5 — Summer** (4–5 weeks before training camp). **Pursue dexterity.** Attain the highest levels of attunement, intentionality and adaptability, with perception, cognition and action tightly coupled to specifying information in the game's relevant problems.

**Phase 6 — Training camp and preseason** (late July to the final preseason game). **Initial tests of dexterity.** Explore and solidify optimal performance routines — warm-up format, away-game habits — and settle on a regeneration and recovery schedule.

**Phase 7 — Season** (September to season's end). Health and highest performance. **The most complete test of dexterity**, with minor adjustments to the problem-solving process throughout. Authentic and honest expression of movement skill.

**Why it works** — The arc is coherent: **open degrees of freedom → couple them to real information → test the coupling under progressively harder conditions.** See [[principle--annual-arc-open-couple-test]].

**When to apply** — As a template for sequencing skill work, and — with dates ignored — as a **return-to-play sequence**, which is the structure it most resembles. An athlete returning mid-season is being asked to traverse phases 1 to 6 in compressed time, and this model at least names what each stage is for.

**When NOT to apply** — Marked **untested**, and the authors are unusually candid about why. It is written from **anecdotal evidence and one practitioner's experience** with individual professional athletes — "a unique context" that "could differ quite significantly from a coach's own in the team sector." Readers are told to **absorb, discard, and add**. Phases 4–7 are also dictated by the NFL calendar and do not transfer as dates. Take the sequence, not the schedule.

**Example** — Its most honest moment: in Phase 2 sub-phase two, Myszka admits to a small amount of **decontextualised, isolated sprinting** because too few players are around at that time of year — "this application violates our ecologically-oriented beliefs and preferences to a great degree." A framework that names where its own principles bend is more usable than one that does not.

# Open, Couple, Test: The Arc of a Skill Year

**What it is** — The three-movement logic that gives [[framework--skill-acquisition-periodization-seven-phases]] its shape, and the part that transfers when the calendar does not.

**Open.** Early offseason work is deliberately **general and non-specific** — natural movement, unfamiliar patterns, activities that "must be coordinated and controlled to perform better as a human being first and foremost." The purpose is to **open degrees of freedom** across perception, cognition and action, and to **add to the abundance of the movement toolbox** — degeneracy that "potentially could (or might not)" contribute later. Note the honesty of that hedge: the value is optionality, not a guaranteed return. Crucially, even here problems stay **alive**; they simply lack specificity and representativeness.

**Couple.** The middle phases tie those opened degrees of freedom to **specifying information in progressively more representative tasks**, exploring the landscape of affordances across contextual slices. Complexity and information are scaled up gradually — 1v1, then 1v2 and 2v2, with fewer players early so the athlete can **actively search the information space** in a problem that is not yet overwhelming.

**Test.** The late phases are explicitly framed as **tests of dexterity** — initial tests in camp, the most complete test in the season itself.

**Why it works** — It puts abundance before adaptability in time, matching the theoretical claim that [[principle--degeneracy-precedes-dexterity]]. You cannot couple degrees of freedom you have not opened, and you cannot test a coupling you have not built.

The quality control that runs throughout: in every small-numbers activity, **watch the interactions closely to ensure they unfold similarly enough to how they could in the full 11v11 game.** The authors call this challenging and critical — it is the same warning as [[principle--complexity-and-information-scaling]], and it is what stops "open" from becoming "irrelevant."

**When to apply** — Any long-horizon skill plan, and especially a **return-to-play arc**, which is this sequence compressed. The mapping is direct: early rehab opens degrees of freedom the injury closed; mid-rehab recouples them to real information; late-stage is testing under progressively representative conditions. Naming which of the three a given week is in prevents the common error of testing before coupling.

**When NOT to apply** — Marked **untested**: the arc is a rationale, not a demonstrated sequence, and no evidence is offered that this ordering beats another. There is a real open question the book does not resolve — whether general "opening" work transfers at all, which is precisely the far-transfer problem the same authors are sceptical about elsewhere ([[principle--far-transfer-is-rare]]). They hedge it ("could, or might not") rather than resolving it. Treat the general phase as plausible and unproven.

**Example** — A returning athlete doing unfamiliar general movement is not marking time before the real work; they are in the *open* phase. But if that phase never gives way to coupling against live information, it has become the isolated training the rest of the book argues against.

# Do Not Plan Too Many Variables, In Too Much Detail, Too Far Ahead

**What it is** — The caveat the authors attach to their own annual plan, and arguably the most useful line in the chapter. **In a sport as physically demanding, grueling and risky as football, it probably does not make sense to plan out too many training variables, in too great a detail, too far in advance.**

Expect each day's training and practice activities to **change considerably** based on:

- **dynamic individual constraints** — fluctuations in player state: readiness, emotions, soreness;
- **the learning trends of each individual's movement system.**

Because the human movement system and the learning process are **nonlinear**. Their summary: the annual approach, micro or macro, "will always be a fluid, dynamic, individualized, and complex process that has more gray than it does black and white." And the line worth stealing — **"Just like with the athletes' skill, adaptability is the only constant."**

**Why it works** — It is the planning-level version of **soft assembly** ([[principle--soft-assembly-and-learner-centred-coaching]]). A session that is fully scripted cannot respond to what unfolds; a year that is fully scripted cannot respond to what a player becomes. Nonlinearity is not an excuse for vagueness — a player may be highly attuned one day and overwhelmed the next ([[heuristic--how-to-watch-film]]) — it is a reason to hold the plan loosely enough to notice.

The authors also model this in how they present their own model: a **30,000-foot global view, for illustrative purposes**, that "doesn't always fit cleanly."

**When to apply** — Whenever you are asked for a detailed twelve-month plan, and whenever you are tempted to write one. The defensible version specifies **objectives per phase** and leaves the daily content to be assembled against what is actually observed. That is what the seven-phase model does, and why it is only objectives.

It applies with double force to a return-to-play timeline. A dated week-by-week plan for a healing athlete is a forecast dressed as a protocol, and everyone treats the dates as promises.

**When NOT to apply** — Marked **supported**: sound reasoning, not evidence, and it can be misused. "Adaptability is the only constant" is a poor answer to a director asking what the plan is, and under-planning has real costs — facility bookings, staffing, and the coordination a team requires cannot be assembled on the day. There is also a genuine tension the book does not resolve: **progressive overload and phase structure require some commitment in advance.** The honest position is to plan the *objectives* and the *constraints of the calendar* firmly, and the *content* loosely.

**Example** — Write the phase objectives for the year and the session content for the week. If the September sessions are already written in March, the plan has stopped being a plan and become a prediction.

===== p195 =====
CHAPTER 8

Practical Changes to One’s Learning Environment

We would like to think that, throughout the previous pages of the book, we have
convinced you of the efficacy of, and the need for, major (maybe wholesale!)
changes and modifications to the ways that you practice to increase the likelihood
of transfer to competition, effectively facilitating the enhancement of movement
skills for the players you work with. However, we know that tradition certainly
runs rampant across the sport of football. Thus, we are being realistic here: we
realize that many of you out there won’t be ready to go ‘all-in’ on adopting many
of the ecologically-oriented changes we’ve suggested up to this point.

We have included this chapter for those of you who would like to wade
into the waters more slowly. It will offer a compromise of sorts, where coaches
and practitioners can begin to adopt more minor practical changes to one’s
training, practice, and learning environment that align more closely to the
ecological approach posited throughout this book. These changes have been
battle tested by the authors with athletes across levels, including the National
Football League (NFL) and other professional players.

Coupling information-movement every chance you can

This one probably won’t come as any shock or surprise! Even though
information-movement coupling has been a focal point of the book, and much
of our unfolding discussions leading to this point have aimed to get you to think
differently about concepts related to it, we still felt it was important to encourage
every reader to start here. Frankly, we strongly encourage you to prioritize setting
more representative, alive movement problems for your players to interact with
so players can search the rich and abundant information present in the
environment, not just during our representative task design but also from the
movement preparation scheme/warm-up protocol on through the very end of
their session. In this way, it requires athletes to be in a true problem-solving state
at all times, ready to perceive, cognize, and act in relation to what’s unfolding in
the world around them. Of course, we believe that we can never require players
to perceive and act in coupled fashions too much; meaning, the more exposure and
experience that players have in solving alive movement problems through
interacting with relevant information present there and thus, perceiving and
ultimately accepting the affordances specified by the information outside of
oneself, the more likely it is that they will be comfortable functionally solving
problems of all kinds on game day.

What could this look like?
Relevant information-movement coupling can be developed by players, so long

195
===== p196 =====
as the principle of representative learning design (RLD) is respected. Using this
ptinciple, coaches can attempt to manipulate constraints in devising problems
that expose players to varying degrees of complexity to stretch their optimal grip
over a landscape of the affordances that could potentially be present within the
unfolding player-environment relationship. And, if you’re ready for this, luckily
we have devoted whole chapters in this book to doing so!

However, if you are not quite as willing to go ‘all-in’ just yet with RLD, the biggest
modification we can suggest is to allow your player’s movement
preparation/warm-up periods to present some unpredictable, living, and
breathing movement problems more frequently. For example, let’s say that a
player is performing a simple shuffle with any number of movement techniques
(e.g., plants, transition steps, re-acceleration strategies) taking place to initiate the
action as well as sequence successively in carrying movement solutions out to
completion. You can modify this so the shuffle (and other common movement
patterns like it too) would be performed with another individual in front of them
in their path, or potentially while moving through traffic, so the player has to
concern themselves with these other moving bodies and couple their movement
to information in an adaptable way.

What could you see emerge?

The players should become much more attuned! And, they should be able to be
tuned in much more frequently. Players will no longer be able to use their
movement preparation time to ‘just warm-up,’ but instead they would need to be
ready to pick-up and detect information that exists outside of them and their
movement at all times. Thus, the coordination and control of their movement
actions in time and space should improve dramatically as should their overall
sense of the unfolding relationship with immediate opponents (or teammates and
boundaries too), all through the emergence of a wider variety of creative
movement actions. The added positive byproduct of this is that when players find
potentially find themselves embedded in more representative tasks that follow,
they will also likely be much more attuned and capable of coupling their
movements tightly to specifying information sources, and ready to organize a

# Movement Ownership Speed

**What it is** — Deliberately operating at a **maximum controllable speed** rather than a maximum speed. The glossary definition: intentionally operating at a velocity deemed maximally controllable, instead of always practising or playing at the highest speeds attainable, so the player can better coordinate and control the most functional solution to a peculiar problem.

The authors know it sounds wrong for football, and argue it anyway. Of course there are moments demanding maximal burst, deceleration or change of direction. But **a player always running around like their hair is on fire — a way of being that football coaches celebrate and reward — can miss perceptual connection to the very information specifying the affordances for the biggest plays.**

The parallel claim about decisions: **the most functional decision is not always the fastest one.** It is the one that sufficiently, accurately and usefully resolves the problem in front of the player.

**Why it works** — Always-on-the-gas produces **a lack of exploratory perceptual search** — no new affordances get perceived, selected or acted on. Slowing to a controllable speed restores the search. And the reported second-order effect is the interesting one: players who practise near movement-ownership speeds **gain confidence and comfort in the face of chaos**, which then shows up as *higher* football speed in games, because the integrated solution fits better ([[principle--gamespeed-vs-stopwatch-speed]]).

**When to apply** — This is the most directly transferable idea in the book for return to play, and it inverts a familiar conversation. Practising below top speed is usually framed as a limitation to be tolerated during rehab. Here it is a **legitimate skill-development mode with its own rationale** — the returning athlete restricted to 70% is not merely marking time, they are in the condition that best supports perceptual search and recalibration ([[principle--affordances-point-both-ways]]).

Coaches should **allow and actively encourage** slower speeds in practice, not merely permit them.

**When NOT to apply** — Marked **supported**: the mechanism is well-argued, the downstream claim ("this may trickle into the game") is explicitly anecdotal, and no evidence is offered that practising slower improves game speed. There is also a real risk of over-application: a player who *only* ever operates at controllable speed never calibrates to the speeds the game demands, and some information is only available at full velocity. Movement ownership is a mode to include, not the only mode.

**Example** — Telling a returning athlete "go at the speed where you still own it" gives them a target that is theirs to judge, rather than a percentage that means nothing to their body — and it happens to be the speed at which they will learn the most.

# Wading In: Modifications for People Who Won't Go All-In

**What it is** — The chapter written for realism. The authors accept that **tradition runs rampant in football** and that many readers **"won't be ready to go all-in."** So they offer a compromise: minor practical changes that move a learning environment toward the ecological approach without requiring anyone to rebuild practice. All of them are described as **battle tested by the authors with athletes across levels, including NFL and other professional players.**

The modifications, each presented with the same three questions — *what could this look like?* and *what could you see emerge?*:

- **Couple information and movement every chance you can** — the umbrella. If you are not ready for full representative learning design, **the biggest single modification is to make the warm-up present unpredictable, living problems** ([[heuristic--alive-warm-up]]). A shuffle becomes a shuffle with someone in your path, or through traffic.
- **Movement ownership** — encourage slower, controllable speeds ([[principle--movement-ownership-speed]]).
- **More movement navigation through the chaos of traffic** ([[heuristic--daily-traffic-navigation]]).
- **Looking to and through** ([[principle--look-to-and-through]]).
- **Changing equipment** ([[heuristic--change-the-equipment]]).
- **Contextual sprint work** ([[heuristic--contextual-sprint-work]]).
- **Bridging the gap** ([[principle--bridging-the-gap]]).
- **Deception and disguise** ([[principle--deception-and-disguise]]).
- **Being able to do the right thing from challenging positions** ([[heuristic--right-thing-from-wrong-positions]]).

**Why it works** — Every item leaves the existing practice structure intact. No period is removed, no install time is lost, no scheme changes. That matters more than the theory when the constraint is political rather than technical — and in most programmes it is.

The umbrella claim is the one that ties them together: **you can never require players to perceive and act in coupled fashions too much.** More exposure to alive problems, from movement prep through the end of the session, means more comfort solving problems on game day.

**When to apply** — When you have limited authority over practice. Pick one item, run it for a block, and let the change be visible before proposing another. The warm-up is the recommended first move, and it is the one nobody objects to.

**When NOT to apply** — Marked **supported**: "battle tested" is the authors' own phrase for their own practice, not evidence. Every "what could you see emerge?" section describes expected outcomes, not measured ones, and they are uniformly positive — read them as hypotheses about what to look for, not as results to expect. There is also a strategic risk the chapter does not name: adopting the modifications without the reasoning produces a coach who adds traffic to a warm-up and believes they have adopted the approach.

**Example** — The order matters. Lead with movement prep and traffic navigation — cheap, visible, uncontroversial. Save equipment changes and deception for after the staff has seen something work.

# Look To and Through

**What it is** — A correction for the most common perceptual fault the authors observe: **players get overly fixated on the most immediate opponent or obstacle in front of them.** The instruction is to look **to** the immediate opponent **and through** to what lies deeper beyond.

Gibson's line is the warrant: **"Perceiving gets wider and finer and longer and richer and fuller as the observer explores the environment."** The authors' shorthand — **wider, longer, and deeper.**

**Why it works** — Because the problem has layers, and the affordance a player should accept often depends on information behind the nearest threat ([[principle--nested-affordances]]). A player reading only the closest defender is solving the local problem in isolation from the global one.

The design consequence is the important half: **you cannot cue this into existence.** The problems presented must *require* looking deeper for the movement to be functionally regulated. Their example: a linebacker moving from behind a defensive lineman, and a safety moving behind the linebacker, against a back navigating a tunnel of traffic between the hashes — roughly 1v3 to 3v3. The layers must be physically present, or "look through" is empty advice.

**When to apply** — Whenever film shows a player consistently beaten by the second defender rather than the first — a tell that attention stopped at the first. Also directly relevant to the [[case-study--saquon-barkley-swot]], whose central weakness was gaze **"anchored too often and too long on the nearest/immediate defender in front of you as if every problem were a 1v1 problem."** That is this fault, named in a real analysis.

For return to play this is a subtle risk. An athlete rebuilt entirely on 1v1 work has been trained, for months, to attend to exactly one opponent — and then returns to a game with layers.

**When NOT to apply** — Marked **supported**: observed and reasoned, not measured, and the predicted outcomes ("you should notice…") are expectations. There is also a real tension with early-stage work: 1v1 activities are the recommended low-complexity staple ([[principle--low-complexity-activities-as-movement-vitamins]]), and they are precisely the format that cannot teach this. Both are right; the resolution is that layered problems must appear in the diet, not that 1v1 work is wrong.

**Example** — The cheapest fix is a third body. A 1v1 with one extra defender standing ten yards behind changes what the ball carrier must perceive, without changing the load, the space, or the intensity.

# Navigate Traffic Every Day

**What it is** — The authors' claim that **traffic navigation is one of the main on-field key performance indicators for American football players at the highest level, regardless of position** — gaps opening and closing, threats from opponents *and* from friendly fire, moving in relation to an opponent while looking through and past traffic. Their recommendation follows: present activities of this kind **very frequently — daily, such as during individual periods — because the return on invested time is almost certainly high.**

**Three grades of traffic**, to be rotated across days:

1. **Stationary traffic** — bodies spread out and not moving, passive participants in the workspace. The player picks and chooses a path, exploring and creating fluidly.
2. **Dynamically moving traffic** — same workspace size, but the traffic now moves in various directions and speeds. The player must pick up others' movement while finding gaps to dart and slice around.
3. **Goal-directed traffic** — blocking teammates and oncoming defenders acting in a tackling-fit fashion, which gives the highest perception-action fidelity.

Chapter 6 supplies the designs: *open field traffic navigation in a tunnel*, *dynamically changing gaps*, *traffic navigation with teammate/opponent layers*.

**Why it works** — The graded structure is the useful part, and it is a clean **complexity ladder that keeps the information intact at every rung** ([[principle--task-simplification-not-decomposition]]). Even stationary traffic presents real spatial information to be read; it simply does not change.

The predicted outcome is a **360-degree perceptual radar** — players comfortable with bodies in front, beside and behind, with fewer close calls, and visibly searching the workspace before moving.

# Change the Equipment

**What it is** — One of the cheapest constraint manipulations available. Players are **particular and often ritualistic** about their helmet and visor, pads, gloves and shoes — they find what they like and then struggle to perform with a different version, or without it. But **the equipment a player wears materially affects how they connect to key information sources** and how they interact with them: shoe-surface interaction is the obvious case; pads change centre of mass and restrict differently by size and type.

Since the goal is adaptability, **do not let players become overly reliant on equipment of any sort.** The modification: **require different equipment on a given day** — a different shoe, a receiver going glove-less when accustomed to gloves.

**Why it works** — Players will **balk, and say they are uncomfortable — which the authors note is precisely the objective.** Discomfort here means the perceptual-motor mapping is being forced to recalibrate, which is exactly [[framework--direct-learning-attention-intention-calibration]]'s third lever. The whole movement problem-solving process gets organised differently as the athlete adapts, which is another instance of *learning to learn to move*.

**When to apply** — Any time you want variability without changing the activity, the space, the numbers, or the time. It is a task constraint hiding inside kit that is already on the shelf.

It also has a specific return-to-play use worth naming. An athlete returning in a **brace, a different shoe, extra taping, or a new pad** is already facing an equipment-changed problem — and it is usually treated as a nuisance rather than as a perceptual change requiring recalibration. Introducing the brace *before* the return, in low-stakes work, means the recalibration happens somewhere other than a game.

**When NOT to apply** — Marked **supported**: reasoned and reported, with no evidence offered. Real limits exist. Some equipment is **protective and prescribed**, and swapping it is not a coaching decision — a mandated brace, a specific helmet fit, or footwear chosen for a healing foot is not a constraint to play with. Kit changes can also raise injury risk directly: unfamiliar cleats on an unfamiliar surface is a genuine hazard, not just a perceptual challenge. And the effect is limited by rules and by what the equipment staff will allow.

**Example** — A receiver who has never caught a ball without gloves has one fewer solution available on the wet day when the gloves stop working. One glove-less session a month is not a training philosophy; it is insurance.

# Contextual Sprint Work: Invite the Sprint, Don't Prescribe It

**What it is** — The authors' position on programmed speed work: **the majority of sprint work should take the form of contextually-driven movement problems** and the solutions that emerge from them. Since coaches are problem-setters who manipulate constraints to channel behaviour — including accelerating over a given distance — **they typically do not have players run sprints for the sake of it.** Instead they design so that sprinting appears as **an affordance** the player accepts within a contextual activity.

The specific recommendation: **place great emphasis on having opposing players chase from behind**, which changes the nature of the problem-solution dynamics.

**Why it works** — A sprint run for its own sake trains the action with the information removed ([[framework--three-types-of-task-decomposition]]). A sprint that occurs because a defender is closing is the same physical output coupled to the thing that regulates it in a game — which is the difference between near and far transfer ([[principle--far-transfer-is-rare]]) and the practical face of [[principle--gamespeed-vs-stopwatch-speed]].

**When to apply** — When designing speed exposure for a field-sport athlete who has other on-field work available, and especially when a chaser costs nothing to add.

**When NOT to apply** — Marked **untested**, and this is the entry where the framework most clearly collides with a well-evidenced neighbouring discipline, so the caution should be stated plainly rather than smoothed over.

**Maximum-velocity sprinting has an independent, well-supported evidence base** in physical preparation — for hamstring injury prevention, for exposing tissue to high eccentric demand, and for developing top speed itself. That literature is not addressed here, and nothing in this chapter provides a reason to abandon it. A contextual problem does **not** reliably produce true maximal-velocity exposure: a player reading a defender will rarely reach the speeds a prescribed fly-in sprint guarantees, and the dose is uncontrolled and unmeasurable.

The authors' own annual plan concedes the point in practice — Phase 2 includes decontextualised linear sprinting, which they acknowledge "violates our ecologically-oriented beliefs" ([[framework--skill-acquisition-periodization-seven-phases]]).

The defensible synthesis: **keep prescribed max-velocity work for the physical adaptations only it delivers, and make the rest of the speed exposure contextual.** Treating this heuristic as a reason to remove sprint training would be a genuine, and foreseeable, harm.

**Example** — A chaser starting five yards behind converts an empty acceleration rep into a problem, at no cost. It does not convert it into a maximum-velocity exposure, and it should not be counted as one.

# Bridging the Gap

**What it is** — An idea borrowed from martial arts (the authors cite Shannon Lee's *Be Water, My Friend*). In combat sports and in most sport research, **the gap** is the space between opponent and self — interpersonal distance, as studied by Pedro Passos and colleagues.

The authors extend it: the gap is **the space between one's emerging integrated movement solution and the disposition of the unfolding problem** — the **informational interface point between the problem and the solver.** Bridging it means closely coupling the solution to the opportunities the opponent presents.

**Why it works** — It gives a single name to the thing all the perceptual work is aimed at, and it converts an abstraction into something a player can be asked to attend to.

**Four things to allow players to do**, if they are to work on it deliberately:

- **(a) Slow down** — operate at movement ownership or sparring speeds, so they can connect to what is truly unfolding *within* the gap ([[principle--movement-ownership-speed]]).
- **(b) Actively explore and search** for different ways of perceptually connecting to the information present.
- **(c) Use movement strategies that disrupt the timing and rhythm** of immediate opponents.
- **(d) Attempt feints and fakes** to draw out behavioural actions from the opponent ([[principle--deception-and-disguise]]).

The prerequisite the authors state: to be attuned to the gap and to related variables — relative velocity, opponent posture and kinematics — a player **must also be capable of executing a wide range of movement strategies.** Perception and abundance are not separable here ([[principle--degeneracy-precedes-dexterity]]).

**When to apply** — As the organising concept for 1v1 work of any kind, and as language athletes tend to take to. The authors report players "resonate with this concept rather well," particularly for educating attention and intention toward what is most specifying in a given situation.

**When NOT to apply** — Marked **supported**, and honestly it is a **reframe rather than a finding** — the extension from interpersonal distance to "the informational interface between problem and solution" is conceptual, and the reported athlete reception is anecdotal. Interpersonal distance itself is well studied (Passos and colleagues), and the caution from [[framework--specifying-variables-in-dyadic-problems]] still applies: **distance alone is usually not sufficient** to coordinate a functional solution. Do not let "the gap" collapse back into "the distance."

**Example** — Point (a) is the one that changes practice. An athlete cannot read what is happening in the gap at full speed, so the instruction to slow down is not a concession — it is the precondition for the perceptual work.

# Deception and Disguise

**What it is** — The observation that in sports outside American football, **creativity and innovation often appear when athletes explore feints and faking actions for intentional, purposeful deception.** In mixed martial arts, skilled performers feint or fake an action **to draw out a behavioural response from the opponent**, then act on the new opportunity — immediately, or later in the contest.

The authors argue the most sophisticated NFL movers already do this across positions, and that **all players should explore it more in practice.**

**Why it works** — It is [[principle--affordances-are-opportunities-for-action]] run in reverse. Normally a player perceives the affordances the environment offers. Deception is the player **manufacturing** an affordance by causing the opponent to move — which follows directly from Gibson's **"behaviour affords behaviour."** It also pairs with [[principle--bridging-the-gap]]: feinting is item (d) in that list, and the authors report that players who feint effectively also exploit the gap well.

**When to apply** — Easiest to introduce in clean 1v1 situations: receiver against defensive back in a route concept, back against linebacker in the open field, defensive end against an offensive lineman in a pass rush. Then extend to layered problems — quarterbacks in particular already have many opportunities to disguise intent.

The barrier is cultural and the authors name it: **many traditionally taught techniques discourage deceptive actions on the grounds that they waste time or energy**, so players "may initially need constant reminding" that this intention is now permitted. That is a permission problem more than a skill problem.

**When NOT to apply** — Marked **untested**: this is an argument from analogy with combat sports plus observation of elite players, with no evidence that training deception improves outcomes and no method offered for developing it beyond "encourage exploration." The traditional objection is also not simply wrong — a feint genuinely does cost time, and against a defender who does not bite it can cost the rep. When deception is worth its cost is exactly the question this entry does not answer.

There is also a real caution for a returning athlete: feints and fakes involve **deceleration, direction change and asymmetric loading** that a healing tissue may not tolerate, and the encouragement to "explore more" should not arrive before the tissue can pay for it.

**Example** — Adding "see if you can get him to commit first" to a 1v1 changes the intention without changing the activity — and the intention is what was missing.

# Doing the Right Thing From the Wrong Positions

**What it is** — The authors take a phrase heard constantly at coaching conferences — *"being able to do the right thing from the wrong positions"* — and point out that the same presenters then coach athletes to adhere to idealised patterns under a technical model. Their question: **"How can we enable players to do these right things from the wrong positions if we never allow or require them to be in these so-called wrong positions?"**

The answer is **differential learning** (Schöllhorn et al., 2012): require athletes to start from compromising, poor, or simply unfamiliar positions and find ways to do things from there.

**The worked example.** Accelerate from a position foreign to the athlete — an extremely unbalanced stance, low and wide base of support, **leaning opposite the direction they intend to go.** Start every repetition of a set from a position like that, **changing it slightly each rep** — width of base, height of centre of gravity, nature of the stance. Then encourage the player to find **as many ways as possible** to accelerate from each: a transition step, an open step, a crossover step. Repetition without repetition ([[principle--repetition-without-repetition]]).

**Why it works** — Football guarantees bad positions. If they never appear in practice, the only place an athlete searches for solutions from them is in a game, at full speed, with consequences. Exposing them deliberately lets the movement system **search for and discover the affordances still present** in a compromised position.

**When to apply** — Late-stage return to play has an obvious use, and the authors' framing is the useful one: this is not about tolerating bad positions, it is about **having options from them.**

**When NOT to apply** — Marked **supported**, and the two cautions the authors themselves attach are the most important lines in the entry, so keep them attached:

1. **They are not advocating positions that carry high risk of something bad happening, or tasks inherently dangerous by design.** Unfamiliar is the target; hazardous is not.
2. **Never require a player to execute from a position they feel overly apprehensive about** — for example significant fear or physical discomfort from a previous injury. Some uncertainty from unfamiliarity is expected and fine; **apprehension is a stop signal.**

That second caution is precisely calibrated for rehabilitation, and it is the one most likely to be skipped by someone who reads only the headline. An athlete's apprehension about a position is information about their calibration ([[principle--affordances-point-both-ways]]), not resistance to be coached through. Note also that differential learning as cited here is a real but contested literature, and no evidence is offered for this specific application.

**Example** — Asking a returning athlete to accelerate from a deliberately awkward stance is legitimate. Asking them to accelerate from the position they were injured in, because "they need to face it," is not what this says.

**Why it works** — Football guarantees bad positions. If they never appear in practice, the only place an athlete searches for solutions from them is in a game, at full speed, with consequences. Exposing them deliberately lets the movement system **search for and discover the affordances still present** in a compromised position.

**When to apply** — Late-stage return to play has an obvious use, and the authors' framing is the useful one: this is not about tolerating bad positions, it is about **having options from them.**

**When NOT to apply** — Marked **supported**, and the two cautions the authors themselves attach are the most important lines in the entry, so keep them attached:

1. **They are not advocating positions that carry high risk of something bad happening, or tasks inherently dangerous by design.** Unfamiliar is the target; hazardous is not.
2. **Never require a player to execute from a position they feel overly apprehensive about** — for example significant fear or physical discomfort from a previous injury. Some uncertainty from unfamiliarity is expected and fine; **apprehension is a stop signal.**

That second caution is precisely calibrated for rehabilitation, and it is the one most likely to be skipped by someone who reads only the headline. An athlete's apprehension about a position is information about their calibration ([[principle--affordances-point-both-ways]]), not resistance to be coached through. Note also that differential learning as cited here is a real but contested literature, and no evidence is offered for this specific application.

**Example** — Asking a returning athlete to accelerate from a deliberately awkward stance is legitimate. Asking them to accelerate from the position they were injured in, because "they need to face it," is not what this says.

CHAPTER 9

Skill Acquisition in Youth Football

This chapter will focus on special considerations for coaching youth football
players. What is the best way to make football practice easier for someone first
learning to play American Football? How about for a younger player that is
physically small in stature or completely new to the game? When should we add
complexity and variability to the practice conditions? How, as a coach, do we
balance the expectations of performance and development? What is the best way
to deal with the expectations of other interested parties (e.g., team managers,
parents). In addition to answering these questions, in this chapter, we will explore
how the ideas discussed earlier in the book can be adapted for coaching flag
football, an increasingly popular sport (particularly for young athletes).

Reducing Task Complexity for a New Learner

Remember back to the very first time you stepped on the field of a football
practice. For most kids this is a very overwhelming experience. Everyone else on
the field seems to know where to be and when to be there. They simply know
where to go and how to move. They know the “proper” way to run, throw, pass
and tackle. You seem to be just in the way all the time! There is so much going
on and it is all happening so fast. It’s just too much. To learn the skills necessary
to succeed in football, we need to make things easier and less complex for a new
learner. No one is denying that!

As discussed in detail in Chapter 1, the traditional approach to addressing
these challenges has typically been using task decomposition in practice. That is,
pulling the “fundamental skills” out of the game so that they can be trained in
isolation. Here, we see young quarterbacks (QB) throwing balls through tires so
they can work on the mechanics of throwing separate from the problem of
perceiving the movement behaviors of the receiver and the opponents on
defense. We have running backs (RB) and wide receivers (WR) run through cones
or agility ladders so they can work on “footwork” without having to avoid being
tackled. As was also discussed in that earlier chapter, there are several limitations
with this “fundamentals’”’-based approach. The most basic issue is that when you
pull a skill out of the game you essentially end up having to train it twice. For
example, for a QB, we first need to train them how to throw (eg., the ideal
technique) then you must train them where and when to throw. That is, after players
have learned how to execute throwing actions to get the ball to different spots on
the field (by practicing a decomposed version of that skill), they will still need to
learn how to pick up relevant information to know when it's appropriate to use
each of these actions. When do I throw the ball on a line? When do I put some
air under it? How much should I lead the receiver? Does it depend on the

209
===== p210 =====
defensive coverage? How can I tell when a receiver is “open’’? The reader can
likely think of several examples of QBs with great throwing technique (i.e., who
have mastered the fundamentals of throwing) that are very poor at making
decisions (i.e., using perceptual information to decide where to throw and when
to throw it). When we separate perception from action through task
decomposition, we do not allow these links between information and movement
to develop—we are essentially just pushing that aside hoping that the individual
player can figure it out later on in their development when they are ready.

content.content:
Task complexity from an ecological dynamics perspective

From an ecological approach, there are three main challenges that a new learner
faces:

1. Educating attention to specifying information

This issue involves learning to use information sources that will allow a task to
be performed successfully across a wide range of conditions. This requires a
player becoming attuned to specifying information sources in the performance
environment. For example, think about the task of receiving a football. To catch
the ball successfully, the player needs to use visual information to close their
hands around the ball at the right time. Closing the hands too soon will result in
the ball bouncing off and falling to the ground while closing too late will mean
the ball is not secured properly to control it. Now, consider two possible options.
Player 1 uses the distance of the ball to time the hand closure—for example, they
start to close their hands when the ball is one foot away from the hands. While
this strategy could be effective if the ball was always thrown at that speed, it would
fail once the speed of the ball begins to vary—as every thrown ball will. In this
example, distance is a non-specfying variable for timing the reception. It does not tell
the player when they need to time the closure of their hands because that will
depend on the ball’s speed. Player 2 uses the perceptual variable /au (illustrated in
Figure 9.1) to control the timing of their hands. This will lead to successful
catches for passes of any speed. Thus, tau is a specifying variable for timing—it is
specific to a particular event (i.e., a tau value of 0.75 always indicates that the ball
will reach the hand in 0.75 seconds, no matter what its speed or distance).

approaches the receiver at a speed of 70 ft/s. It's time to contact (i.e., when it will arrive
at the hands) is specified by the optical variable tau. See text for details.

Research has shown that when first learning a new skill like catching a
football, it is very common for performers to use non-specifying information
(Fajen & Devaney, 2006; Jacobs et al., 2011; Smith et al., 2001). This is, in a large
part, encouraged by the traditional way we practice—using low variability,
blocked conditions (e.g., the ball always being thrown at the same speed and same
location when practicing catching) allows for success when using a non-specifying
information in that it makes it useful for that particular task. But this information
will not be useful when conditions become more variable, like within most game
situations. A key part of becoming proficient at a skill like catching a football (and
others across the sport) is the player moving away from using less useful, non-
specifying information to more useful specifying information (e.g., from using

distance to using tau). In ecological dynamics, we call this process the education of
attention (Jacobs & Michaels, 2007).

2. Solving the degrees of freedom problem

As first identified in the seminal work of Bernstein (see Bernstein, 1996), another
challenge for a new learner is solving the degrees of freedom problem. This can be
stated as: among the almost infinite possible ways (e.g., combinations of joint
angles, forces, speeds) a task can be performed, how does the performer choose
the way to execute? Consider the task of learning to throw a football. As
illustrated in Figure 9.2, you can do this in almost an infinite number of different
ways. You could just rotate your arm around your shoulder joint (A). Or you
could use some shoulder rotation plus some added lower arm rotation around
your elbow joint (B). Or you could combine rotation around the shoulder,
rotation around the elbow joint, and rotation of your hand around the wrist joint,

211
===== p212 =====
with a host of different choices for the amounts of each (C). These different
rotational movements that can be used are what Bernstein called degrees of
freedom—you are free to choose the values that they have. This becomes an even
bigger problem when we add in the possible movements of the lower body
involved in throwing a football. Of course, the complex nature of this degrees of
freedom problem ramps up even further when we think of how perceptual and
cognitive degrees of freedom need to be reciprocally coordinated alongside
movement actions when a player attempts to solve an alive movement problem
on the field, as discussed extensively in Chapter 2.

A B C

Rate Limiters

A rate limiter is an individual constraint that limits the rate at which a performer
acquires and develops a movement skill through exploration of the solution space
(Seifert et al., 2014; Moy et al., 2024). An individual constraint is a physical or
psychological characteristic that influences the movement solution available to a
performer. In football, common rate limiters for young, developing players
include the fear of being hit and the fear of jamming one’s fingers when catching
the ball. These fears can limit the extent to which a young player will explore the
solution space when learning these skills. Now that we have identified the main
challenges associated with being a youth football player, let’s look at some of the
ways that they can be addressed.

Task Simplification: The Ecological Way to Make the Task Easier

In the ecological approach, we are still faced with the same problem introduced
at the start of this chapter—playing football is far too complex for a new learner
to start playing the full game right away. We still need some alternatives to make
it easier for them. But, in the ecological approach, we are not going to achieve
this by breaking things apart. Instead of using task decomposition, we are going
to use task simplification, which we originally discussed in Chapter 5. We want to
make it easier while keeping it whole but making it simpler. Stated another way:
we should make the task easier while still meeting the key criteria of
representativeness we discussed in Chapter 5. Let’s look at some examples of how
this can be achieved using the constraints-led approach (CLA).

1. Shifting action boundaries by scaling equipment

One of the main challenges that can occur for a new learner (especially one who
is younger and less physically developed) is that the movement solution needed
to produce a basic level of proficiency is beyond their action boundaries. For
example, a regulation-size football may be difficult to throw accurately for a

213
===== p214 =====
young QB who has lesser hand size and grip strength or for a WR or RB to catch
successfully when they have smaller hands. One of the most effective ways to
combat this is through equipment scaling (i.e., reducing the size of a football as is
now commonly done in many youth leagues). Figure 9.3. shows how the
recommended football size is typically scaled (i.e., increase in size proportionally)
with age.

2. Removing rate limiters by changing the rules

As mentioned, one of the things that can greatly limit a youth players’ exploration
of the solution space is the fear of contact. This can be understood in terms of
Gibson’s affordance theory (extensively discussed in Chapter 3). As outlined by
Gibson (2015, p. 119), “the affordances of the environment are what it offers the
animal, what it provides or furnishes, either for good or ill.” Just as affordances
can invite opportunities for action with positive outcomes (e.g., running through
a gap for a touchdown), they can also present opportunities to avoid actions that
will produce a negative outcome (e.g., failure, pain or injury). To deal with this
rate limiter, a coach may need to modify the constraints to reduce the strength of
the negative attractor. Here, beyond playing a non-tackle version of the game
(e.g., flag football or two-hand touch), the coach can also reduce the size of the
field and/or the number of players so that there is less momentum involved in
the hits. Additionally, the coach could also have the players already begin an
activity in initial starting positions where the information is scaled and intensity is

214
===== p215 =====
lessened such as the various examples offered in the Blocking and Tackhing Skill
section of Chapter 6.

Another example of a rate limiter that can affect football performance is
fear of failure. In a recent study by Moy et al. (2024), the authors proposed that
the rule which allows only one serve in volleyball (in contrast, to tennis, where
two serves are allowed) may be such a rate limiter. The rules that permit only a
single serve may be actively discouraging the performer from exploring their
action capabilities and taking risks to search for alternative movement solutions

# Specifying vs Non-Specifying Information

**What it is** — The sharpest and most precise idea in the book, and the mechanism behind several of its other arguments.

Take catching a football. The player must close their hands at the right moment — too early and the ball bounces off, too late and it is not secured. Two players solve it differently:

- **Player 1 uses distance.** They begin closing their hands when the ball is a foot away. This works while the ball is always thrown at the same speed, and **fails the moment speed varies** — which it always does. Distance is a **non-specifying variable** for timing: it does not tell you when the ball will arrive, because arrival depends on speed too.
- **Player 2 uses tau.** Tau is the optical variable specifying time-to-contact. **A tau value of 0.75 always means the ball reaches the hand in 0.75 seconds, whatever its speed or distance.** It is a **specifying variable**, and it works for passes of any speed.

**Why it works — and the claim that should change practice.** Research shows that new learners **commonly latch onto non-specifying information** (Fajen & Devaney, 2006; Jacobs et al., 2011; Smith et al., 2001). And the authors name the culprit: **this is in large part encouraged by the traditional way we practise.** Low-variability, blocked conditions — the ball always thrown at the same speed to the same place — **make the non-specifying variable work**, and so teach the player to rely on it.

That is a stronger indictment than "blocked practice is less effective." It says blocked practice can actively install a strategy that will fail in the game. Becoming proficient means **moving from less useful, non-specifying information to more useful, specifying information** — the **education of attention** (Jacobs & Michaels, 2007), given a concrete, testable meaning here.

**When to apply** — Whenever an athlete performs well in a controlled drill and poorly in the game. That is the signature of a non-specifying variable that the drill made viable. The diagnostic question: **what could they be using here that would stop working if I varied the speed?**

For return to play this reframes the fixed-condition rep. A ball machine at constant speed does not merely fail to build the coupling; it can teach the wrong one.

**When NOT to apply** — Tau is well established for interceptive timing, but do not over-generalise: for most football problems **nobody has identified which variable is specifying** ([[framework--specifying-variables-in-dyadic-problems]] lists candidates, from other sports, explicitly as hypotheses). So you can usually apply the *logic* — vary the conditions so a non-specifying variable cannot survive — without being able to name the right variable. That is fine, and it is the practical form of the idea.

**Example** — The test is one rep. Throw the next ball harder. If the catch falls apart, the player was timing on distance, and no amount of hand-position coaching will fix it.

# Rate Limiters: Fear Constrains the Solution Space

**What it is** — A **rate limiter** is an individual constraint that limits **the rate at which a performer acquires and develops a skill through exploration of the solution space** (Seifert et al., 2014; Moy et al., 2024). An individual constraint is any physical or psychological characteristic influencing the movement solutions available.

In football, the rate limiters the authors name for young players are **fear of being hit** and **fear of jamming one's fingers when catching.** Both **limit how far the player will explore.**

**Why it works — the affordance account of fear.** Gibson: "the affordances of the environment are what it offers the animal, what it provides or furnishes, **either for good or ill.**" Affordances invite actions with positive outcomes *and* present **opportunities to avoid actions that produce a negative outcome** — failure, pain, injury. Fear is therefore not a psychological add-on sitting outside the perception-action system; it is a **negative attractor inside the landscape of affordances**. The coaching move follows: **modify constraints to reduce the strength of the negative attractor.**

**Ways to reduce it:**
- Play a **non-tackle version** — flag football, two-hand touch.
- **Reduce field size and/or player numbers**, so there is less momentum in the hits.
- **Start activities from positions where information is scaled and intensity is lessened** (see the blocking and tackling activities in Chapter 6).
- **Smaller, softer ball** — directly addresses the jammed-finger fear ([[heuristic--equipment-scaling]]).
- **Change the rules** to remove fear of failure. Moy et al. (2024) is the cited evidence: 40 high-school students played a regulation single-serve volleyball game and a modified **two-serve** game, counterbalanced. In the two-serve game, first serves were **significantly faster, less accurate, and included significantly more jump serves** — the rule change produced exploration of the solution space. The football analogue the authors suggest: **add an extra down**, so young players explore passing, running and receiving without the pressure of a turnover on downs.

**When to apply** — This is the most important entry in the book for return to play, and it deserves to be stated in those terms. **An athlete returning from injury has an acquired rate limiter.** Their apprehension is not a compliance problem or a mindset problem — it is a negative attractor that will measurably shrink how much of the solution space they explore, and therefore how much they relearn. Waiting for confidence to return does nothing. **Reducing the strength of the attractor** — fewer bodies, less space, less momentum, softer equipment, a rule that removes the cost of failure — is a design action you can take this week.

**When NOT to apply** — Marked **supported**: the concept is well-founded and the Moy evidence is real, but it is **volleyball, 40 high-school students, a single acute session** — not football, not injured athletes, and not a learning outcome. The football extrapolations (extra down) are the authors' suggestions, untested. And fear after injury is not identical to a novice's fear of contact: sometimes apprehension is accurate information about tissue that is not ready, and the right response is to respect it, not engineer it away ([[heuristic--right-thing-from-wrong-positions]] draws exactly this line).

**Example** — "He's tentative" is a description. "His fear of re-injury is a rate limiter, so we reduce the momentum in the problem until he explores again" is a plan.
